No shame in that, though the purists among us will insist a quiet weekend is merely a duck biding its time. 📋 Week in Summary One duck from two matches is a modest return by Linton standards, but early season is early season — the real hunting rarely begins before the wickets have dried out and the confidence has grown. 4 ducks

Two fixtures, four ducks, and the archives creaking under the weight of history — a proper vintage weekend for the exclusive zero club. 🏏 Saturday 26th — 1st XI v A.Trembeths Robert Wood battled to the crease at seven, dug in gamely, and was eventually undone c P. Rye b C. Rye — the Rye family clearly operating a closed shop that afternoon. It's his 5th duck of the season and 7th of an illustrious career, good enough for 31st on the all-time list of 726. Robert is also a paid-up member of the Debutante Duck club from a duck-on-debut long since consigned to history — not this one, but the badge stands. He now joins the Victorian great A Startup on exactly 7 career ducks — a man who played 1868–1963... sorry, 1868–1882, took Duck of the Year honours three separate times, and once strung five ducks in a row. Alan Wilkes opened and departed first ball region c John Abnett b Terry Whittaker — his 3rd of the season and 11th of a career now sitting a lofty 15th of 726 all time. Alan is a double Only Two Quacks honouree, paired separately with Bob Arnold and John Ames — both of whom, delightfully, ducked in this very same innings, reuniting all three on the honours board in the flesh. Bob Arnold, at three, fell b Tony Tipples for his 5th of the season, moving to a barely believable 31 career ducks — 2nd of all 726 in club history, second only to the legendary Tim Thirkell-tier company. Bob owns Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) and shares Only Two Quacks with Alan Wilkes, his batting partner in ignominy this very afternoon. His own executioner, Tony Tipples, has a habit of this fixture — he too made a duck against Linton Park CC on this day back in 1953. John Ames, two down, fell b Alan Wilkes for his 3rd of the season and 20th career — 4th of 726 all time, and a Homebody Duck top-tenner to boot. He shares Quacking Together honours with none other than Roy Clarke, who currently tops this season's leaderboard — proof that good company follows a man even into the zero column. 📊 Week in Summary Four ducks from two matches, three of them arriving in a single Sunday innings — a rare cluster that would have made fine viewing for the purists. 5 ducks
Week 20 · 12 Sep 1959 – 13 Sep 1959
Two fixtures at Linton Park this weekend, and the zero club welcomed five new entries to its ledger, all from the 1st XI. A tidy reminder that late September shows no mercy to the specialist blocker. 🏏 Saturday 12th September — v Bowaters CC (home) S Lusher, in at seven, was stumped by John Woollett off Bernard Collins to open his LPCC duck account. It is duck number one of the season and number one of a career just five innings old, placing him 296th of 726 in the all-time table. He arrives alongside - Dampier, whose sole Linton duck came in 1952 and came, rather ominously, with a Debutante Duck, a One and Done, and a presumptive Retirement Duck all in the same afternoon. Lusher, we trust, has a rather longer stay in mind. 🏏 Sunday 13th September — v Tunbridge Wells CC (home) A grim afternoon in the middle order and beyond, as four Linton batsmen queued up for the walk back without troubling the scorers. John Ames was stumped by Don Glanvill off John Piper for his 2nd duck of the season and 19th of a long and distinguished career, good enough for 4th on the all-time list. A fully paid-up member of Ducks in a Row and the Homebody Duck top ten, Ames also extends his Quacking Together partnership with Roy Clarke, who joined him in the pavilion in this very innings. Robert Wood fell lbw to Mike Willard, his 4th of the season and 6th of a career that began, fittingly, with a Debutante Duck some years back. He draws level on career ducks with D Sells (1943-44), who reached six in just 14 innings and wore the Duck of the Year crown in 1943. Roy Clarke, caught and bowled by Mike Willard, brought up his 9th duck of the season, a tally already leading the current Duck Hunting Season table by some distance, and his 16th career duck, 6th on the all-time roll of dishonour. 1959 is officially Clarke's year: he holds the Duck of the Year 1959 title, and duly proved it by quacking together with John Ames for the second time in the innings. He is level on career ducks with the mighty Stan Wratten (1943-59, 172 innings), and joins a small dynasty of Clarkes, sibling H Clarke having chipped in two career ducks of his own. John Abnett completed the rout, bowled by Mike Willard for his 4th duck of the season and 14th of his career, good for 11th all-time. A charter member of Ducks in a Row, Abnett is now level with Frank Sutton (1925-49), twice Duck of the Year in the 1940s, who took 62 innings to reach the total Abnett has managed in 36. 📋 Week in Brief Five ducks from two matches, four of them arriving in a single Tunbridge Wells innings. Mike Willard alone accounted for three, a spell the Linton dressing room will not remember fondly. Bowaters, by contrast, got away with contributing just the one. 0️⃣ Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Roy Clarke — 26 inns, 9 ducks (34.62%) 2. Tony Snell — 7 inns, 5 ducks (71.43%) 3. Slim pickings from Linton Park this week — two fixtures, and the zero club managed to smuggle just the one specimen through customs. But what a specimen, ladies and gentlemen. 🏏 Saturday 18th July — 1st XI v Rumwood CC (home) In at five and out for nought, Bob Arnold departed courtesy of a sharp take from D- Land off the bowling of G- Wood — c D- Land b G- Wood in the book, and another line added to what is fast becoming Linton's most distinguished ledger of failure. This is Bob's 3rd duck of the season and, remarkably, his 29th for the club — good enough to hold him at 2nd of 722 in the all-time standings. Only one man in the club's entire history has collected more noughts than Bob Arnold, which is either a tremendous achievement or a tremendous cause for concern, depending which side of the boundary rope you're stood on. Bob arrives at this milestone already a fixture of the honours board, a veteran of the exclusive Ducks in a Row club for four consecutive quacks in his time, and a founding member of two of the more sociable categories going — Only Two Quacks alongside Alan Wilkes, and Quacking Together with John Thirkell. Company, it seems, is never far away when Bob walks back. And in a pleasing quirk of the calendar — on this day in 1954, five years almost to the very date, John --'s Taylor (1949–1958) also strolled back for nought, albeit against John Larkings rather than Rumwood. The art of not scoring, it appears, has its own anniversaries. 📊 Week in Summary One duck from two matches is a quiet week by Linton's usual generous standards — but when the sole entrant is the club's number two all-time collector adding to an already gilded résumé, quality has rather made up for quantity. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Roy Clarke — 5 ducks in 19 innings (26.32%) 2. Brian Mills — 4 ducks in 7 innings (57.14%) 3. Michael Fagg — 3 ducks in 5 innings (60.00%) 4. William Buck — 3 ducks in 9 innings (33.33%) 5. Bob Arnold — 3 ducks in 10 innings (30.00%) A tight scrap for top spot, with Michael Fagg's frankly alarming 60% duck rate keeping the whole table honest. 🦆 Roll on the next fixture — the ducks are surely only resting, not retired. Bring your bat, and bring your sense of humour. 5 ducks

A fine early return for a man who is, naturally, a paid-up member of the Debutante Duck club, having opened his LPCC account the very same way some years back. This is the same operator who claimed Duck of the Year in 1958, once reeled off four ducks in a row, and famously went that entire season without troubling the scorers — a genuine grandmaster of the art of not scoring, and another name drawn to this date alongside Stan Wratten. Sunday 12 July — Tovil (Away) - John Ames, stumped off R- Brigden, notched his 1st duck of the season and 18th of his career from 133 innings — a mighty 4th of 722 all-time. Few names carry more silverware in this club: Ducks in a Row, a place in the Homebody Duck top 10, and three separate Quacking Together partnerships across the decades, Stan Wratten among them. - William Buck, bowled by Brian Fridd, took his 3rd duck of the season and 14th of his career from 204 innings — 10th all-time, and already honoured on the Quacking Together board alongside John Thirkell. He now sits level on 14 with Frank Sutton, who played 1925 to 1949 across 62 innings and twice took the Duck of the Year crown. Week in Summary Five ducks from three matches, every one of them landing in the Tovil double-header — the third fixture kept an entirely clean sheet. A week where the club's elder statesmen did the heavy lifting, with two top-ten all-time names, John Ames and Tony Snell, both walking back for nought within a day of one another. 🦆 Duck News — 27–28 June 1959

4 ducks
Week 9 · 27 Jun 1959 – 28 Jun 1959
Two fixtures on the books this week, and while Saturday passed off refreshingly duck-free, Sunday's trip to face A.Trembeths turned into a proper cull — four Linton batsmen shuffled back for nought in the very same innings. The art of not scoring, on full display. 1st XI — away to A.Trembeths The rot set in at four, where Michael Fagg was run out for nought — his 2nd duck of the season and 2nd of a young career already standing at 5 innings, good enough for 127th on the all-time list. Fagg is also a paid-up member of the "Retirement Duck" honours board from a past farewell innings, so he keeps distinguished, if scoreless, company there. Four down the order at number 8, John Abnett fell caught for his 2nd duck of the campaign and his 12th for the club in just 34 innings — enough to hold a lofty 13th all-time. Abnett also carries the "Ducks in a Row" honour, having once reeled off four consecutive noughts, a feat of dogged consistency this correspondent can only admire from a safe distance. One place later, Roy Clarke went the same way, caught for his 5th duck of the season — extending his lead at the top of this year's Duck of the Year table — and his 12th in a 59-innings career, level with Linton greats Bert Buckoke (1928–1953) and Jack Fryer (1881–1906), and now rank 14 all-time. Clarke's name already sits on the "Quacking Together" board alongside John Ames, and with sibling H Clarke also holding a career duck of his own, the noughts evidently run in the family. To complete the set, Richard Harris departed at 10 for his 1st duck of the season, his 29th in a 155-innings career — remarkably good enough for 2nd on the all-time list, trailing only the mighty John Thirkell. One wonders how long Harris can hold off the summit. Fittingly, this very day in 1882 also saw a Linton batsman fall for nought against Marden CC, Kent — J Sedgwick, whose brief 1881–82 career yielded 4 ducks and the 1881 Duck of the Year crown. All four of Sunday's fallen share that same anniversary. Something in the Kent air, perhaps. Week in Summary Four ducks, two matches, and every single one arriving in one innings — the top order survived, the middle and lower order did not. A collapse of genuinely ceremonial proportions. 🦆 Duck Report — Weekend of 13–14 June 1959

3 ducks
Week 7 · 13 Jun 1959 – 14 Jun 1959
A quiet weekend for the fowl-hunters by recent standards, but the exclusive zero club never fully closes its doors, and the 1st XI kept the lights on across both days out. Saturday 13th — 1st XI away at Headcorn CC Number eleven Peter Hughes wasted no time announcing himself, bowled by W- Ward for nought on his very first senior appearance. A debut duck is one of cricket's purest ironies and Peter is now formally inducted onto the Debutante Duck board, taking up residence at 277th of 718 in the all-time ledger. Splendidly, on this exact date back in 1943 Herbert Sunley was doing much the same against the Home Guard's Maidstone 11th Battalion, en route to five career ducks of his own — so there's a precedent, Peter, for turning a rough start into a proper collection. Sunday 14th — 1st XI away at Halfway House Opener Stan Wratten fell early, bowled by Don Capeling, his first duck of the summer but his 16th for the club overall — enough to keep him parked at a mighty 5th of 718 all-time. Stan remains a proud member of the Quacking Together board alongside John Ames, proof that misery enjoys the best company. Neatly, on this very 14th of June back in 1882, C Gibbs was contributing his own nought against Boxley CC's 1st Innings — his career amounted to just the one duck against Stan's sixteen, so consistency of a very particular kind clearly runs deeper in some than others. He had company in the returning-hut. At number nine John Abnett also departed for nought, bowled by Peter Bedelle, his 11th career duck from a brisk 33 innings — good enough for 14th on the all-time list and a place on the Ducks in a Row board for four consecutive noughts, a genuine feat of sustained failure. Fittingly, John shares his on-this-day company with C Gibbs too, who was busy not scoring against Boxley on this same date in 1882. Two Linton men, 77 years apart, united in nought. Week in summary Three ducks from two matches, all shouldered by the 1st XI, and all three victims caught, bowled or otherwise dismissed without so much as troubling the scorer — a clean sweep for the bowlers, a triumph through adversity for the club's honours boards. 2 ducks

Two fixtures on the books this weekend, and the exclusive zero club held its ceremony at just one of them, Tilling Steven away, where the 1st XI queue formed early and often. 1st XI, away to Tilling Steven Brian Mills, promoted to first drop, made scarcely more of his innings than the walk out and back, bowled by F- Baker for his 3rd duck of the season and 3rd of a still-young senior career, 5 innings in and already 71st of 716 on the all-time list. A debut innings, and therefore an instant, involuntary enrolment onto the Debutante Duck board (rank 222 of 715) — there are faster ways to make your mark, but few so memorable. Fittingly, his fall shares its calendar date with Frank Sutton's 1943 effort too — some days are simply built for it. - Arthur Cradduck rounded things off, run out for nought by a mix-up nobody present is owning — his 1st duck of the season and 8th career nought from 47 innings (rank 25 of 715). A past Duck of the Year himself back in 1951, Arthur joins the Sutton parallel for a third time this innings. 🍩 Family honours: a proper Two of a Quack — H and Roy Clarke, brothers both back in the hutch to Farrow inside the same innings. The Duck Club doesn't get to toast a bloodline double often; Saturday obliged in style. Sunday 31 May — Folkestone CC (home) - William Buck opened and closed his account almost immediately, bowled John Spanswick for his 2nd duck of the season and 13th career nought from a substantial 201 innings — a lofty 10th of 715 all time, and half of a standing Quacking Together pairing with John Thirkell. 🦆 Duck News — 2 & 3 May 1959 🦆

6 ducks
Week 1 · 2 May 1959 – 3 May 1959
Six into the book across two outings for the 1st XI this weekend, the exclusive zero club welcoming old faces and one very new one. The art of not scoring, alive and well at Linton Park. Saturday 2 May — Bearsted CC (h) Frank Brattle survived two deliveries before Peter Longley had the last word, bowled for his 1st duck of the summer and 8th of a lengthening career (52 innings, 24th in the all-time table). He now sits level with Alan Wilkes, who played 1953–1959 and reached the same 8 in a brisker 41 innings — and, for the genealogically minded, Frank's forebear Percy Brattle already carries 4 career ducks of his own, so the family name is no stranger to the honours board. Brian Mills provided the day's real occasion — out first innings, first ball faced, first everything, bowled Alan Fagg without troubling the scorers. A genuine arrival into the Duck Club, and he goes straight onto the Debutante Duck board for it. He joins the select company of the 1952 debutant "- Dampier," who also opened his and closed his entire Linton career on a single duck — Brian, one hopes, has rather more cricket ahead of him. Roy Clarke departed caught behind off Ian Lambert for his 8th career duck, and with 1959 barely a month old already sits proudly atop this year's Duck of the Year table — a crown he'll be defending all summer. He too draws level with Alan Wilkes on 8 apiece. Tony Snell rounded off the innings at number 11, bowled by Bryan Elswood for his 14th career duck from just 45 innings — form that earned him the Duck of the Year gong in 1958 and a place in the Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) hall of infamy. He now stands shoulder to shoulder with Frank Sutton, twice Duck of the Year in the 1940s, who reached 14 in 62 innings. Sunday 3 May — Harrietsham CC (a) Tony Tipples was caught and bowled by C Stitchman for his 7th career duck. Neat historical footnote: on this very date back in 1953, club legend John Ames also trudged off for nought, against Hunton Wanderers CC. And then the headline act. John Thirkell, LBW to D Hampshire, notched his 41st career duck — and yes, that keeps him firmly at number 1 of 712 in the entire Linton Park record book. A three-time Duck of the Year (1952, 1954, 1955), permanent fixture of the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens, Thirkell remains the undisputed monarch of the zero club. Fittingly, he shares his duck's date with the very same John Ames who also fell on 3 May 1953. Week in brief Six ducks, two matches, the entire haul claimed by the 1st XI — the 2nd, 3rd and 4th escaped entirely unscathed this week, which either means discipline or simply that they weren't watching. Nobody managed the ignominy of a golden duck this time round — every one of our six at least troubled the bowler for a delivery or two before departing. Small mercies. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. Brian Mills — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 2. Tony Snell — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 3. Tony Tipples — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 4. Frank Brattle — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% 5. John Thirkell — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% Early days yet in the 1959 campaign, but the leaderboard is already crowded. Next fixture awaits — who fancies joining the club? 🦆🍩0️⃣

🦆 Duck Club Report — 27–28 September 1958 🦆

9 ducks
Week 23 · 27 Sep 1958 – 28 Sep 1958
As the 1958 season draws towards its curtain, the Duck Club staged its own closing ceremony — nine gloriously scoreless departures across two matches. The art of not scoring, it seems, never takes a day off. Saturday 27th — 1st XI v A. Trembeths - Terry Whittaker (no. 9) fell b J- Mortlock for the very first duck of his 10-innings career, 297th on the all-time list — and a lifetime member of the "Quacking Together" honour shared with one Brian Relf, who would renew that partnership in spirit come Sunday. - Tony Snell (no. 11) departed b v- Chance, his 5th duck of the season and 13th of a career that now stands 9th all-time. Runs this season: none whatsoever — his board already confirms a full "Runaway Duck" campaign, and the reigning Duck of the Year 1958 shows no sign of loosening his grip on the crown. Both fell on the very date that, back in 1953, Tony Tipples (1952–58) also quacked against Linton Park CC — the fixture list has a long memory for these things. Sunday 28th — v Linton Park CC (Unknown XI, Married & Singles) - Len Conway (Unknown XI, 2) b Alan Wilkes — season duck #1, 4th of his career, 60th all-time, and a paid-up Debutante Duck club member. - Ray Howard (Unknown XI, 3) lbw b Gordon Fenner — his 2nd this season, 6th career, 37th all-time. - John Waters (Unknown XI, 5) b Gordon Fenner — 3rd career duck, 81st all-time. - John Abnett (Unknown XI, 10) b Alan Wilkes — 2nd of the season, 10th career, up to 18th all-time, and already a name on the honours board for four Ducks in a Row. - J Lea (Unknown XI, 11) b Alan Wilkes — an eye-watering 4th duck of the season, 5th career, 44th all-time — see the leaderboard below, he's earned his place. - Tony Levick (Married, 5) b Ray Howard — proof Ray can dish it out as well as collect it — 2nd of the season, 7th career, 31st all-time. - Brian Relf (Singles, 3) b G Martin — 3rd of the season, 5th career, 41st all-time, a long-standing Debutante Duck alumnus whose "Quacking Together" honour pairs him with none other than Terry Whittaker, out himself just a day earlier — kindred quackers across the weekend, if not the crease. Spookily, this same date in 1952 saw Ray Tippen also fall to Linton Park CC — some fixtures simply have the duck's scent about them. Week in summary: 9 ducks from 2 matches, with Alan Wilkes and Gordon Fenner each claiming a brace — Linton Park CC's attack plainly fancied its chances this weekend. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 🥇 1. Tony Snell — 8 inns, 5 ducks (62.5%) 2. John Ames — 19 inns, 5 ducks (26.32%) 3. Roy Clarke — 27 inns, 5 ducks (18.52%) 4. J Lea — 6 inns, 4 ducks (66.67%) 5. Stan Wratten — 16 inns, 4 ducks (25.0%) Tony Snell sits top of both the table and the Duck of the Year race — can anyone reel him in before 1958 draws stumps for good? Same ground, same fixtures, more nought-shaped glory awaits next time out. 🏏🍩0️⃣

🦆 Duck News — 20-21 September 1958

4 ducks
Week 22 · 20 Sep 1958 – 21 Sep 1958
A quieter weekend for the Club numerically, but a rich one thematically, with the 1st XI supplying the entire haul and Tilling Steven proving a positively fowl venue for Linton's middle order. 🏏 Saturday 20th — Bearsted CC (away) Batting at 11 with little left to protect, Tony Snell departed caught Ian Lambert bowled Bryan Elswood without adding to the total. It's his 4th duck of the campaign and his 12th in a 43-innings career, good enough for 11th of 710 in the all-time reckoning — and it draws him level on tally with Bert Buckoke, who played 1928–1953 and reached his dozen in 55 innings. Snell also extends his run to four ducks in a row, a streak that would make a hen proud, and with "Duck of the Year 1958" already on his honours board he heads into the run-in as the man to catch this season. The "Runaway Duck (a whole season without a run)" honour, too, sits uncomfortably close should he keep this up. 🌱 Sunday 21st — Tilling Steven (home) If Saturday was a solitary quack, Sunday was a full chorus. Three Linton batsmen fell without scoring in the same innings against Tilling Steven, a genuine gathering of the clan. Stan Wratten went first, run out for nought at number 2 — his 4th of the season and 15th of a 161-innings career, 6th of 710 all-time. On this very day in 1957, Richard Harris (1940–1958, 28 career ducks, 2nd of 710) also strolled back for a duck, so the calendar keeps good company. John Ames followed, lbw to F. Baker at 6, his 5th duck of the season and 17th of the career from 121 innings, 4th of 710 — a lofty position, backed by a place in the Homebody Duck top 10. Ames and Wratten renew their "Quacking Together" partnership in fine style this week, both falling in the same innings as history suggested they might. Roy Clarke completed the set, bowled by the same F. Baker at 7, his 5th season duck and 7th career one from 43 innings, 30th of 710. Clarke, too, shares "Quacking Together" honours with Ames — and true to form, the pair obliged together at Tilling Steven. 📋 Week in Summary Four ducks from two matches, every one of them a 1st XI affair, and three of the four arriving in a single unhappy innings at Tilling Steven. Not quite family, but certainly friendly. 🥇 Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - John Ames — 18 inns, 5 ducks, 27.78% - Roy Clarke — 25 inns, 5 ducks, 20.00% - Tony Snell — 7 inns, 4 ducks, 57.14% - Bob Arnold — 15 inns, 4 ducks, 26.67% - Stan Wratten — 15 inns, 4 ducks, 26.67% Next fixture looms and the exclusive zero club never closes its books early. Bring your bats, gentlemen — someone's got to keep the honours board honest. 🦆🍩0️⃣

🦆 Duck News — 13-14 September 1958 🦆

5 ducks
Week 21 · 13 Sep 1958 – 14 Sep 1958
Two fixtures at the tail end of the season, but it was Sunday's trip to Tunbridge Wells CC that did the real damage — five ducks in a single innings, a proper cluster of quacks to close out the week. 1st XI v Tunbridge Wells CC (away) - Stan Wratten opened and departed early, caught Woodland bowled Hall — his 3rd duck of the season and 14th of a steadily swelling career, good for 8th of 709 all time and level with both Frank Sutton (1925–1949) and Gordon Fenner (1941–1958). Spookily, this very date in 1957 saw Bob Arnold post a duck of his own against Bowaters CC — September has form. - John Ames, at five, fell to William Isard for his 4th of the season and 16th of his career, climbing to 4th on the all-time list. A card-carrying member of the Homebody Duck top ten and the exclusive Ducks in a Row club, Ames also holds Quacking Together honours with both Stan Wratten and Roy Clarke — and remarkably both obliged him in this very innings, the set completed live in front of the Tunbridge Wells fielders. - Cliff Anscombe followed soon after for his 3rd of the season and 7th career duck, 27th of 709 all time, level with Arthur Cradduck (1950–1953) and Frank Brattle (1937–1958). A Debutante Duck by trade and Duck of the Year back in 1957, Cliff shows no sign of slowing this fine tradition. - Roy Clarke made it four for the season and six for his career, 35th of 709 and level with current-era regulars Tony Levick and Tony Tipples. His own Quacking Together pact with Ames rang true once more, the two men departing within the same innings. - Last man John Lea, on debut, was bowled by Charles Wicker without troubling the scorers — a genuine baptism into the Debutante Duck club, and 1958's newest recruit to the One and Done register. Whether he stays a member of one is entirely up to him. Week in summary: 5 ducks from 2 matches, the entire haul arriving in one innings at Tunbridge Wells. Three of the five — Wratten, Ames and Clarke — share mutual Quacking Together honours that all rang true in the same innings, a rare triangle of shared ignominy 🍩🍩🍩. 🦆 Duck News — Saturday 6th & Sunday 7th September 1958

3 ducks
Week 20 · 6 Sep 1958 – 7 Sep 1958
A quiet weekend for the club at large, but the 1st XI kept the zero club ticking over nicely with three fresh entries to the ledger of dubious distinction. 🏏 Saturday — Away at Tovil John Ames opened the weekend's account, lbw to F- Goldsworthy at number 5. It's his 3rd duck of the season and 15th of a storied career, good enough for 5th on the all-time list from 119 innings — a genuine club institution, already carrying "Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive)" and a Homebody Duck top ten spot on his honours board, alongside standing "Quacking Together" pairings with Roy Clarke and Stan Wratten. Ames keeps fine historical company. 🌱 Sunday — Home to Anchorians CC Sunday's home fixture proved a productive one for all the wrong reasons, with Anchorians CC claiming a brace. Cliff Anscombe went first, bowled by J Toon, for his 2nd duck of the season and 6th of his career — 29th all time. Cliff is a long-standing Debutante Duck club member, having marked his very first senior innings with a nought, and was Duck of the Year back in 1957 for good measure. Fittingly, it was on this same date in 1957 that Frank Brattle (1937–1958, 7 ducks, 27th all time) was last seen making an identical contribution against Tovil. At the other end of the innings, last man Alan Wilkes was bowled by Don Wykes for his 1st duck of the season and 8th career nought, moving him to 22nd all time. Wilkes' honours board already carries two "Only Two Quacks" partnerships — with Bob Arnold, and with Saturday's own John Ames — proof that the zero club runs in company as much as in solitude. Like Cliff, Wilkes joins Frank Brattle's 1957 vintage on the calendar of shared infamy. 📋 Week in Summary Three ducks, two matches, one club — with the 1st XI shouldering the entire burden this week and Anchorians CC doing the double on Sunday. No golden ducks, no pairs, no family affairs to report — just solid, dependable failure to trouble the scorers. Roy Clarke — 3 ducks, 21 innings (14.29%) J Lea's 60% strike rate remains the one to watch — at this rate the season's Duck of the Year race may be settled well before the last ball is bowled. 🍩 Next fixture looms, and with it, further opportunities for enshrinement. Get your ducks in a row, gentlemen — the honours board never sleeps. 🦆

🦆 Duck Report — 30–31 August 1958

6 ducks
Week 19 · 30 Aug 1958 – 31 Aug 1958
Two fixtures, six ducks, and the ghost of John Thirkell walking arm in arm with every one of them — the great man (1943–1958, still an imperious 40 ducks, all-time #1) made his own duck on this very date back in 1952, once at Hunton Wanderers, once at A Levick XI. History has a wicked sense of timing. 🏏 Saturday 30th — 1st XI v W. Buck's XI (h) John Abnett departed for nought, caught Beale bowled Ames — his 1st duck of the season and 9th of a career now 21st all-time, a paid-up member of the "Ducks in a Row" club, four on the spin at his peak. Tony Snell followed him back, caught Morris bowled the same J. Ames, for his 3rd of the season and 11th career, 14th all-time. Snell wears the 1958 Duck of the Year sash and, more remarkably, the "Runaway Duck" honour — a whole season so far without a run to his name. Ames, whose afternoon's work sent both men packing — a surname Linton would hear from again rather sooner than expected. 🏏 Sunday 31st — 1st XI v Halfway House (h) Four fell in this one, headlined by our own John Ames, bowled Colin Robinson for his 2nd of the season and 14th career, 7th all-time — a committed Homebody Duck top-tenner who rarely troubles the away tally. Moments later Roy Clarke was run out for his 3rd of the season, 5th career, 44th all-time — and in doing so completed the "Quacking Together" honour shared with Ames, the pair now officially quacking as one. Lea, bowled Allsworth, notched his 3rd of the season and 4th career, 57th all-time — sharing his method of dismissal with Childs, both undone by the same probing spell. 📊 Week in Summary Six ducks from two matches, all at home, all 1st XI — a rare weekend where the seconds and thirds kept their heads down and let the top team do the collecting. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Bob Arnold — 4 ducks, 13 inns, 30.8% - J Lea — 3 ducks, 5 inns, 60.0% - Tony Snell — 3 ducks, 6 inns, 50.0% - Roy Clarke — 3 ducks, 20 inns, 15.0% - John Thirkell — 3 ducks, 25 inns, 12.0% Arnold sits imperiously atop the pile, but Snell, Lea and Clarke are queuing up behind him. 4 ducks

Two fixtures, four ducks, and the exclusive zero club took in a full house this weekend. Linton's top order continues to demonstrate that consistency of a very particular kind. 🏏 Saturday 16th — away to Bowaters CC Bob Arnold departed at four, bowled by Eric Wilson, for his 4th duck of the season and 26th of a career now bedding into the all-time top three — 3rd of 706, no less. This one extends his "Ducks in a Row" board to four on the bounce, a feat requiring real discipline to sustain, and keeps him in company on the "Only Two Quacks" honour with Alan Wilkes and "Quacking Together" with John Thirkell. Stan Wratten fell at three, bowled by S. Kitchin, his 2nd duck of the season and 13th of a career that sits him 8th of 706 — a lofty perch. He shares the "Quacking Together" board with John Ames. On this day back in 1957, John Thirkell was also enjoying the poultry treatment, against Bowaters CC no less — 40 career ducks and still Linton's undisputed number one. Roy Clarke followed at five, caught P. Jordan bowled A. Olsen, his 2nd of the season and 4th career duck, 61st of 706 — and, like Wratten, a fellow member of "Quacking Together (with John Ames)". Kitchin, taking his season tally to a debut-of-the-week 1 but his career tally to a startling 28 — good enough for 2nd of 706 all-time, agonisingly close to the summit. Another nod to Thirkell's 1957 vintage duck completes the set. 📊 Week in Summary Four ducks from two matches, three of them arriving in the same Mote A innings — S. Kitchin doing the damage twice over. Bob Arnold quietly extends his consecutive-duck streak while Richard Harris continues his relentless march up the all-time table. 🦆 Duck Report — 9th–10th August 1958

5 ducks
Week 16 · 9 Aug 1958 – 10 Aug 1958
A quiet weekend at Linton Park by match count, but a vintage one for the ledger — five new entries to the zero club, four of them courtesy of a single ruthless Headcorn attack. 🏏 Saturday — 1st XI v Headcorn CC (h) Opening the batting and opening the day's account, John Thirkell fell caught Farrance bowled Kemp without scoring. The club's ledger has been counting on his behalf for years — this is his 3rd duck of the season and takes him to 40 for his career, top of the all-time chart at rank 1 of 706, a record about as secure as records get. He arrives already garlanded with Duck of the Year honours from 1952, 1954 and 1955, plus permanent residency in the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens. On this very day in 1904, Jack Fryer made his own duck against Leeds Castle CC's House Team — some traditions run deep. Robert Wood followed, bowled Murrell for nought, his 2nd of the season and 2nd of a career just seven innings young, rank 135 of 706. His Debutante Duck board records that his first-ever senior innings, some years back, was also a blob — today's simply adds to the collection. Jack Fryer, 1904, keeps him company on the calendar once again. Then Bob Arnold, caught Farrance bowled Murrell — the same Farrance who'd already pouched Thirkell, evidently having a fine afternoon in the slips. Arnold's 3rd of the season moves him to 25 career ducks, rank 3 of 706, well inside his own Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) territory, and formally Quacking Together with Thirkell — a partnership the pair have now honoured twice, on this very afternoon. Fryer's 1904 duck obliges the pattern again. Brian Relf closed the innings out, caught Wilkinson bowled Kemp, his 2nd of the season and 4th career duck, rank 47 of 706. His Debutante Duck and Retirement Duck boards are standing honours from a career with its own bookends, nothing to do with today — alongside Quacking Together with Terry Whittaker. Fryer's 1904 shift echoes once more down the decades. Four ducks, two bowlers — Kemp and Murrell shared the spoils evenly, with Farrance doing the honest work at slip twice over. 🌱 Sunday — 1st XI v Harrietsham CC (h) Roy Clarke was bowled by D La Plain for nought, his 1st duck of the season and 3rd of a 34-innings career, rank 86 of 706. His Quacking Together board names John Ames, a partnership from a different vintage. On this day in 1895, J Lampard also made a duck, against Maidstone CC. 📊 The Week in Brief Five ducks from two matches, all in the 1st XI, all on home soil — Headcorn's attack claimed four of them between just two bowlers. Quality over quantity, as the zero club likes to say. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Bob Arnold — 3 ducks, 12 innings (25%) 2. John Thirkell — 3 ducks, 21 innings (14.29%) 3. C- Haylor — 2 ducks, 3 innings (66.67%) 4. J Lea — 2 ducks, 4 innings (50%) 5. Brian Relf — 2 ducks, 5 innings (40%) See you next weekend, when the zero club will no doubt be recruiting again. 🦆🍩 --- One unrelated housekeeping note: a teammate's machine (Kleptocrat1) is 151 commits behind — worth a nudge to them to start a session when you get a chance, nothing needed on your end.

🦆 Duck Report — 26th–27th July 1958

5 ducks
Week 14 · 26 Jul 1958 – 27 Jul 1958
Two fixtures graced the calendar this weekend, but only one needed the record book out: Linton's 1st XI capitulated against Tovil on the Saturday for FIVE ducks in a single innings, the kind of collective effort the exclusive zero club exists to celebrate. Fittingly, this very calendar date in 1940 also claimed a Linton batsman for nought — J Short, undone without score against Boughton Monchelsea, proving the 26th of July has form. 1st XI v Tovil William Blight departed at number three, bowled by Hitchin, for his 1st duck of the summer and 10th of a career that now sits 18th on the all-time roll of dubious distinction. Brian Relf followed moments later, also bowled by Hitchin, his 3rd career duck in just 12 innings. Relf remains a paid-up member of the Debutante Duck club from his early days at the crease, and carries the rarer Quack-to-Quack distinction besides — a duck on debut, with the "farewell" half presumably still some way off. No danger of that today, at least. R. Bailey then took the ball and simply helped himself. G Abel edged behind for his 2nd duck of the season, his career tally now 2 from 7 innings — a startling 28.57% strike rate that leaves him 3rd on this season's leaderboard. Bob Arnold was caught off Bailey for his 23rd career duck, a genuinely fearsome tally ranking 3rd of all 706 names in the club's nought-book, and a proud holder of the "Ducks in a Row" honour for four on the spin. Last man Tony Snell was bowled by Bailey for his 2nd of the season, his 10th career duck overall. It puts him firmly in this season's Duck of the Year 1958 conversation, with the ignominious "Runaway Duck" — a whole season without troubling the scorers — still tantalisingly on the cards. Hitchin (2) and Bailey (3) shared the spoils of an afternoon Tovil will remember fondly and Linton would rather forget. 📋 Week in Summary 5 ducks, 2 matches, all five arriving in the same doomed innings. The other fixture passed off disappointingly fowl-free. 🥇 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. J Lea — 2 ducks / 4 inns — 50.0% 1. Tony Snell — 2 ducks / 4 inns — 50.0% 3. 🦆 Duck Report — Weekend of 19–20 July 1958

2 ducks
Week 13 · 19 Jul 1958 – 20 Jul 1958
Two Linton fixtures across the weekend, and the club's enduring gift for the naught stayed firmly switched on for one of them. Saturday's outing passed off disappointingly duck-free, but Sunday's visit from J G Larkings more than made up for it, with two names freshly inked into the ledger of dubious distinction. 🏏 1st XI v J G Larkings (Sunday 20th, home) First up was Tony Levick, trapped lbw by D. Goodliffe without troubling the scorers. His first duck of the summer, and his sixth for the club in 108 innings, which lodges him 34th of 706 in the all-time table — respectable company for a man who otherwise knows which end of the bat to hold. Splendidly, this very fixture falls on a haunted date: on this day in 1906, R W Mitchell (1903–1909) also strolled back for nought, against the Royal West Kent Regiment CC Officers XI, en route to 2 career ducks and 130th on the all-time list. Fifty-two years apart, same calendar square, same outcome. Not long after, Goodliffe struck again, bowling John Thirkell outright for his second duck of the week — and, with rather greater ceremony, his 39th career duck in 263 innings. That is enough to make John the club's outright record holder, sitting at #1 of 706 all-time, a throne he has occupied with some style having already been crowned Duck of the Year in 1952, 1954 and 1955. He also holds permanent residency in the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens, and carries Quacking Together honours alongside old teammates Bob Arnold and William Buck — a man who has mastered failure from every conceivable angle. Fittingly, he too shares this weekend's ghostly echo of R W Mitchell's 1906 duck, out on the same date 52 years prior. Two wickets, one bowler, no complaints from D. Goodliffe, who evidently fancied his afternoon's work against the Linton middle-to-lower order. 📊 Week in Summary Two matches, two ducks, both claimed by the same bowler in the same innings — a rare case of Larkings doing the club's collecting for it. 5 ducks

5 ducks

Best of all, D Young marked his very first senior innings with a golden entry into the record books — caught and bowled by J Ellis without troubling the scorers, a genuine Debutante Duck. 4 ducks

A three-time Duck of the Year (1952, 1954, 1955) and fixture of the Ducks on the Road, Homebody Duck and Lone Duck top tens, Thirkell's "Quacking Together" board now ticks over nicely alongside Buck. Completing the Allsworth treble was Michael Morton, bowled at five for his 2nd duck of the season already — 8th of his career (17th of 670, 46 innings). Morton draws level with George Champion, who mustered the same eight across a marathon 1886–1912 stint. With a live Duck of the Year 1956 board to his name, Morton is very much one to watch in this year's race for scoreless glory. 🌱 Sunday 27th — Ron Aiston XI (Home) C- Haylor continued a lean run, run out for nought at number eight — his 2nd duck of the season and 4th of his career (39th of 670, just 9 innings — a rate that raises eyebrows). A paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from a past farewell, Haylor can at least take comfort that on this very day in 1950, John --'s Taylor was also trudging back for nought, against Hunton Wanderers CC no less. History does love to rhyme. 📋 The Week in Brief Four ducks, two matches, and one bowler doing the lion's share of the damage. 🦆 Duck Club Dispatch — Weekend of 12th & 13th May, 1956

3 ducks
Week 3 · 12 May 1956 – 13 May 1956
A modest but perfectly formed haul this week — three noughts across two 1st XI outings, the exclusive zero club welcoming its latest inductees with the usual pomp. More strikingly, this is career duck number 24 from 118 innings, which plants him at a formidable 2nd of 668 on the all-time list — one of the most decorated members the club has ever produced, and he isn't finished yet. Like Piercy, Harris shares his duck-day with D H Luck's 1906 vintage against Town Malling — Saturday the 12th evidently has previous. Sunday 13th May — 1st XI at home to West Farleigh CC Ray Howard, batting four, was trapped lbw by R- Kemp for his first duck of the campaign and his first in senior colours — 1 from 16 career innings, ranking 262nd of 668. On this same date in 1950, D Simmons was similarly dismissed for nought against Bearsted CC, racking up what would become 4 ducks across his 1949–53 career and a rank of 39th — Howard has some catching up to do if he fancies that company. Week in summary Three ducks, two matches, one common thread — the 1st XI carried the weekend's entire quota single-handedly. Richard Harris' back-to-back pair of noughts is the standout, a serious early marker in the race for this season's crown, while Piercy and Howard both open their season accounts in style — or rather, in its total absence. 🦆 Duck Report — 5 September 1954

4 ducks
Week 19 · 5 Sep 1954
A single fixture on the books this week, away trade forgotten, as the 1st XI hosted Gillingham CC, Kent — and Gillingham's bowlers found the home dressing room in generous mood. Four ducks recorded, three of them falling in a tidy little cluster. 1st XI v Gillingham CC, Kent (home) John Larking opened up and didn't last, bowled by J Tansley for his very first LPCC duck — a debut entry on the nought column in just his 8th innings, landing him 215th of 650 in the all-time list. Curiously, this very date has previous: on 5 September 1953, John Thirkell was also trudging off for nought, that time against Yalding CC. History, it seems, likes this fixture week. Then O Barden got to work, and got to work thoroughly. Number six John Thirkell fell to him for a 7th duck of the season, his 26th in an LPCC career now 150 innings deep — a total that keeps him imperiously parked at #1 on the all-time chart. Thirkell already carries Duck of the Year honours from 1952 and, on this season's evidence, is mounting a serious defence of the 1954 crown too. He's a fixture of the Ducks on the Road, Homebody Duck and Lone Duck top tens besides, with shared quacking history alongside Bob Arnold and William Buck. On this same day in 1953, J Barclay was likewise dismissed for nought against Yalding — Barclay finished his short career on exactly 7, precisely where Thirkell now sits for the season alone. O Barden wasn't done. Richard Harris, in at seven, followed his captain back for a 5th duck of the campaign, taking him to 19 career ducks from 96 innings and into 2nd place all-time — Thirkell's shadow lengthens behind him. Like Larking, Harris finds company on this calendar date in Thirkell's 1953 effort at Yalding. And to complete the set, John Abnett went at eight, O Barden's third scalp in a row, for his 1st career duck in only his 2nd senior innings. He arrives with a "Ducks in a Row" board credit already to his name for a run of four in swift succession — a man clearly not afraid of type-casting. Another entry for the 5 September file, joining Thirkell's 1953 quack at Yalding. Week in brief: one match, four ducks, and O Barden helping himself to three victims on the spin — Thirkell, Harris and Abnett walking back in convenient single file. A tidy afternoon's work for Gillingham, a less tidy one for the LPCC top order. Arnold's honours cabinet is already groaning: Ducks in a Row (four consecutive, a feat of remarkable consistency of a very particular kind), Only Two Quacks alongside Alan Wilkes, and Quacking Together with John Thirkell. And yes — by pleasing coincidence, 1869's J Amies strikes again as this day's historical companion in futility. Sunday 11th — vs Selstead (Away) At Selstead, R- Waters departed bowled by H- Denham, batting at three. This was his 1st duck of the season and, notably, his 1st career duck from just 3 innings — the art of not scoring, freshly discovered. He lands at 247th of 648 in the all-time standings, and joins the Retirement Duck ranks as a standing club honour, entirely unrelated to any suggestion he's finished playing. On this same day in 1943, Stan Wratten was falling for nought against the Royal Artillery Wing — a fellow member of the Quacking Together honours, paired with John Ames. The Week in Summary Three ducks from two matches — a modest but respectable haul. All three fell to attacking bowling rather than run-outs or misadventure, and both Muir and Arnold shared the same wrecking-ball in Chance. Triumph through adversity remains the house motto. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Peter Weedon — 5 innings, 3 ducks (60%) - Bob Arnold — 10 innings, 3 ducks (30%) - William Blight — 12 innings, 3 ducks (25%) - L Skinner — 5 innings, 2 ducks (40%) - Robert Muir — 8 innings, 2 ducks (25%) Weedon leads the charge with a frankly heroic 60% strike rate for failure, but Arnold's weekend haul keeps him snapping at his heels. Plenty of season left for the standings to turn. Next fixture looms, and with it, the inevitable next instalment of the zero club. Bring your bats, gentlemen — or don't bother. 🦆🍩0️⃣

3 ducks

A quieter week in the hunting grounds, but the 1st XI still managed to keep the exclusive zero club ticking over with three fresh inductions across two fixtures. His first duck of the season and only his second in a 25-innings career, rank 105 of 648, though he's already a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from a past farewell innings. Sunday 4 July — home to S.Kimmins William Blight, at six, fell to D- Altham for his third duck of the season and, remarkably, his third in a career that has produced nothing else — every one of his 28-innings career's noughts arriving inside this single summer. Rank 66 of 648 and climbing fast. On this same date in 1904, Arthur Cornwallis was doing likewise, a two-time Duck of the Year in his own right back in 1888 and 1904, playing on from 1884 to 1909. Week in summary Three ducks, two matches, all honours claimed by the 1st XI, who evidently fancied sharing the misery about equally home and away. Triumph through adversity, as ever. The Duck Club Gazette — 12th and 13th September, 1953

0 ducks
Week 20 · 12 Sep 1953 – 13 Sep 1953
A quiet week, and a disappointing one for connoisseurs of the duck's egg. Across both fixtures played this weekend, the club's watchful eye — ever hopeful, pencil poised over the honours board — found not a single nought worth the recording. Every man who walked to the crease departed, sooner or later, with at least one run to his name, which is all very well for the scorebook but leaves this correspondent with precious little to celebrate. One might almost suspect a conspiracy of straight bats and watchful footwork about the ground this week, though it is more likely simple ill fortune for the Duck Club, whose members hunt in vain whenever an eleven insists on playing sensibly. The tail, we are reliably informed, wagged rather than folded, and not a man among either side troubled the exclusive zero club these two days. Still, one barren weekend does not empty the trophy cabinet, nor dim the lustre of those already enrolled in the club's dubious distinction. The season's leading exponents of the art of not scoring remain handsomely in credit, and the list below stands as testament to sterner, more fruitful days for the pursuit of nought. The Duck Club Gazette — 5th and 6th September, 1953

4 ducks
Week 19 · 5 Sep 1953 – 6 Sep 1953
A brace of fixtures this week, and the eleven found four ways to depart without troubling the scorer. The exclusive zero club, ever discerning in its membership, drew its new candidates from both ends of the county this week. 1st XI At Yalding, John Thirkell strode out first wicket down and returned bowled by D. Brooker, his fifth duck's egg of the summer and the nineteenth of a long and eventful career — a career distinguished chiefly by its studious avoidance of runs. He sits alone at the head of the club's roll of honour, first of 639, and carries into every innings the laurels of Duck of the Year 1952, a place among both the Ducks on the Road and the Homebody Duck top tens, and shared quacking honours with Bob Arnold and William Buck besides. A gentleman for whom the long walk back has become almost a habit of residence. Further down the order, J Barclay followed him to the pavilion, bowled by G. Davis, his sixth duck of the season and sixth of his career, good enough for twentieth on the all-time list and this year's Duck of the Year honour already resting on his shoulders. He is besides a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from a past farewell. He now stands level on six career ducks with D Sells, who played his own quiet innings of failure between 1943 and 1944 — kindred spirits separated by a decade but united in arithmetic. At Gillingham the following day, the eleven suffered a curious symmetry: Richard Harris and Gordon Fenner, batting at six and seven, were both bowled by R. Beckenham within the same innings. Harris departed for his second duck of the season, his thirteenth in a career of seventy-six innings and fourth on the club's roll of shame. Fenner followed directly behind him, his fourth duck of the summer and also his thirteenth for his career, third all-time — and now drawing level with Harris himself, the two gentlemen sharing both a bowler's figures and a lifetime tally within the space of a single over. Fenner, it may be added, keeps failure rather in the family, his brother Joe carrying five ducks of his own. The Week in Brief Two matches, four ducks, and something of a pattern: three of the four fell to the bowled dismissal, and Gillingham's R. Beckenham managed the rare distinction of accounting for two Duck Club members in a single innings. A sticky wicket for the top and middle order alike, and no mistake. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - J Barclay — 20 innings, 6 ducks, 30.00% - John Thirkell — 28 innings, 5 ducks, 17.86% - Gordon Fenner — 12 innings, 4 ducks, 33.33% - John Ames — 15 innings, 4 ducks, 26.67% - Gerald Wright — 13 innings, 3 ducks, 23.08% The season's honours board continues to fill most satisfactorily, and the eleven take the field again next week with every confidence that fresh candidates will present themselves. The Club awaits them, as ever, with open arms and a duly sharpened pencil.

The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, 29th August 1953

5 ducks
Week 18 · 29 Aug 1953
A single fixture, away to Hunton Wanderers, yet the eleven contrived five entries in the ledger of nought. A sticky wicket indeed, and the zero club welcomes its latest subscribers. 1st XI - John Thirkell, in at three, was taken by Reg Oldfield off J Ludden for his fourth duck of the season and eighteenth of his career — top of the all-time table at 1 of 639, a Duck of the Year laureate of 1952 and a fixture of the Lone Duck and Homebody Duck top tens. He and Bob Arnold, old campaigners of the Quacking Together honours board, duly quacked together again this very afternoon. On this same date in 1949, one E Simmons also strolled back for nought against Town Malling CC — the calendar has its favourites. - N Simmons followed at five, bowled by J Ludden, his maiden season duck and maiden career duck alike in only his fourth innings — rank 222 of 639, and already a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from some past and presumably distant farewell. Like his captain, he shares his date with E Simmons of 1949. - Bob Arnold, at seven, fell leg before to R Venner for his second duck of the season and ninth of his career, tenth on the all-time roll and holder of Ducks in a Row, four consecutive — a spell so barren it merits its own trophy. His Quacking Together honour with Thirkell was renewed in the same innings. - G- Tompkinson, promoted to nine, was caught by J Foley off J Ludden in his very first innings for the club — a debut duck, and entry into the Debutante Duck club at the first attempt. He joins the select fellowship of One and Done for 1953, season and career alike consisting, so far, of a single nought — the purest of beginnings. - Gerald Wright closed the innings at eleven, leg before to R Venner, his third duck of the season and fifth of his career, twenty-third on the all-time table. Like every one of today's unfortunates, his fall echoes E Simmons on this same date in 1949 against Town Malling CC. Five ducks from a single match, top and tail of the order both accounted for, and J Ludden the chief tormentor with three scalps. The eleven may reflect that a duck's egg is at least honestly come by. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. J Barclay — 19 innings, 5 ducks, 26.32% 2. John Ames — 15 innings, 4 ducks, 26.67% 3. The Duck Club Gazette — Week Ending 22nd August 1953

1 duck
Week 17 · 22 Aug 1953
A modest week for the eleven, home to Charles Arkcoll, yielding but a single fresh entry to the Zero Club's ledger. Modest in number, never in ceremony — the club has always held that one duck properly honoured is worth more than a dozen let pass unremarked. 1st XI J Barclay, promoted to number eight, offered a return catch that Stan Wratten was only too glad to accept — c & b Stan Wratten, and back to the pavilion without troubling the scorers. It is his fifth duck of the season and stands as the twenty-fourth entry on the club's all-time roll of dubious distinction, a list now numbering 638 names in all. With the season itself bearing the same number, 1953, Barclay's effort must be counted toward this year's Duck of the Year — a title awarded not for runs made but, in the club's own particular reckoning, for runs conspicuously not made, and he goes into the reckoning as a serious contender. He remains besides a long-established member of the Retirement Duck fellowship, a past farewell recorded on the honours board from an earlier chapter of his cricketing life, and no reflection upon this week's proceedings. Most curiously of all, on this very date in 1903, a full half-century before, one W Peach fell in precisely the same manner against the 1st Innings of the Kent County Constabulary — the art of not scoring, it seems, keeps a faithful calendar. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, and a single name added to the ledger — the eleven played a generally straight bat this week, leaving the Zero Club's secretary with rather less to record than usual. Whether this reflects improved batting or merely a quiet fixture, the committee declines to speculate. 3 ducks

Two fixtures in the diary this week, but the duck's egg made its appearance in only one of them — the visit of Mote A, where the home eleven contrived three ways of getting back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer. Bryant for his fourth duck of the summer — the fourth of a season that continues to test his patience, and enough, by the club's own ledger, to make it "Ducks in a Row," four in succession, a feat few would boast of but none can deny. It is his fourth career nought in thirty innings, thirty-first — no, forty-first — in the all-time order of six hundred and thirty-eight, and he remains a fixture of the Homebody Duck company besides sharing past quacking honours with Roy Clarke, Stan Wratten and Alan Wilkes. Curiously, on this very day in 1893, one George Champion also strolled back for nought, against the Free Foresters. - John Thirkell, in at four, fell to J. Coomber for his third duck of the season and his seventeenth in a long and distinguished career of one hundred and nineteen innings — a career which, remarkably, sits him at the very head of the club's all-time table, first of six hundred and thirty-eight. A former Duck of the Year, and a name long resident in the Lone Duck and Homebody top tens, he adds merely another line to an already formidable record. He, too, shares his day with George Champion's duck of 1893. - L Skinner, batting at ten, was bowled by S. Capon for his maiden duck of the season, and the first of his short career so far — one nought from two innings, placing him modestly at two hundred and eleventh of all who have ever made the walk. He carries, from some past and unrecorded reckoning, a place among the Retirement Duck company, though we trust his innings with the club is far from concluded. He, like his colleagues, kept company with George Champion's ghost of 1893. The Week in Brief Three ducks from two matches, the whole clutch laid in a single innings against Mote A — a fine morning's work for the visiting bowlers, and a poor one for the home order's middle and lower reaches. 5 ducks

The Duck Club Gazette — the 2nd and 3rd of August, 1953

2 ducks
Week 14 · 2 Aug 1953 – 3 Aug 1953
Two fixtures over the weekend, and two subscriptions paid into the exclusive zero club, that place of dubious distinction where consistency of a very particular kind is celebrated rather than mourned. 1st XI - J Barclay, turning out against Birchington Wanderers on the Saturday, came in at number six and was bowled by J Ince without troubling the scorers unduly — hardly the straight bat the eleven had hoped for. It is his fourth duck of the season and the fourth of a career of fifteen innings, placing him thirty-seventh in the club's all-time roll of the dismissed for nought. As it happens 1953 is very much his season for it, and this latest nought keeps him snugly inside the Duck of the Year honours he already carries for the year in question. He remains, besides, a long-standing member of the Retirement Duck club, having bowed out on a duck in an innings some while back — a badge worn with the quiet pride of the veteran. Curiously enough, on this very date in 1944 one E- Humphreys performed the identical trick against the National Fire Service Overseas Contingent, proving that some anniversaries keep themselves. - John Thirkell, a day later against the Lord Cornwallis XI, came in at the same number six and departed caught by a- Milsted off the bowling of K- Goodwin, for nought. It is only his second duck of the present season, but a rather more imposing sixteenth in a career now standing at one hundred and fifteen innings — figures that install him, with a certain grim majesty, at the very summit of the club's all-time table: first of six hundred and thirty-seven, a record the rest of the eleven can only regard from a respectful distance. A fixture of the Ducks on the Road, Homebody Duck and Lone Duck top tens, and a name twice bracketed under Quacking Together, with Bob Arnold and with William Buck besides, Thirkell wears his Duck of the Year 1952 as history now rather than news. Fittingly, on this same day in 1952 Gordon Fenner — no mean hand at the art of not scoring himself — was also making his own quiet way back to the pavilion. A modest week by the club's usual standards: two matches, two ducks, one apiece between Saturday's and Sunday's elevens, and neither a pair nor a family affair to report. The ducks came singly this time, which by this club's lights counts almost as restraint. The Duck Club Gazette — 25th to 26th July, 1953

2 ducks
Week 13 · 25 Jul 1953 – 26 Jul 1953
🦆 Two more names are inscribed upon the ledger of the scoreless this week, both from the 1st XI's excursion to Folkestone, and both, it must be said, achieved by rather more decorous means than the customary golden blob. No first-ball ignominy here — merely two batsmen undone after settling their guard, which the club regards as scarcely better consolation. 1st XI — away to Folkestone CC, 26th July Tony Levick, at number five, played on to a leg-before decision off D Morton and trudged back having troubled the scorers not at all. This is his second career duck in five-and-thirty innings for the 1st XI, placing him 104th of 637 in the club's all-time roll of the dismissed-for-nought — a position he now shares, at exactly two apiece, with a positively distinguished company including Arthur Ash, B Lloyd of the Debutante Duck club, and B- Vince, who once carried off the Duck of the Year honour itself in 1941. By curious coincidence of the calendar, on this very date in 1940 one J Short likewise trudged home for nought against Boughton Monchelsea CC — proof, if any were needed, that the ducks of Linton Park stretch back through the decades in unbroken and faithful procession. Bill Hall, sent in at number eight, was stumped by Len Godden off the same D Morton — a dismissal requiring, one notes, rather more effort from the opposition than the standard variety, though the result upon the scorecard is identical. It is his maiden duck of the season and of his one-and-twenty-innings career, seating him 130th of 637 on the all-time list, level on a single career duck with a full company of one-time offenders, several of them Debutante Duck men and one-season wonders besides. Mr Hall is additionally a paid-up member of the club's Retirement Duck honours board, a distinction earned on some past and presumably dignified departure from the crease — not, it should be stressed, this week's affair, upon which no comment as to his continuing career shall be ventured. He too finds his name matched against J Short's duck of the 26th of July, 1940, against Boughton Monchelsea CC. The week in summary A modest haul: two ducks from two fixtures, both from the 1st XI, both at Folkestone, and both, pleasingly, struck by different means of dismissal — the straight bat undone by swing, and the wandering foot undone by wicketkeeper's swiftness. No pairs, no golden ducks, and no family gatherings at the crease this week — the ducks, for once, kept to their own company. Until then, may your bats stay straight and your stumps stay standing.

A single fixture against John Larkings, and the home eleven contrived to lose three wickets without troubling the scorers at all. The zero club welcomes its latest subscribers. His brother Joe, himself no stranger to the zero club with five career ducks to his name, will doubtless offer what sympathy the tea urn allows. The weightier honours of the Quack-to-Quack and the Retirement Duck must wait upon further innings, and further seasons, before either can be fairly claimed. He too walks in step with F M Hills, whose Boxley duck of 1902 falls on this same calendar day. The Week in Brief Three ducks from one match, and John Larkings' bowlers plainly found Linton Park's order much to their liking. No pairs this week, and no families united in shared misfortune — merely three gentlemen, each dismissed without addition, doing their part for the club's proudest and most peculiar tradition: the fine art of not scoring. LPCC Duck Club — Weekly Gazette, 11th July 1953

0 ducks
Week 11 · 11 Jul 1953
🦆 A quiet week at the crease, ladies and gentlemen. For once the eleven kept their bats straight and their heads down, and not a single member of the club presented himself for induction into the exclusive zero club this week. Whether by sound technique, good fortune, or the bowling simply not being up to the task of separating a batsman from his wicket without troubling the scorer, the ducks evaded capture entirely. One match was played in the period, and it passed — remarkably — without incident. The committee notes this with a mixture of relief and mild disappointment, for a week without a nought is a week without a story, and this gazette rather prefers its heroes fallen. Let it be recorded, all the same, that the season's stalwarts of self-inflicted misfortune remain hard at work elsewhere, quietly compiling the sort of figures that keep this column in business. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Ames — 10 innings, 3 ducks, 30.0% - Michael Morton — 12 innings, 3 ducks, 25.0% - J Barclay — 14 innings, 3 ducks, 21.43% - Gerald Wright — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - Gordon Fenner — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% Mr Wright leads the percentage table with a positively alarming 40 per cent strike rate for nought, a consistency of a very particular kind that the rest of the eleven would do well to study, if only to avoid. Two fixtures were played this week, and though the exclusive zero club is rarely quiet for long, it was the 1st XI alone who furnished business for the honours board — three names added in a single afternoon away to Charles Arkcoll. At seven, G- Neighbour fell to John Ames, likewise for nought — a maiden season's duck, and but the first blot on a young ledger of three innings, 179th of the 636. He carries already the Retirement Duck honour from a past farewell of his own, a solemn distinction best left where it belongs, in history rather than this week's account. He, too, finds himself keeping company with Cornwallis, who trod the same lonely path back to the pavilion on this date in 1904. And at eight, Michael Morton went the same way — bowled John Ames — for the third time this season, and the third duck of a career built upon a dozen innings, 58th of the all-time company. Two wickets to Ames inside the same short spell was triumph through adversity for the bowler and a sticky wicket indeed for the middle order. Morton, like his colleagues above, shares his date with Cornwallis's duck of 1904 — a coincidence the honours board will note with quiet satisfaction. Week in summary Three ducks from two matches, all struck from the one innings against Charles Arkcoll, with John Ames doing for two batsmen what most bowlers manage only once in an afternoon. The tail, it must be said, did not so much wag as fold quietly. The Duck Report — 20th to 21st June, 1953

0 ducks
Week 8 · 20 Jun 1953 – 21 Jun 1953
A curious week to set before you, gentlemen, for the eleven took the field twice over these two days and not a single batsman was persuaded to walk back for nought. The zero club, that most exclusive of pavilions, reports no new admissions. Whether this reflects a sudden and regrettable outbreak of good batting, or merely that the bowlers of the opposition were having an off week of their own, the committee declines to speculate. It happens, now and again, that the ducks give the fielders the slip entirely — a fortnight's respite from the art of not scoring, and no doubt a source of quiet disappointment to those who follow this report chiefly for its casualties. Let it be recorded, in the spirit of honest chronicle, that on this occasion every man who came to the crease left it having troubled the scorers for at least one run. A sticky wicket for the Duck Club correspondent, if for nobody else. We shall not want for material long. The season's leading exponents of the golden art remain very much in form, and a glance at the honours below should reassure members that ignominy is never far away.
