The Duck Club Gazette — 6th and 7th June, 1953

1 duck
Week 6 · 6 Jun 1953 – 7 Jun 1953
A modest despatch this week, for the ducks proved shy quarry across both fixtures, yielding but a single egg to the collector's net. 1st XI At the wicket on the 7th, in the match against Old Shooterhillians, Richard Harris came in at number seven and departed without troubling the scorers, caught J Cooper, bowled G Bird. A tidy piece of bowling and a plucky if fruitless knock, and so the season's first duck's egg is chalked up against his name. It is, mind you, no stranger to him — his twelfth for the career now, in sixty-two innings, which places him a most distinguished fourth of six hundred and thirty-three in the club's roll of honour, a perch few gentlemen ever reach and fewer still would boast of. In doing so he draws level on that very tally of twelve with one Jack Fryer, who wore the same figure with equal good humour between 1881 and 1906 across sixty-seven innings, and who twice carried off the Duck of the Year, in 1891 and again in 1900. Mr Harris now walks in distinguished if unscoring company. The Week in Brief Two matches played over the weekend, and only the one duck laid between them — the eleven, on the whole, kept a straight bat and the tail need not have wagged at all. A quiet week for the club's own particular scoreboard, though the season's leading exponents of the art of not scoring continue to press their claims below. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Gerald Wright — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent - John Ames — 6 innings, 3 ducks, 50.00 per cent - Stan Wratten — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.00 per cent - Michael Morton — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.22 per cent - J Barclay — 12 innings, 2 ducks, 16.67 per cent Gerald Wright leads the field by some distance, though John Ames's three eggs in half a dozen visits to the crease is a rate of failure not easily bettered, and the whole quintet may consider their positions far from safe with the season yet young. The eleven take the field again shortly, and the club's honours board stands ever ready to welcome whichever unfortunate soul the bowlers next dispatch for nought. Until then, keep a wary eye on the sticky wickets.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the days of the 30th and 31st of May, 1953

2 ducks
Week 5 · 30 May 1953 – 31 May 1953
A quiet couple of days for the exclusive zero club — only the First Eleven troubled the scorers with their particular brand of nothing, but they made it count with a fine display of team spirit in adversity against the Old Williamsonians. 1st XI — v Old Williamsonians CC, 30th May Opening the innings and opening the account for the wrong side of the ledger was Basil Sears, caught Saunders, bowled Trower, for his 1st duck of the season and the 4th of a career now standing at a very respectable 28th of 630 on the all-time roll — a batsman who has, over 63 innings, made a habit of occasionally forgetting to trouble the scoreboard. He finds himself level on career ducks with a whole gallery of old and new names alike, joining the likes of Gerald Wright and the long-serving John --'s Taylor on exactly four apiece — kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. And by happy coincidence of the calendar, on this very day in 1943 one Frank Sutton, twice Duck of the Year and second on the all-time list with fourteen to his name, was himself walking back for nought against Home Guard - D Company — the ghosts of duck-outings past keeping Basil fine company. Following him back to the pavilion in short order was John Thirkell, bowled Trower without troubling the scorers, his 1st duck of this season but the 15th of an extraordinary career that sits him proudly — or perhaps not so proudly — at the very summit of the all-time table, 1st of 630. A paid-up member of the Duck of the Year honours board for 1952 and a fixture of the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens, Thirkell also shares the rare distinction of Quacking Together with both Bob Arnold and William Buck in seasons past. Like his opening partner, he too finds himself keeping step with history — for on this same 30th of May in 1943, Frank Sutton was again making his own duck's egg against Home Guard - D Company, proof that some dates simply attract the duck. A sticky sort of morning for the top of the order, then, with the innings undone before it had properly begun — but a straight bat and better fortune will surely follow at the crease before long. A brief accounting: two ducks recorded across two matches this week, both falling to the bowling of Trower and both from the top of the 1st XI order — a fine piece of new-ball work by the visitors, and a sobering reminder to Linton Park's openers that the art of not scoring requires no invitation. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard — 1953 - John Ames — 3 ducks in 5 innings (60.0%) - Gerald Wright — 2 ducks in 3 innings (66.67%) - Stan Wratten — 2 ducks in 4 innings (50.0%) - Michael Morton — 2 ducks in 8 innings (25.0%) - J Barclay — 2 ducks in 10 innings (20.0%) The season presses on, and with it the Duck Club's ever-watchful ledger. Members of the Eleven are respectfully reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for fresh nominations to this most singular of honours boards — until then, may your bats stay straight and your stumps stay standing.

The Duck Report — 23rd to 25th May, 1953

3 ducks
Week 4 · 23 May 1953 – 25 May 1953
A quiet week for the eleven, yet not so quiet as to spare the honours board a fresh entry or two. Three ducks fell across three fixtures, and one gentleman contrived to visit the pavilion twice in as many days. The First Eleven Gerald Wright made unwanted history this week, twice undone for nought inside two days — a feat the club's ledger records plainly as a pair, that grim double which no batsman sets out to achieve. On the Saturday, at home to Gore Court CC, he was bowled by Peter Holmes batting at number ten, his first duck of the season and the third of a career now numbering seven innings. Curiously, on this very day in 1943, one K- Symonds likewise departed for nought, against Royal Artillery Wing 48. Wright returned to the crease on the Sunday against Halfway House, in at number eleven, and was run out without troubling the scorers — his second duck in as many days and his fourth for the career, a tally that places him 34th of the 628 gentlemen who have made this particular journey. By a pleasing coincidence, this same 24th of May in the year 1882 saw F Foster fall for nought against Collier Street CC — proof, if any were needed, that the art of not scoring respects no calendar. William Buck, opening at number two against Halfway House on the Sunday, was likewise run out without scoring — a plucky enough start undone by a mix-up in the running. It is his second career duck in a lengthy innings of sixty-five, and places him 107th of the 628 in the club's all-time reckoning. Buck is, besides, a paid-up member of the "Quacking Together" fellowship alongside John Thirkell, two names forever bound by shared misfortune on the honours board. And here too the calendar plays its game — on this same 24th of May back in 1882, F Foster made his own duck against that same Collier Street CC. The Week in Brief Three matches, three ducks, and a certain want of communication in the running between wickets seems to have been the villain of the piece — both Sunday dismissals at Halfway House came by the run out, a sticky wicket of a different sort. Gerald Wright's pair is the week's chief curiosity, two ducks laid inside a single weekend being a distinction few would seek and fewer still achieve twice running. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Ames — 5 innings, 3 ducks, 60.0% - Gerald Wright — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% - Stan Wratten — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0% - Michael Morton — 7 innings, 2 ducks, 28.57% - J Barclay — 8 innings, 2 ducks, 25.0% The eleven takes the field again shortly, and the club has every confidence that fresh candidates will present themselves for the honours board in due course. Until then, the exclusive zero club extends its sympathies, and its congratulations, in equal measure.

The Duck's Egg Gazette — 16th and 17th May, 1953

5 ducks
Week 3 · 16 May 1953 – 17 May 1953
Two fixtures, one melancholy thread running through both: five eggs laid for the 1st XI across Gore Court and Mote A, and the exclusive zero club welcomes its members back with the usual solemn ceremony. Gore Court CC, 16th May Michael Morton, at four, was undone by a smart catch from Peter Holmes off T Clinch's bowling — his second duck of the season, and the second of a career now five innings long. He stands 92nd of 627 in the club's grand and dubious ledger. Curiously, on this very day in 1943, one L- Breedon walked back for nought against the Royal Army Service Corps 533 Division — the calendar, it seems, has a long memory for the art of not scoring. J Barclay, at seven, was caught and bowled by Peter Holmes for his maiden career duck — though the celebrations proved premature, as the reader shall discover below. Barclay already carries this season's Duck of the Year honours, and is a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from some past and presumably final innings, though nobody present this week saw him bow out for good, so we shall say no more on that score. His fall, too, echoed L- Breedon's 1943 vintage against the Service Corps. Mote A, 17th May The very next day brought Stan Wratten to the crease as opener, only to be bowled by Mac Harden without scoring — his second duck of the summer, and the seventh of a career that has now seen him dismissed for nought seventy-seven times over, fourteenth on the club's all-time list of the ignominious. Wratten holds his "Quacking Together" honours jointly with John Ames, and fittingly the pair renewed the acquaintance this very afternoon, Ames following him back to the pavilion at four, bowled by J- Coomber for his third duck of the season and his third of a career now eighteen innings long. Ames, a fixture of the Homebody Duck top ten and no stranger to four ducks in a row, continues to prove that consistency in this club comes in more than one flavour. Both men might reflect that on this same date in 1941, Herbert Rayner made his own duck against the Royal Army Ordnance Corps — some anniversaries simply will not be shaken off. And J Barclay, not content with Saturday's disappointment, returned at number eight to be caught by J- Waters off Mac Harden for his second duck of the week and his second of the season — a grim pair across the two fixtures that places him firmly among the week's most decorated failures. The Week in Brief Five ducks fell across two matches, both played away from home, and Mote A alone accounted for three of them — a sticky afternoon for top and middle order alike. Barclay's pair was the week's sternest reminder that misfortune, like rain, rarely falls but once. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. John Ames — 3 innings, 3 ducks, 100 per cent 2. Stan Wratten — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent 3. J Barclay — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40 per cent 4. Michael Morton — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40 per cent The eleven takes the field again next week, and the zero club stands ready, as ever, to welcome whichever gentleman finds the art of not scoring rather too easy to master.

The Duck Club Gazette — 9th to 10th May, 1953

2 ducks
Week 2 · 9 May 1953 – 10 May 1953
Two fixtures graced Linton Park this weekend, and though bat generally had the better of ball, the eleven surrendered a brace of duck's eggs to keep the Club's ledger in its accustomed good order. 1st XI On the Saturday, against Bearsted CC, Michael Morton came to the wicket at number four and departed without troubling the scorers, bowled by G. Hawkins. A first duck's egg of the season for him, and the third innings of a still-young career — the 212th such dismissal on the Club's long and honourable roll. He now keeps company with the departed - Dampier, who managed exactly one duck in his single season of 1952 before quietly retiring the bat for good, a paid-up member of both the Debutante Duck and the Retirement Duck fraternities, though Morton, one trusts, has rather more cricket left in him yet. The Sunday brought Folkestone CC to the Park, and with them the second instalment of John Ames's week, bowled by Jim Gordon at number five for his second duck of the season and second of a seventeen-innings career — a tidy 87th on the all-time roll. Ames arrives in distinguished if faintly cursed company: he sits within the Ducks in a Row quartet, keeps a place among the Homebody Duck top ten, and shares his solitary quacks with Alan Wilkes, with Roy Clarke, and with Stan Wratten besides — a man who rarely ducks alone. Curiously, on this very day a twelvemonth before, in 1952, Bob Arnold too strolled back for nought against Bearsted CC, a small coincidence of the calendar the Club notes with quiet satisfaction. The Week in Brief Two matches, two ducks, one apiece — a modest yield by the Club's exacting standards, but honest toil against two visiting sides, and proof enough that the art of not scoring remains very much alive at Linton Park. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard, 1953 1. John Ames — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 2. Stan Wratten — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% 3. Michael Morton — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33% The season is young yet, and the wicket at Linton Park has shown no particular favour to anyone this week. The Duck Report — 3rd May, 1953

2 ducks
Week 1 · 3 May 1953
🦆 A fine Sunday at Linton Park, and the eleven welcomed Hunton Wanderers CC to the home ground — a fixture that, for two of our number, will be remembered less for runs scored than for runs decidedly not scored. The art of not scoring was practised with quiet distinction. 1st XI John Ames, sent in at five, played a firm enough looking guard before M Owen had him bowled without troubling the scorers — his first duck's egg of the 1953 season, and the sixth of a career now sixteen innings long. He takes his place at 198th of 627 in the club's long and honourable roll of failure, and does so as a paid-up member of several standing societies of the nought — the Homebody Duck top ten among them, and a fellow traveller in "Quacking Together" with both Roy Clarke and Stan Wratten, which made for interesting company in the pavilion this week. Curiously, on this very date last year, the redoubtable John Thirkell — second on the all-time list with fourteen ducks to his name — was likewise dispatched, against West Farleigh CC. History, it seems, keeps a calendar. Not to be outdone, Stan Wratten followed him back to the pavilion one place down the order, also bowled by M Owen, also for nought. A sticky wicket for the middle order, evidently. This was Wratten's first duck of the season but his sixth in a career of seventy-five innings, lodging him firmly at 19th of 627 on the all-time roll — rarefied air indeed, and he now stands level on career ducks with the venerable W H Fryer of 1867-85 vintage, among other distinguished company. Fittingly, he too shares the on-this-day misfortune with Thirkell's 1952 duck against West Farleigh. Two batsmen, one bowler, one unhappy coincidence of dates. The Week in Brief A single fixture, a brace of ducks, and one bowler — M Owen of Hunton Wanderers — who may fairly claim to have enjoyed his afternoon rather more than the home order did. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family affairs to report this week, the ducks arriving individually rather than in convenient bundles. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Ames — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Stan Wratten — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect start to the season's ignominy for both, and plenty of fixtures yet to come in which either might improve his figures — or, this being the Duck Club, cheerfully fail to. The eleven return to the field next weekend, and the Club awaits its next candidates for the exclusive zero club with its usual warm and undiscriminating welcome.

The Duck Club Bulletin — 28th September 1952

1 duck
Week 23 · 28 Sep 1952
A single entry only graces this week's ledger, but the exclusive zero club never turns away a new subscription, however modest the week's takings. Singles - Ray Tippen, batting at number two in a home fixture against Linton Park CC, was undone by a smart piece of work behind the stumps — caught by John Taylor off the bowling of Gordon Fenner — and made the familiar walk back to the pavilion. It is the first duck's egg of his season and the third of a career now standing at seven-and-twenty innings, placing him 55th of the 625 names inscribed upon the club's roll of dubious distinction. Mr Tippen is also, from a season long since concluded, a member of the Retirement Duck honour board — a gentleman who once bowed out of the game upon a nought — though this week's failure is no such farewell, merely another instalment in a long and honourable acquaintance with the art of not scoring. He now sits level with A Kent, who compiled his own three ducks in a brief season of 1893 and was that year's Duck of the Year, kindred spirits separated by the better part of sixty summers yet united upon the very same tally. The Week in Summary One match, one wicket falling for nought, and the credit goes to Gordon Fenner — a name that will be seen again below, for he numbers among this season's most industrious duck-hunters, having evidently dispensed more trouble with the ball than he has met with the bat. The Duck Club Gazette — 20th to 21st September, 1952

1 duck
Week 22 · 20 Sep 1952 – 21 Sep 1952
🦆 A quiet week upon the Linton Park square, ladies and gentlemen — the eleven, by and large, played the straighter bat this weekend, and the Duck Club's tellers were left twiddling their thumbs through the greater part of two fixtures. But the club never closes its doors entirely, and one gentleman of the 1st XI has this week paid his dues to the exclusive zero club. 1st XI Away in the field against Hayle Party — beg pardon, Hayle Place CC — on the 21st, Richard Harris strode out at number seven and departed caught H Gosling, bowled G Ashby, without troubling the scorers. Not a golden duck, mind — he faced at least the one delivery before submitting to the inevitable, which in this club counts as a plucky show of resistance. This is his second duck of the summer of 1952 and his eleventh in a career now stretching to fifty-one innings, which plants him a very respectable 5th of 625 on the club's all-time roll of dishonour. He joins none other than the venerable Bert Buckoke — a two-time Duck of the Year, no less, in 1928 and 1950 — on exactly eleven career ducks apiece, and there can be no finer company in which to sit becalmed on a duck's egg. The week in summary Two matches played, and but a single duck laid between them — a lean week indeed for the collectors among us, proof if proof were needed that the art of not scoring is not to be rushed. No pairs, no golden ducks, no family affairs to report this time round. The ducks, it seems, took the weekend off — though Mr Harris was good enough to keep the tradition alive single-handed. The Duck Club Gazette — 13th and 14th September 1952

0 ducks
Week 21 · 13 Sep 1952 – 14 Sep 1952
A quiet week at the crease, gentlemen. Two fixtures were played across the weekend, and for once the exclusive zero club found no new candidates for its rolls. Not a single duck's egg was laid, not one batsman was required to make that shortest and most melancholy of walks back to the pavilion. Whether this speaks to a sudden outbreak of straight bats and sound judgement, or merely to the bowlers having an off couple of days, the committee declines to speculate. The art of not scoring, it seems, took its rest this week — though the club has every confidence the ducks will return before the season is out. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's honours remain keenly contested, and this week's inactivity has done nothing to trouble the standings: - John Thirkell — 32 innings, 8 ducks, 25.0% — the season's most reliable attender of the zero club, sitting a comfortable distance clear at the head of affairs - Gordon Fenner — 11 innings, 3 ducks, 27.27% — a fine strike rate of failure, rather better than his rivals manage in their sleep - Bob Arnold — 13 innings, 3 ducks, 23.08% — quietly keeping pace, a plucky knock away from respectability on any given Saturday - Don Hartridge — 22 innings, 3 ducks, 13.64% — the most measured of the leading pack, his ducks arriving with a certain dignified restraint - Gerald Wright — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0% — fewest innings of the five yet half of them ending at nought, a sticky wicket indeed for so brief an acquaintance with the crease Members will note the table stands exactly where it did — a week's grace for the bowlers, no doubt, rather than any lasting reform among the batting order. The eleven return to the field next weekend, and the committee trusts that the ducks, having evaded capture this week, will not make a habit of it. Should any gentleman fancy his chances of a fresh entry to the rolls of dubious distinction, the wicket awaits him. Until then, we remain, as ever, watchful.

THE DUCK CLUB GAZETTE — Saturday, the 6th of September, 1952

0 ducks
Week 20 · 6 Sep 1952
A quiet week, gentlemen, and a rare one at that. Your correspondent has combed the scorebook from Saturday's fixture with the diligence of a man searching for his spectacles, and must report, with no small measure of disappointment, that not a single member of the eleven troubled the umpires for the zero. Every batsman who walked to the crease walked back again having troubled the scorers at least once, however modestly. The exclusive zero club, so often swelled on a Saturday afternoon, gains not one new subscription this week. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming outbreak of application at the crease, a touch of luck on a summer wicket, or merely the bowlers having an off day, history does not record. The art of not scoring, so lovingly cultivated by this club's membership, was for once left unpractised. One suspects it was but a brief truce, and that ambition for the duck's egg will return with the first ball of the next fixture. A single match played, not a duck to show for it — a sticky wicket indeed for the chronicler with nothing to chronicle. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the week ending the 31st of August, 1952

3 ducks
Week 19 · 30 Aug 1952 – 31 Aug 1952
A modest week for the exclusive zero club, but a memorable one, for one member of the 1st XI contrived to visit us twice inside a single weekend. 1st XI John Thirkell opened proceedings on the 30th, away to Hunton Wanderers CC. Sent in at four, he was bowled by R Venner without troubling the scorers — his seventh duck of the season and the thirteenth of a career that stands second in the whole Club register of 625 hopefuls. He was not to be outdone by himself. The very next afternoon, at home to A Levick's XI and promoted to first wicket down, he was bowled again, this time by John Ames, for his eighth of the summer and fourteenth for his career — a grim pair taken across two days and two grounds, the sort of feat that asks a great deal of a man's patience and rather more of his sense of humour. In arriving at fourteen he draws level with the great Frank Sutton, who carried the same tally through a career from 1925 to 1949 and was twice crowned Duck of the Year for his trouble. Thirkell, for his part, already wears this year's Duck of the Year sash, sits proudly among the top ten Lone Ducks, the top ten Homebody Ducks and the top ten Ducks on the Road, and shares the honours board twice over in Quacking Together, with both Bob Arnold and William Buck. H Newport followed him back to the pavilion on the same afternoon, number ten, caught D Latham off the bowling of the ever-busy R Venner, for nought — his second duck of the season and sixth of a career now twenty-four innings long, good enough for seventeenth place in the Club's grim ledger. He sits on precisely the same career total as D Sells, who plied his trade between 1943 and 1944, gathered his own six ducks in fourteen innings, and was Duck of the Year in 1943 besides. Newport is, we might add, a long-standing member of the Retirement Duck club, an honour recording some distant and presumably premature farewell rather than any valediction of his own this week. The week in brief Two fixtures, three ducks, and one gentleman of the 1st XI shouldering two of them single-handed — proof, if proof were wanted, that the art of not scoring is best practised with commitment. R Venner of Hunton Wanderers CC may fairly claim the ball of the week, having accounted for both of Saturday's victims. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Thirkell — 29 innings, 8 ducks, 27.59% - Gordon Fenner — 11 innings, 3 ducks, 27.27% - Bob Arnold — 12 innings, 3 ducks, 25.00% - Don Hartridge — 22 innings, 3 ducks, 13.64% - Gerald Wright — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.00% The season stands at a lively pitch, and with fixtures yet to be played there is every confidence the honours board will find fresh names to add. Members are warmly encouraged to attend the next match, bat straight, and, failing that, to fail with style.

The Duck Club Gazette: 23rd–24th August, 1952

4 ducks
Week 18 · 23 Aug 1952 – 24 Aug 1952
Two fixtures took the field this week, and one of them proved uncommonly generous to the exclusive zero club. Four eggs were laid in a single innings against Charles Arkcoll on the Saturday, while Sunday's match passed the ducks by entirely, to the quiet relief of at least eleven gentlemen. The First Eleven - D Simmons, in at first wicket down, was caught by Humphrey Morris off the bowling of Stan Wratten — a plain enough dismissal, honestly earned. His third career duck in fifteen innings settles him at 48th of 624 on the club's roll of dishonour, drawing him level with the venerable A Kent, whose own trio of noughts were gathered in a single unhappy season back in 1893. - Three places along, Gordon Bugge fell to the very same Stan Wratten, whose afternoon was plainly a rewarding one for all the wrong reasons. This too was his third career duck, and he joins Simmons in keeping curious company with A Kent on that count — two members of the present eleven, fifty-nine years and one bowler apart, arriving at the identical figure by rather different roads. - At number six, Bob Arnold was bowled by Gordon Fenner for his third duck of the season and his seventh of a career that continues to write itself firmly into the honours boards. He remains a proud holder of Ducks in a Row for four consecutive eggs laid without troubling the scorer, and stands paired for perpetuity in Only Two Quacks with Alan Wilkes and in Quacking Together with John Thirkell — evidently a man who prefers not to fall alone. His seventh career duck draws him level with the formidable A Startup, whose own seven noughts between 1868 and 1882 earned three Duck of the Year honours and a place in the five-consecutive company of Ducks in a Row — a target Arnold may yet have designs upon. - Last man in, Gerald Wright was bowled by John Ames for his second duck of the season and his second in a mere four innings played, a strike rate for failure that would give a lesser man pause. He joins A S Day on that same tally of two. In sum, four wickets fell to nought in the one innings on Saturday — Messrs Simmons, Bugge, Arnold and Wright strung from number two clean through to number eleven, wanting only the middle order to make the collapse entire. Gordon Fenner, who appears further down this very report as a leading light of the season's duck-getting, spent his Saturday afternoon adding to the ledger from the bowling end instead, claiming Arnold's wicket while presumably hoping his own name might rest quiet a while longer. The LPCC Duck Report — 10th August 1952

Week 15 · 3 Aug 1952 – 4 Aug 1952
A quiet weekend for the exclusive zero club, but what it lacked in numbers it made up for in doggedness. Two matches, two ducks, and both laid by the same unfortunate hand. 1st XI Number ten Gordon Fenner opened proceedings on the Saturday, stumped by E Webb off the bowling of D Thomas — undone not by rash stroke but by a wandering foot outside his ground. His second duck's egg of the season, and the eighth of a career now stretching to sixty-three innings, which places him level with the venerable George Champion (74 innings, 1886–1912) on exactly eight career ducks — fine company for a fine failure. Curiously, on this very day in 1903, one H G Smith trudged back for nought against the same opposition, 1st Innings Rochester CC, a reminder that the club has been repeating itself for the better part of fifty years. A day was not enough to shake the habit. Sent in last man on the Sunday against Lord Cornwallis's XI, Fenner was bowled by J Larking for his third duck of the season and his ninth of a career that now stands ninth on the all-time list of some six hundred and twenty-three names — drawing level, by neat coincidence, with B Westover's wartime tally of nine. The scorebook records the weekend plainly as a pair, that grimmest of doubles, two ducks laid within twenty-four hours of one another, though happily neither was a golden one — Fenner played himself in each time before the axe fell, triumph through adversity of a very particular kind. It may be noted, for those who like their history layered, that on this same date back in 1869 one W H Fryer made his own duck against Horsmonden CC — the ritual, it seems, is older than the club itself. Members with long memories will also recall that Fenner's brother Joe carries five career ducks of his own — evidently a family with an inherited gift for the art of not scoring. The week in brief Two matches, two ducks, one player — a rare instance of a gentleman keeping the whole week's dismissals entirely to himself. Whether this counts as generosity or simple bad luck is left to the reader's judgement, though the sticky wicket of consistency clearly runs in the Fenner blood. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. A Quiet Afternoon at the Crease A single fixture came and went this week, and — remarkably, gallingly, almost suspiciously — not a single duck was laid to rest. The eleven went about their business with bats held reasonably straight, and the club's fielders of misfortune were left kicking their heels in the pavilion. Even the season's most reliable suppliers of nought could not, on this occasion, be tempted into their old habits. A sticky wicket for the Duck Club itself, one might say — the ducks evaded capture entirely, and went home to lay another day. We shall not pretend to manufacture drama where none occurred. The honours boards stand untroubled, the pairs list unmarked, and no family took the field only to walk back together in shared ignominy. A rare week indeed, and one the club records with a mixture of relief on behalf of the batsmen and mild disappointment on behalf of the chroniclers. The LPCC Duck Club Chronicle — a report for the 10th and 11th of May, 1952

3 ducks
Week 3 · 10 May 1952 – 11 May 1952
Three eggs were laid this week, gentlemen, all by the 1st XI, and all away from home — which will not surprise those who hold that a duck travels better than it bats. Bearsted CC, Saturday the 10th Bob Arnold, sent in at number ten, was undone by the bowling of Snook and returned to the pavilion with nothing to show for his trouble — his first duck's egg of the season, and the fifth of a career that now stands nineteenth of all six hundred and sixteen who have ever failed in this particular art. His name already sits in the book alongside Alan Wilkes and, as it happens, John Thirkell, and he remains a charter member of the noble "Ducks in a Row" — four in unbroken succession, a feat requiring a consistency few possess. He now stands level with Allan Peach, who managed the very same five between 1903 and 1907, proof that the art of not scoring is handed down the generations with scarcely a stroke lost. Folkestone CC, Sunday the 11th John Thirkell, at five, played on to J Court without troubling the scorers — his third duck of a summer already generous with them, and the ninth of a career placing him a lofty seventh on the all-time roll. He carries this season's Duck of the Year honours into the match and remains a fixture of the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens alike — evidently a man equally at ease failing on his own doorstep or abroad. He draws level on nine with B Westover, who played between 1940 and 1945. One place below him, Don Hartridge fell to the very same J Court without scoring — the two gentlemen departing in harness to a bowler plainly in irresistible form that afternoon. It was Hartridge's second duck of the season and his ninth in a career of sixty-six innings, sixth of all time, and he too finds himself keeping company with B Westover on nine. The week in summary Two matches, three ducks, and Folkestone CC may fairly claim the day's honours — J Court removing two LPCC batsmen without a run between them inside a single innings, a sticky wicket indeed for numbers five and six. No golden ducks this week, no pairs and no king pairs — the tail, such as it was, at least troubled the bowlers for a ball or two before departing. The Duck Club Gazette — Week Ending 27th April, 1952

1 duck
Week 1 · 27 Apr 1952
A modest week's business for the exclusive zero club, but modest is not the same as idle, and the honours board has had one fresh entry made upon it. 1st XI John Thirkell went in at number five against Maidstone Trades at home, and there met his end bowled by S. Crump for a duck's egg — the first such visitation of his season, and the seventh in a career now sixty-two innings long. That places him tenth of the six hundred and fourteen who have ever made the walk back for nought, and puts him well in the early running for the Duck of the Year honours of 1952, should the summer continue in this vein. He is, besides, no stranger to distinction of this particular sort: a fixture of both the Lone Duck and Homebody Duck top tens, a name that appears among the Ducks on the Road, and one half of two separate Quacking Together pairings from seasons past, with Bob Arnold and with William Buck respectively. On this occasion, though, he finds company rather further afield — his tally of seven draws him level with the celebrated A Startup, who compiled his own seven ducks in a mere eleven innings between 1868 and 1882, and sits eighth on the all-time list. A comparison spanning the better part of a century, and one Mr Thirkell need not blush at. The week in summary One match, one duck, one gentleman keeping solitary vigil in the nought column. The tail did not so much wag this week as fail to appear at all — a sticky wicket, evidently, though the rest of the eleven seem to have played rather straighter bats than Mr Thirkell managed. Consistency of a very particular kind continues to be his stock in trade. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - John Thirkell — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A leaderboard of one is a leaderboard nonetheless, and Mr Thirkell presently has it entirely to himself, an honour he may not wish to keep for long. The club awaits the next fixture with its usual quiet confidence that further additions to the nought column cannot be far off. Members are reminded that the art of not scoring is one practised by only the bravest, and the Gazette will be watching closely.

0 ducks

🦆🏏 Well now, members. A curious thing has happened, and it happened by not happening at all. Not a single batsman troubled the exclusive zero club this Sunday. Whether this be a triumph of application at the wicket or simply a lull before the storm, this correspondent cannot say. Even Arthur Cradduck, that most dependable of contributors to the season's tally, appears to have played rather too straight a bat for once. Let it be recorded plainly: a week without a duck is a rare thing indeed, and the Committee trusts the Eleven will not make a habit of it. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1951 - 🥇 Arthur Cradduck — 11 innings, 3 ducks, 27.3% - 🥈 J Enfield — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% - 🥉 H Newport — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - Gordon Bugge — 8 innings, 2 ducks, 25.0% - Bob Arnold — 10 innings, 2 ducks, 20.0% Young Enfield's figures bear particular scrutiny — two ducks from two innings is a perfect record of a very particular kind, the art of not scoring practised with unerring consistency. Cradduck remains the season's most prolific contributor to the noble tradition, and one suspects it is only a matter of time before he adds to his tally once more. The next fixture awaits, and with it, no doubt, fresh candidates for the honours board. Members are invited to attend, bat bravely, and — should fortune desert them — do so with the good grace this club has always demanded. The Duck Club will be watching, as ever, with quiet anticipation.

23rd–24th June, 1951 A quiet week on the honours board, but the zero club never quite closes its doors, and one member was admitted all the same. 1st XI At Tovil on the 23rd, John Thirkell came in at four and departed bowled by F. Archer, back to the pavilion with the eleven's fortunes still to be settled by others. By a pleasing trick of the calendar, on this very day in 1906 one Jack Fryer also strolled back for nought, against Leeds Castle CC — a reminder that the art of not scoring has been quietly practised on this ground for the better part of half a century. 1 duck
Week 8 · 16 Jun 1951 – 17 Jun 1951
Two fixtures were played this week, and of the many gentlemen who took guard between them, the club's records show but a single name added to the roll of the dismissed for nought. Hadlow. It is his second duck of the season, and the fourth of a career that now stands at thirteen innings, placing him twenty-third of the six hundred and twelve names who have ever graced this exclusive company. Mr Arnold may take comfort, or possibly alarm, in walking so precisely in such footsteps. The eleven may reflect that a straight bat and a plucky knock were the order of the day elsewhere — Mr Arnold excepted, whose bat on this occasion proved rather less straight than F. Hadlow's aim. The Duck Club Gazette — 9th and 10th June, 1951

3 ducks
Week 7 · 9 Jun 1951 – 10 Jun 1951
A quiet weekend for the eleven at large, but Saturday's meeting with East Peckham & Nettlestead CC proved no friend to the lower order. Three eggs were laid before the innings closed, and the exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers. 1st XI Mr Richard Harris, in at number six, was bowled by K Taylor without so much as troubling the scorebook — a first duck of the season for him, and the sixth of a career now standing at nine-and-twenty innings. He takes his place thirteenth upon the club's roll of nought, a rank he has occupied with the quiet dependability of a man who knows his own game. Curiously, this very date in 1950 saw Joe Fenner make an identical journey back to the pavilion against Lloyds Social Club — the calendar, it seems, keeps its own fixtures. Mr Arthur Cradduck, sent in at ten, was caught by C Dengate off the bowling of R Cox for nought — his second duck of the summer, and the third of a career of fifteen innings, good for thirty-seventh in the all-time table. He carries, this very season, the honour of Duck of the Year 1951, a crown he appears intent on defending with real application. He too shares his date in the history books with Fenner's effort of a year before. Bringing up the rear, Mr H Newport was caught by H Green off R Cox, also for nought — a second duck of his own campaign, and the third of a career of eleven innings, forty-sixth on the board of dubious distinction. From an earlier season he remains enrolled among the Retirement Duck club, that most solemn of honours reserved for those who once bowed out upon a duck, though nothing here suggests he means to repeat the gesture just yet. Like his colleagues above him, his name now stands alongside Fenner's on this same June date. Between them, positions six, ten and eleven accounted for all three ducks of the period — a sticky wicket for the tail, which did not so much wag as fold quietly away. The second fixture of the period passed, by contrast, entirely untroubled by the art of not scoring. The Duck Club Gazette — for the week of 26th to 27th May, 1951

0 ducks
Week 5 · 26 May 1951 – 27 May 1951
A curious thing occurred over the weekend's two fixtures, and it is this: nothing occurred at all. Not a single member of the eleven, on either side of the ropes, contrived to walk back for a duck's egg. The bowlers toiled, the fielders crouched in expectant hush around the bat, and still the naught eluded every hand that reached for it. One almost suspects the batsmen of having taken instruction, though the Club trusts this is merely a passing aberration and not a change of habit. It falls to your correspondent to report, with as much good grace as can be mustered, that the ducks have gone to ground. Two matches played, and not one egg laid. The exclusive zero club, so accustomed to welcoming new and returning members most weekends, must this week close its doors for want of custom. Consistency, it seems, took the week off along with the ducks. We are assured this dry spell is temporary. The wicket will turn sticky again in due course, a promising young batsman will play across a straight one, and the roll of dishonour shall resume its stately growth. Until then, we record the quiet with the same solemnity we would a triumph, for the art of not scoring a duck is, after all, still a species of cricketing accomplishment. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard, 1951 - J Enfield — 2 innings, 2 ducks, a scarcely believable 100 per cent. A batsman playing a lone and unrelenting hand against fortune. - Gordon Bugge — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent. Two eggs from three visits to the crease, and a name the bowlers must relish seeing walk out. - E Goodall — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. A short career thus far, and a naught to show for the whole of it. - Gordon Fenner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. Cut from similar cloth to Mr Goodall, and welcome to keep him company. - E Lockyer — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33 per cent. The most restrained of this company, and rather better for it. The Committee extends its compliments to these five gentlemen, who between them have kept the season's honours board from gathering dust while the rest of the eleven behaved themselves. We trust the coming fixture will furnish fresh candidates for the register, and members are respectfully reminded that a straight bat is no guarantee against a wandering one. Until the next match, the Club remains, as ever, at the batsman's peril.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 19th and 20th May, 1951

1 duck
Week 4 · 19 May 1951 – 20 May 1951
A gentle week, this, for the connoisseurs of the duck's egg. Two fixtures were played between the 19th and the 20th, and for once the bowlers of the district found the Club's collectors uncommonly hard to catch out. Only one nought was recorded in the whole of the period, and it fell, as these things generally do, to a man already well acquainted with the pavilion steps. The First Eleven On the Saturday, against Aylesford Paper Mills CC, Mr Gordon Bugge came to the crease at number five and departed run out, the identity of the fielder responsible left to the scorer's honest shrug of "Unsure." It was a plucky sort of dismissal, if a fruitless one, and it stands as his second duck's egg of the summer and the second of a career now twenty-four innings long. That places him seventieth of the six hundred and twelve names on the Club's roll of dishonour, a position he shares, as it happens, with one A S Day, who between 1944 and 1949 contrived to collect his own pair of noughts in a mere eleven innings. The two now sit level upon the tally of shame, kindred spirits separated by the better part of a decade but united in the art of not scoring. A quiet week all told. One duck's egg laid across two matches is a modest harvest by the Club's usual standards, and whether it speaks of improving technique at the crease or merely indifferent bowling elsewhere, the Committee is not minded to say. The tail, such as it was, wagged undisturbed. A quiet couple of days in the field, but the zero club is never wholly idle, and this week it welcomes one more name to the roll of honour. 1st XI J Enfield strode out at number six against West Farleigh CC on the 5th of May and was undone by George Reffell's bowling, clean bowled without troubling the scorers — though not, mercifully, first ball, so no golden ignominy to report here, merely the ordinary sort. This stands as his first season's duck and the second duck of a career now numbering two innings, placing him 177th of 611 in the club's long and honourable ledger of failure. He joins a considerable and eclectic fellowship on exactly one career duck apiece — from the venerable A Barker, who first achieved the feat between 1885 and 1904, down to the present-day Arthur Cradduck, still active and himself the reigning Duck of the Year for 1951. Fine company for a man just beginning to make his mark on the honours board of the unmarked. The Week in Brief Two fixtures played, and for all the eleven's application at the crease, only the solitary duck to show for it — a week in which the wicket, evidently, favoured application over abandon. West Farleigh CC can claim the credit, George Reffell the wicket, and the Duck Club a single, dignified new entry. No pairs, no family affairs, no golden ducks to speak of this time round — the eggs, it seems, proved harder to lay than usual. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - J Enfield — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect record of imperfection so far this season, and nobody yet to challenge him for it. The table awaits fresh contenders, and with the season young there is ample opportunity yet for others to test their technique against the bowler's guile and their own concentration. The eleven takes the field again shortly, and the Duck Club, ever watchful from the boundary's edge, confidently expects further additions to its distinguished and dubious roster before long.

The Duck Club Gazette — 29th April, 1951

0 ducks
Week 1 · 29 Apr 1951
A quiet week to report, and for once the quiet is not our custom subject. One fixture was played in the period under review, and — remarkable as it may seem to the seasoned student of ignominy — not a single member of either eleven contrived to depart for a duck's egg. Every batsman who walked to the crease this week troubled the scorers, however modestly, before his eventual return to the pavilion. The exclusive zero club, so rarely short of new applicants, finds its books unopened this Sunday. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming outbreak of competence, or merely a sticky wicket that favoured caution over adventure, your correspondent cannot say. We prefer to think of it as the calm before the storm — for a season is young yet on the 29th of April, and history teaches that the ducks are never far from home. The Committee views the development with polite suspicion and awaits next week's card with its usual keen appetite. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard The 1951 table stands empty at the time of writing — no innings yet posted to nought, no name yet entered upon the honours board for the current campaign. A blank page, gentlemen, and a challenge to us all. The season is but a single match old; there is time enough, and eleven need not fear for long. So to the players of Linton Park we say: enjoy the reprieve while it lasts, for the Duck Club's memory is long and its standards forgiving of nothing. The next fixture will surely furnish fresh material for these pages, and we shall be watching every ball with the keenest and least charitable of interest. Until then — play straight, and mind the honours board does not miss you for long.

1950 Season 11 reports

The Duck Club Gazette — the week ending 2nd September, 1950

2 ducks
Week 19 · 2 Sep 1950
A single fixture, a single afternoon at home to Bowaters CC, and yet the 1st XI's eleven found room enough for two duck's eggs to be laid before the same bowler. John Ibbotson, it seems, had their measure entirely. Let the record show it. 1st XI Brian Relf, promoted to first wicket down, was undone by John Ibbotson and sent back to the pavilion without score on what was, by the book, his very first innings for the club. A debut of the purest kind — he joins the Debutante Duck club on the strength of it, and all-time sits a respectable 117th of 610 in the club's long ledger of noughts. He is already down, too, as a paid-up member of the Quack-to-Quack fraternity and the Retirement Duck honours, though we trust those are honours earned in some earlier innings of the club's history and not a hint that we shan't see him again — Sunday next will tell. He shares, besides, a "Quacking Together" entry with Terry Whittaker from some previous rendezvous with nought. Curiously, this very day in 1945 saw D Clark similarly recalled to the pavilion without troubling the scorers against 1st Innings MCPC — five years apart, but evidently kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. Bert Buckoke followed at number eight, likewise accounting for John Ibbotson's figures, and made rather a habit of it — his third duck of the season and his tenth in a career now spanning forty-one innings. Third of all 610 in the club's history is no small distinction, and a man who already carries the Duck of the Year honour from 1928 must fancy his chances of adding the 1950 crown to the mantelpiece before the summer is out. As with his colleague, this same date in 1945 found D Clark similarly dismissed for nought against 1st Innings MCPC — the calendar, it seems, has long memory for these things. A modest week, all told: one match, two ducks, one common executioner in Mr Ibbotson, and the tail — such as it was at eight and three — offering little resistance either side of it. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. Bert Buckoke — 4 innings, 3 ducks, 75.0% 2. E Lockyer — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.3% 3. Joe Fenner — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.2% 4. John --'s Taylor — 11 innings, 2 ducks, 18.2% 5. - Hooper — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% The season's honours board continues to reshuffle itself most satisfyingly. Members are warmly invited to the next fixture, where further plucky knocks, sticky wickets and the occasional duck's egg may confidently be expected.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette

2 ducks
Week 9 · 24 Jun 1950 – 25 Jun 1950
A Chronicle of the Nought — for the week of the 24th to 25th June, 1950 Two matches, two ducks: a modest catch for the Club's watchful eye, but the register of dubious distinction never turns away a subscription however small, and grows steadier for it week upon week. The First Eleven Saturday, at home to Tovil, and Arthur Cradduck came to the crease at number six only to be run out before he had troubled the scorer, the confusion at the striker's end being a matter for the fielding side's conscience rather than his own. It is his first duck of the season, and the first of a career now five innings old — he takes his place 112th of the 607 gentlemen who have gone before him into this exclusive company, and joins - Gaskin, whose own single career nought (from one solitary innings back in 1949) sits him at exactly the same tally. A fine beginning to a collection, Cradduck, and may it grow no further this season. Sunday brought the Desert Rats to Linton Park, and Don Hartridge, holding the same number six berth, was given out leg before to the bowling of W Hall. A first duck of this season for him, though scarcely his first acquaintance with the Club — his fifth career nought from thirty-nine innings sees him installed 14th of all 607 on the all-time roll, a lofty and rather melancholy perch. He draws level on five career ducks with Allan Peach, who compiled his own quintet of noughts between 1903 and 1907 — good company for a man who evidently prefers his straight bat kept for other occasions. The Week in Summary A quiet week by the Club's usual bustling standards: two matches, two ducks, no pairs and no family gatherings to report. The rest of the eleven, it would seem, kept their straight bats about them and left only Cradduck and Hartridge to carry the Club's colours. Consistency, as ever, comes in a great many forms, and not all of them are welcome at the crease. The Duck Gazette — Linton Park, 18th June 1950

1 duck
Week 8 · 18 Jun 1950
Only one soul answered the call of the zero club this week, but a lone duck flaps just as proudly as a flock, and the honours board takes note regardless of numbers. 1st XI, at home to Hambros Bank In strode Joe Fenner at first wicket down, and out he went again lbw to the bowling of F Chapman, without so much as a run to his name. It is his second duck of a summer already turning quackish, and the fifth of a career now thirty-three innings deep — enough to see him settle at 17th of 607 in the club's whole solemn history of the dismissed-for-nought. A Fenner trait, this: his brother Gordon sits on an identical five career ducks, so whatever it is that lands a Fenner back in the pavilion without scoring, it does appear to run in the blood. And by a pleasant quirk of the calendar, on this very day in 1949 John Thirkell was performing precisely the same trick against Bowaters CC — a small fraternity of the nought, scattered across the years but united in feeling. The week in brief One match, one duck, one Fenner walking back with his straight bat unrewarded. A quiet week for the club by its own modest standards, though quiet weeks have a habit of being followed by louder ones. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the week of the 10th to 12th of June, 1950

3 ducks
Week 7 · 10 Jun 1950 – 12 Jun 1950
Three fixtures were contested this week, and though two of them passed with every egg intact, the First Eleven's outing at Lloyds Social Club furnished the exclusive zero club with three fresh entries in a single sorry innings. 1st XI, away to Lloyds Social Club, 10th June Joe Fenner, promoted to first wicket down, was bowled by J. Stevens for a duck's egg — his first of the summer, and the fourth of a career now two-and-thirty innings deep, good enough for 28th place of all 606 names on the club's roll of dishonour. He keeps company with C. Amies, who played between 1867 and 1870 and sits on the very same tally of four, proof that the art of not scoring has never gone out of fashion. Cricketing kinship runs in the family too — his brother Gordon carries five career ducks of his own, so the Fenners are building quite the joint estate in nought. Down at number eight, Bert Buckoke was run out without troubling the scorers — his first duck of the season, and the eighth of an illustrious career, illustrious in this particular currency at any rate, leaving him fifth of all 606 in the club's history. A two-time Duck of the Year, in 1928 and again this very season of 1950, Buckoke wears his ignominy like a badge of office. George Champion, who turned out between 1886 and 1912 and gathered his own eight ducks across seventy-four innings, keeps him honest company on the same career total. At number ten, E. Lockyer departed caught by S. Jarrett off the bowling of J. Ibbotson — his second duck of the season, and remarkably his second career duck too, in only five innings played, a rate of failure that ought to have the selectors reaching for the smelling salts. That places him 63rd of all 606, level on career ducks with A. S. Day, who managed the same modest tally between 1944 and 1949 in eleven innings. The week in summary Three matches, three ducks, all laid in the one basket at Lloyds Social Club — the other two fixtures passed off without a single egg to report, which speaks either well of the batting or poorly of the bowling, depending on one's allegiance. A middle-order man, a lower-order man and a tail-ender all present at the same funeral suggests the Lloyds attack had the measure of the innings from top to bottom. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. 5 ducks

A record of the Eleven's dealings with nought, 27th–29th May 1950 Three fixtures fell to the Eleven this week, and five gentlemen returned to the pavilion without troubling the scorer — a fine haul for the exclusive zero club, that place of dubious distinction where consistency of a very particular kind is its own reward. 1st XI Opening the account against Hunton Wanderers CC on the 27th, John --'s Taylor was undone lbw to R Moon — his first duck's egg of the season and the first of his career in seven innings, placing him 183rd of 603 on the club's long roll of failure. He joins - Gaskin, of the 1949 season, level on a tally of exactly one. A duck on debut is a bittersweet welcome, but Hooper's name now sits, 95th of 603, in the Debutante Duck gallery, keeping company with the One and Done roll for 1950 and the Retirement Duck honours board, though the Eleven trusts he shall have rather more to say for himself before any retirement is confirmed. Like Taylor, he sits level with - Gaskin on a single career duck. No pairs and no family affairs to report this week, which the Eleven considers, on balance, a mercy. A lean week for the connoisseurs of nought, two fixtures played and but a single egg laid between them. Still, quality over quantity, as any true student of the art of not scoring will tell you. The First Eleven Mr John Thirkell, at four in the order and away from home against Charles Arkcoll's eleven, was undone in the accustomed fashion — caught Humphrey Morris, bowled Stan Wratten — and trudged back to the pavilion to add his name to the season's roll of honour. It is his first duck's egg of the 1950 season, and the third of a career now twenty-four innings long, which plants him a solid 44th of 602 in the club's all-time list of dubious distinction. A long-serving member of several standing companies besides — the Ducks on the Road top ten, the Homebody Duck top ten, and the Lone Duck top ten among them — Mr Thirkell has twice before shared the ignominy in company, once with Mr Bob Arnold and once with Mr William Buck, though neither companion troubled the scorers alongside him on this occasion. He joins, on exactly three career ducks apiece, the name of A Kent, who managed the same tally for the 1893 eleven and was crowned that year's Duck of the Year for his trouble — kindred spirits fifty-seven years apart, bound by the same modest total. In Summary One duck, two matches, and precious little else to report — the ducks, it seems, mostly evaded the net this week. A quiet round for the club's least-wanted trophy, but the season is young yet. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - D Simmons — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - John Thirkell — 5 innings, 1 duck, 20% The eleven takes the field again presently, and the Duck Club's scouts will be watching every departing batsman with their usual keen and faintly ghoulish interest. THE LPCC DUCK CLUB GAZETTE — 13th to 14th May, 1950

1 duck
Week 3 · 13 May 1950 – 14 May 1950
A quiet week upon the whole, with only two fixtures played and but a single name added to the register — though a solitary duck, dear reader, is no less an occasion for ceremony than a dozen. 1st XI At Bearsted, on the 13th, D Simmons strode to the crease at number seven and departed for nought, run out by a fielder whose identity the scorebook, in its wisdom, declined to record — "Unsure" being, on reflection, rather a fitting epitaph for the whole sorry business. This is the first duck's egg of the season for Simmons, and the second of a career now standing at six innings — a rate of failure that places him a very respectable 59th of 601 in the club's long and honourable roll of the dismissed. Not yet a name for the honours boards, but a promising apprenticeship in the art of not scoring is plainly under way. Curiously, on this very day in 1940 — a full decade before Simmons's own contribution — B Westover likewise trudged back for nought, against the George Fenner XI, one of nine such innings that yet sees Westover installed in fourth place of all time. The zero club, it seems, keeps its calendar as faithfully as its ledger. The Week in Summary One duck from two matches is a slim harvest by the Club's usual generous standards — the eleven, on the whole, appear to have played rather too straight a bat this week for our purposes. Still, where Bearsted is concerned, Simmons alone flew the flag for failure, and flew it with a certain understated dignity. No pairs, no families of ducks, no golden eggs to report — merely one plucky, if fruitless, contribution to the great tradition. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - D Simmons — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, an easy table to top, and Simmons finds himself there by simple virtue of being the only contender who troubled the scorers this week — in the wrong direction. Whether he can be caught, or indeed whether he shall wish to be, remains a question for the fixtures ahead. The season is young yet, and the wicket at the far end has a way of producing further candidates. Members are warmly encouraged to keep their bats straight — or, in the finer traditions of this Club, resolutely otherwise — for the next match promises the eleven every opportunity to add to this modest register.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Tuesday, the 29th of April, 1950

0 ducks
Week 1 · 29 Apr 1950
A quiet week to report, and for once the quiet is the story. The eleven took the field on Saturday last, and by close of play not a single member of the batting order had contrived to depart for nought. A clean sheet. A whitewash of the wrong sort, from the Duck Club's point of view. We confess to a certain flatness in the clubhouse at this news. The exclusive zero club thrives on adversity nobly borne, and this week adversity simply declined to show up. Bats were played straight, singles were taken where ducks might once have been laid, and the tail — usually so reliable a source of comedy — wagged its way to respectable scores instead of the pavilion steps. One rather suspects the wicket was too kind for its own good. Still, the committee takes the long view. A team cannot manufacture failure to order, however much tradition might wish it, and a season is a long business with many a sticky wicket yet to come. The ducks have merely gone to ground this week, not retired from the field altogether, and past form suggests they will be back among us directly. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard Nothing yet to report here either — the season's honours board stands empty of any fresh entries, awaiting its first candidate for 1950. A blank ledger is a rare sight in these parts, and we shall watch with interest to see whose name is first to grace it. We look ahead, then, to the next fixture with the club's usual mixture of hope and mild anticipation of disaster. Someone, somewhere, is surely due a duck's egg before the season is very much older — and when he finds it, this gazette shall be first to mark the occasion with the ceremony it deserves. Until then, the members of the Duck Club remain, as ever, in cheerful reserve.

1 duck

A quiet couple of days for the eleven, but the honours board never truly rests — one gentleman did make his way back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer, and here his innings, such as it was, is recorded for posterity. 1st XI Down at home against British Legion Boughton Monchelsea on the 18th, in strode Gordon Fenner at number nine, and out he went too, bowled by J Genn, though not first ball — a duck earned with at least a modicum of application, if not of runs. This was his fifth career duck in forty-two innings, placing him a respectable 14th of 599 in the club's ledger of shame, a position he holds with the quiet dignity of a man who has been here before and shall doubtless be here again. He now joins the estimable Allan Peach, who plied his trade for the club between 1903 and 1907, on exactly five career ducks apiece — kindred spirits separated by four and a half decades but united in the art of not scoring. Those keeping half an eye on family form may note his brother Joe Fenner already carries three ducks of his own, so the appetite for nought appears to run in the blood. The Week in Brief Two matches played, and but a single duck's egg laid between them — the ducks, on the whole, evaded capture this week, content to leave Mr Fenner to fly the flag alone. Whether this reflects a sudden outbreak of watchfulness at the crease, or simply a want of opportunity, the Duck Club declines to speculate. The eleven take the field again shortly, and history suggests the honours board will not stay quiet for long — do come along and see who joins it next.

Down at Maidstone the eleven found the going sticky, and the away trip against Maidstone YMCA CC yielded not one but four fresh entries for the honours board of dubious distinction. He now sits level on career ducks with the venerable A Startup, whose seven noughts between 1868 and 1882 earned him three separate Duck of the Year titles and a place in the Ducks in a Row club — distinguished company for a distinguished failure. At number ten, C Horton went lbw to - Hooper, his 2nd duck of the season and, remarkably, his 2nd career duck from only 3 innings — a rate of attrition that has already earned him the Duck of the Year 1949 board and, more strikingly still, the Runaway Duck honour for an entire season without troubling the scoreboard. 58th of 598 all time and rising fast — one suspects the club secretary is keeping a weather eye on him for the season's top honours. Last man in, H Newport, went lbw to T- Hendley's bowling for his 1st career duck in 5 innings, a modest addition that nonetheless places him 164th of 598 and, by virtue of standing membership, alongside the Retirement Duck club — a board reserved for those whose final innings closed on a duck, though nothing in today's proceedings suggests Newport is bound for the exit just yet. The Week in Brief A single fixture, four ducks, and the whole quartet falling to catches, bowled and leg-before dismissals without a run between them — a clean sweep for the bowlers and a testing afternoon for the eleven. No pairs and no family affairs to report this week, though with Horton and Buckoke both compiling their second duck of the season inside one innings apiece, the exclusive zero club shows no sign of admitting fewer members before autumn draws in. 3 ducks

A modest but not unremarkable weekend for the Eleven, in which the tail end of the innings against East Peckham & Nettlestead CC surrendered three wickets for three duck's eggs, each duly inscribed into the club's book of dubious distinction. 1st XI — v East Peckham & Nettlestead CC (home, 4th September) - P- Martin, sent in at number nine, contrived the rare and faintly comic feat of falling hit wicket b J Walker — undone, it would seem, by his own footwork rather than the bowler's craft. It is his first duck of the season, his first in two innings for the club, and lifts him to 112th of 597 on the all-time list. It does his claim to Duck of the Year 1949 no harm whatsoever, and he is shaping into a strong contender for the Runaway Duck honour — a whole season without a run — should fortune not soon turn his way. He too finds himself level with Gaskin on career ducks, the newest recruit setting rather a brisk pace for them both. - Last man - Gaskin completed the rout, bowled by W Saunders, a duck's egg on his very first appearance for the club. He joins the shade of - Mill upon the honours board, whose own solitary duck stood unaccompanied since 1943 until being joined this very afternoon. With three wickets down for nothing added, the tail declined to wag at all, and the innings closed rather sooner than the Eleven would have wished. A single fixture accounted for the whole of this week's harvest of three — the second match of the period passed by, mercifully, without addition to the book. A modest tally by the club's own exacting standards, though Martin's manner of dismissal, out by his own hand rather than the bowler's, must be a strong candidate for the season's most inventive. At Hunton Wanderers on the Saturday, Richard Harris was given out lbw to J Ludden, his bat proving more ornamental than useful on the day. Peter Weedon, at eight, fell identically to Simmons, his second career duck in nine innings and 79th on the all time list, a name long since entered upon the club's roll of Retirement Ducks from a farewell some seasons past. A week, then, in which the art of not scoring was pursued with real dedication — six ducks in three matches, four of them arriving together at Town Malling, rather like buses. The Duck Club Gazette — 6th and 7th August, 1949

3 ducks
Week 10 · 6 Aug 1949 – 7 Aug 1949
A trying Saturday for the lower order down at Sharps Kreemy Works, where the zero club welcomed three new subscriptions in the space of a single innings. The 1st XI's tail did not so much wag as fall clean off. 1st XI — away to Sharps Kreemy Works, 6th August - P Clark (No. 8) departed caught Lamb, bowled Roche, without opening his account — not a golden duck, he had at least troubled the bowler before troubling the scorebook not at all. It is the 1st of the season for him and the 1st of his career in five innings, a debut of the least welcome kind, placing him 192nd of 589 in the club's long ledger of noughts. He now keeps company with a wide and distinguished field sitting on exactly one career duck apiece, among them the estimable - Mill of 1943, whose solitary innings and solitary duck have stood unchallenged for six years. - M- Hughes (No. 9), turning out for the very first time, marked his arrival in the most traditional fashion — caught Gray, bowled Knell, for nought. A plucky start to a career it was not, though he too avoided the golden duck's particular disgrace, having faced enough of an over to be dismissed rather than simply removed. First innings, first duck, and straight in at 184th of 589 on the all-time list — a debut the club will remember rather more fondly than the player will. Like Clark before him this same afternoon, he joins the modest fraternity of one-career-duck men alongside - Mill of 1943. - M- Harden (No. 10), last man in, went the same way as his colleagues — caught Hayman, bowled Roche, for a duck's egg of his own. His second career innings and his first career duck, which lands him 183rd of 589, a whisker ahead of young Hughes on the ignominious table. He, too, finds himself level with - Mill on a single career duck, making it three of the eleven drawing that particular comparison in one unhappy afternoon. The week in summary Two fixtures were played over the weekend, and it was the Saturday trip to Sharps Kreemy Works alone that yielded the club's harvest — three ducks in the space of three wickets, numbers eight, nine and ten falling in short order as the innings ran out of partners rather more than it ran out of overs. Sunday's fixture, by contrast, passed without a single addition to the register, for which small mercy the committee is grateful. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. John Thirkell — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0% 2. John Yeo — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% 3. M- Hughes — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% 4. M- Harden — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% 5. P Clark — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.3% The committee looks forward, with its usual mixture of dread and delight, to the next fixture, when the eleven will doubtless offer up fresh candidates for this most exclusive of clubs. 2 ducks
Week 11 · 25 Jul 1948
A quiet Sunday at Linton Park, and yet the eleven found room, as ever, for two additions to the club's most curious ledger. West Farleigh CC provided the opposition, and Kent hospitality, it must be said, extended rather too generously toward wickets taken. The 1st XI Mr Richard Harris, sent in at number six, played what one hopes was a straight enough bat before being taken by Harry Webb off the bowling of George Reffell. Not a first-ball departure, this — he troubled the crease a while before troubling nobody's figures — but a duck's egg all the same, his first of the season and the third of a career now numbering nine innings, which places him a respectable forty-fifth of the five hundred and seventy-six gentlemen who have ever walked back for nought at this ground. Curiously, this very date in 1925 saw a Mr W Turner similarly dismissed for a duck, against Bearsted CC of all sides — history, it seems, is fond of its small rhymes. Then came Mr C Newman, in at number ten, bowled by G Page without troubling the scorebook at all. A maiden appearance for the club, and what a maiden appearance — his very first innings yielding his very first duck, which is either the unluckiest or the most efficient way to begin a cricketing career, depending on one's temperament. He is welcomed forthwith into the club's roll of honour, sitting joint one hundred and eleventh of five hundred and seventy-six on debut alone. He keeps notable company on the calendar too: this same 25th of July, back in 1925, one W Turner also strolled back for nought against Bearsted CC, a full twenty-three summers before Mr Newman's own introduction to the art of not scoring. The Week in Brief One match, two ducks, both from the home eleven's middle and late order against West Farleigh — a modest bag by the club's standards, but every egg counts toward the season's basket, and a debutant duck is always worth a raised eyebrow in the pavilion. The Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Sessions — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C Newman — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Richard Harris — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A tightly-fought summit this season, with the field level at a perfect record of failure. The Duck Gazette — Saturday, 15th May, 1948

1 duck
Week 1 · 15 May 1948
A single entry finds its way into the book this week, but a rare and memorable one for all that — a maiden appearance settled in the most economical fashion imaginable. 1st XI Away from home comforts and into the record books went Sessions, sent in first wicket down against Herne Bay CC and undone by the bowling of Gv Gethin before he could trouble the scorebook. A plucky attempt at a straight bat, no doubt, but the wicket proved sticky enough to see him back to the pavilion without a run to his name. What makes the occasion noteworthy is that this was no seasoned campaigner's misfortune but his very first innings for the club — a debut duck, and there can be few less auspicious ways to begin a cricketing career, nor few more splendid ways to begin a duck-hunting one. He enters the exclusive zero club at the first time of asking, his maiden knock now his maiden nought, career figures reading one innings, one duck, and a seat at number 87 of 571 on the all-time roll of honour. Early in the season it may be, but for now Sessions stands quite alone atop the ledger for Duck of the Year 1948 — a lead he holds only by virtue of being first through the gate, and one the rest of the eleven will no doubt be keen to contest before the summer is out. A pleasant curiosity of the calendar attends the occasion: on this very day in 1943, Gordon Fenner — who between 1941 and 1947 assembled four such noughts of his own, good enough for 24th of 571 on the all-time list — likewise made his way back to the pavilion without scoring, against Maidstone Fire Service. Certain dates, it would seem, carry a duck-shaped destiny all their own. The Week in Summary One match, one duck — a quiet week by the Club's usual standards, but quality over quantity has always been the Duck Club's watchword, and a debutant's egg is worth more column space than a dozen ordinary noughts from the regulars. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Sessions — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% The book stands open and the ink is barely dry. Members are warmly reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for further additions to this most select of registers — may the bowling be hostile and the concentration lapse where it matters most.

0 ducks

A single fixture took the field this week, and — remarkable as it may seem to the connoisseur of the duck's egg — not one batsman among either eleven contrived to be dismissed for nought. The bowlers, for all their guile, went home with their appeals unanswered on this particular front, and the exclusive zero club must report, with no small disappointment, that its books remain unopened for the period. It is not for want of trying, one assumes. Every innings carries its share of jittery starts and playing-and-missing, yet on this occasion the tail wagged, the middle order held firm, and even the customary nervous newcomer seems to have got off the mark. A sticky wicket, evidently, was navigated by all with rather more application than the club prefers. We shall not pretend to be anything but a little put out. The pursuit of the duck's egg is, after all, the purest sport this club knows, and a blank week denies us both ceremony and comedy alike. Still, patience is a virtue long practised on the boundary's edge, and the season is young yet. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's roll of dishonour has, as yet, no entries to publish. Members are reminded that the game continues, and with it the ever-present hazard of the first ball, the leaving stroke gone astray, and the confident forward defensive that meets rather more swing than bargained for. The next fixture will surely furnish the club with fresh material, and your correspondent awaits it with quiet and entirely unsporting optimism.

A chastening afternoon at Gore Court, where the 1st XI's card was inked no fewer than five times with the duck's egg, and the home attack took what can only be called a proprietary interest in the business. 1st XI, away to Gore Court CC Bert Pierce, in at four, played on to Brian French — his first duck of the season and the second of an eleven-innings career, good enough for 53rd of the 559 names on the all-time roll. Pierce carries the Retirement Duck honour on his card, a distinction we trust describes some distant future rather than this one. A twice-crowned Duck of the Year, 1940 and now 1946 besides, Sutton wears his nought with the quiet authority of a man who has made a study of it. Mitchell's 1906 shade walked with him too. Bert Buckoke followed at seven, bowled by the same Whibley, for a fifth career duck and thirteenth of 559 — himself a Duck of the Year, 1928 vintage, and evidently still game for the honour. Mitchell, 1906, once more for company. At eight, N Young opened his innings account, such as it was, with a debut duck — bowled by Whibley for the third time that innings, and straight in at 178th of 559. A first taste of the club's particular hospitality, and, as it happens, on the same calendar date Mitchell once knew in 1906. Stuart Thirkell, in at nine, was bowled by Alec E Allsworth for a debut duck of his own, taking 197th place of 559 — two new members inducted in the one innings, a rare and generous double for the membership secretary. Mitchell's 1906 duck falls on this same date yet again. The week in summary Five ducks from one match is a harvest by any reckoning, and three of them fell to Whibley's bowling alone — the man might fairly be issued honorary membership himself. Two debuts, one duck's-egg apiece, and the eleven's lower order left looking distinctly threadbare by the close. The ducks, we are confident, are merely resting — and your correspondent stands ready, pen in hand, for their inevitable return to the square.
