The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 8th and 9th September, 1945

4 ducks
Week 19 · 8 Sep 1945 – 9 Sep 1945
A brace of fixtures graced the closing days of summer, and the zero club welcomed four new entries to its rolls — every one of them, as it happens, procured in the single encounter with the 8th Sherwood Foresters. The Sunday match passed, most unusually, without a single addition. 1st XI — v 8th Sherwood Foresters (home, 8th September) - Stan Wratten, promoted to first wicket down, was smartly taken by Heath off Fisher's bowling — his third career duck in six-and-thirty innings, and the 45th man of 551 to grace the club's long and dubious roll. He now stands level with A Kent, of the 1893 vintage, both gentlemen holding exactly three apiece across the decades. A veteran of the "Quacking Together" honour alongside John Ames, though that particular double stayed politely dormant this week. - Jimmy Jameson came and went two places later, bowled by Fisher for his second duck of the season and fifth of an increasingly distinguished career in noughts — 28 innings played, and already installed as Duck of the Year for 1945, a crown he shows no sign of relinquishing. He joins Allan Peach, of the Edwardian era, on five career ducks apiece, and sits 14th of 551 in the club's gloomy ledger. Two blanks from four innings this season is form of a very particular kind. - J Jerman, at number six, fell to Carr for his maiden career duck — a solitary blemish on four innings otherwise played with a straight bat. He joins the shade of "- Mill", of 1943, on one apiece, and enters the book at 160th of 551. - Peter Weedon, further down the order, likewise succumbed to Carr, his first career duck from just two innings, drawing level with "- Mill" once more. Weedon is already a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck honour from some earlier and more distant chapter of his cricketing days — the club's records, as ever, running back rather further than any single afternoon. The week in summary Four ducks in two matches, the whole crop harvested in one innings, with Carr and Fisher sharing the bowling honours two apiece on what was evidently a sticky proposition for the home order. Sunday, mercifully or otherwise, offered the zero club nothing at all to report. A Chronicle of the Nought — 5th September, 1943 A single fixture was played this week, and — remarkable to relate — not one soul among either eleven was persuaded back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer. The zero club, so often busy with new subscriptions, finds its ledger unchanged this week. Whether this speaks of straight bats generally applied, or merely of the bowling having an off day, the Gazette shall not speculate. The art of not scoring, it seems, was set aside in favour of the plainer art of scoring something. We shall not pretend to mourn overlong. A quiet week for the duck's egg is no bad thing, and the exclusive zero club can certainly bear one Saturday's want of new members. Let it be recorded, for the curious, that the ducks were abroad somewhere in Kent that afternoon, merely not at Linton Park. Herbert Sunley and Frank Sutton continue their steady, patient accumulation of noughts across a long season, proof that the duck's egg is a dish best served often. W Bunting brings up the rear of this select company, though with the season yet to run its course there is time enough for him to close the gap, should fortune or the bowling favour him. The Gazette must record, too, that a quiet week is rarely a lasting one. History and the LPCC batting order both suggest the ducks are merely gathering themselves for the next appointment. 31st July – 2nd August, 1943 Three fixtures, five ducks laid down for the record — the honours board grows heavier by the week. 1st XI At home to the RAF on the 31st, Herbert Rayner played on to Jerman for nought, his second duck of the season and the fourth of a career now stretching to forty-six innings, the twenty-first most prolific egg-layer among our five hundred and twenty-five. On this very day in 1895, Ernest Cruttenden was likewise trudging back against Headcorn CC, proof that late July has always had a taste for feathers. Down at number ten in that same innings, B Westover fell to the same bowler for the same reward, his fourth duck of the summer and eighth of a career now standing fourth in the club's entire history, a distinction few would covet and fewer still could match. Cruttenden's shade of 1895 walked beside him to the pavilion once more. Against the 53rd Divisional Signals on the 1st, opener W Bunting was caught behind off Skilton without troubling the scorers, his third duck of the season and his career total besides, the forty-fourth name on the roll. The Reverend F A Leveson-Gower kept him company across the decades, having done precisely the same against Maidstone Conservative Club in 1910. At the other end of that innings, D Sells was bowled by Skilton for his fifth duck of the season, and remarkably his fifth in only eight innings played, a rate of failure so pure it already carries him to this season's Duck of the Year, with the Ducks in a Row now standing at four in succession. Eleventh of all who have ever turned out for the club, and young yet in his cricketing life. The good Reverend's 1910 shade attended this dismissal too. Completing the week's misfortune, against H Murray's XI on the 2nd, Bert Pierce was bowled by Moore for his very first duck, entering the list at ninety-eighth of all comers. He joins, on the honours board if not yet in practice, the ranks of the Retirement Duck club, a distinction earned by others' farewells, and no cause yet to fear for Bert's continued service with the bat. On this day in 1882, W H Fryer suffered similarly against Boxley CC. The Week in Brief Five ducks across three matches, and the tail seemed rather fonder of the pavilion steps than the crease — three of the week's five fell at number ten or below. The Signals match alone furnished two, Skilton claiming both with commendable economy. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. D Sells — 8 innings, 5 ducks, 62.5% 2. Herbert Sunley — 13 innings, 5 ducks, 38.46% 3. B Westover — 10 innings, 4 ducks, 40.0% 4. Frank Sutton — 16 innings, 4 ducks, 25.0% 5. W Bunting — 11 innings, 3 ducks, 27.27% The eleven takes the field again before long, and the Gazette has little doubt the list above will want updating. Members are cordially invited to the next fixture, if only to see who joins it.

The Duck Club Gazette — a week of note, 24th–25th July 1943

4 ducks
Week 11 · 24 Jul 1943 – 25 Jul 1943
🦆 A wet ball and a straighter one from the Home Guard bowlers, and the exclusive zero club welcomes four new subscriptions this week. The tail did not so much wag as fall clean off, and the honours board creaks under fresh dubious distinction. 1st XI Saturday against Tovil brought Dennis Smith to the crease at number eight, only to depart bowled by Alexander for his 1st duck of the season, the 3rd of an accomplished career now standing 32nd of 525 all-time. Curiously, on this very day in 1909 one Charles Wycherley also trudged home for nought, against Barming Asylum CC of all opponents — some dates simply attract the duck's egg. Sunday's fixture against Home Guard D Company was a sticky wicket indeed, claiming three wickets for nothing at all. Gordon Fenner, caught by Sergeant Smith off X Elwell, notched his 2nd duck of the season and his 2nd of the career — 55th of 525 on the all-time roll, and a chip off a duck-shaped block, his sibling Joe Fenner carrying three career noughts of his own. Frank Sutton followed, bowled by L Wynn, for his 4th duck of the season — a plucky sequence of failure that brings his career total to 11, good enough (or bad enough) for 2nd of 525 all-time, and a returning name on the Duck of the Year 1940 board. And D Sells completed the rout, lbw to Wynn, for his 4th duck of the season and, remarkably, his 4th career duck from a mere seven innings — 17th of 525 all-time, freshly minted onto both the Duck of the Year 1943 board and the rare Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) honour, a run of futility so unbroken it deserves its own regimental colours. All three Sunday duckers share their on-this-day cousin in the 1925 vintage, when W Turner also fell without scoring against Bearsted CC. The week in summary Four ducks in two matches — a quiet week by the standards of a club that treasures its failures, but a concentrated one, with three of the four falling in a single innings against the Home Guard. The art of not scoring was practised with particular conviction on Sunday. The First Eleven Against the Royal Army Service Corps at home on the 17th, two of the Eleven found the scorebook thoroughly unaccommodating. Both he and Sunley, on the 18th, kept company with one J Danells, who managed the very same trick in 1883 against the Maidstone Junior Liberal Association. The Week in Summary Two matches, four ducks, and Herbert Sunley generous enough to supply half the total himself, a pair spread neatly across successive afternoons. Neither the Corps nor the Home Guard troubled themselves unduly, and the tail, such as there was of it, wagged only feebly against both. 🦆 The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 11th July 1943 🦆

4 ducks
Week 9 · 11 Jul 1943
A Report on the Week's Additions to the Exclusive Zero Club The Royal Artillery Wing paid a visit to the ground on Sunday, and while the eleven acquitted themselves with the usual mixture of pluck and misfortune, four of the home side's number found the art of not scoring rather too easy for comfort. A grave day for the scorebook, and a fine one for the Club. 1st XI Opening the innings and, alas, opening the Club's account for the day, Stan Wratten was taken by Steel off the bowling of Tiplady without so much as troubling the scorers 🍩. His second duck's egg of the season and the second of his career in a dozen visits to the crease — he now stands 77th of 525 in the club's long and dishonourable roll, and remains, by virtue of past company, a paid-up member of Quacking Together with John Ames. He joins the venerable Arthur Ash, of the 1934–41 vintage, in sitting on exactly two career ducks apiece — kindred spirits level on noughts, though separated by the better part of a decade. At number two, George Winter was run out in circumstances the scorer records only as "Unsure" — a fitting epitaph for a first career duck, his maiden entry into the Club after five innings of otherwise blameless service. He arrives at position 135 of 525 all-time, and finds instant company with the newly-minted "- Mill", also on a solitary duck this very season. Down at number nine, W Bunting played on to Tiplady via a catch to Phillips 0️⃣, his first career duck in ten innings — a long and patient wait for infamy, now rewarded, and he takes his place at 194th of 525. And last man in, Gordon Larking, went the way of so many number elevens before him — trapped leg-before to Tiplady for his first career duck in only three innings 🏏. He joins the same crowded ledger as Winter and Bunting on one apiece, and enters the all-time list at 137th of 525. Tiplady, it must be said, had rather a field day — three of the four ducks bear his name in the wicket column, a spell the Club salutes with considerably more enthusiasm than the batting side will muster. Week in Summary Four ducks from a single fixture is a solid week's work by the Club's standards — none of them golden, all falling to a straight ball, a sharp bit of fielding, or the umpire's raised finger. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family affairs to report this time; simply four honest men undone by four honest deliveries. A sticky wicket, by the look of it, for anyone batting first wicket down through to last. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard — 1943 - B Westover — 6 innings, 3 ducks, 50.0% - Herbert Sunley — 9 innings, 3 ducks, 33.33% - Frank Sutton — 10 innings, 3 ducks, 30.0% - D Sells — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - L Ricketts — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% The Club extends its compliments to all four gentlemen above, and looks forward, with its usual mixture of dread and delight, to whatever the next fixture may add to the honours board. 4 ducks

Two fixtures, four eggs laid, and the exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers with the usual mixture of ceremony and sympathy. The First Eleven At Bearsted CC on the Saturday, the last pair went in quick succession to the bowling of W E Weber, each man contributing nothing but his wicket. N- Parr, at number ten, was bowled for his very first innings in senior colours — a debut duck's egg, no less, and one that sets him down at 160th of 510 in the club's long and undistinguished roll. He joins A Barker, of the 1885 to 1904 vintage, on precisely one career duck apiece — Barker, it might be noted, once carried off the Duck of the Year honour in 1885, so N- Parr keeps distinguished if unfortunate company. B Westover followed him back to the pavilion at number eleven, bowled by the same hand — a tidy piece of bowling by Weber, and a tidier collapse by the Eleven. This was Westover's sixth career duck in seventeen innings, and his second of the season already, which places him a lofty sixth of 510 on the all-time list — level with F Danells, who managed the same feat across eighteen innings between 1881 and 1904. The Sunday brought the Royal Artillery Wing 48 to the home ground, and the home side found the art of not scoring just as readily as the visitors had. K- Symonds, first wicket down at number three, was leg-before to a Dillon delivery for nought — his maiden innings for the club, and thus a debut duck to match Parr's, good enough for 151st of 510 on the roll and the same one-duck company of A Barker. Later, at number six, Herbert Sunley was caught by Peach off the bowling of Black, his first duck in three innings for the club, ranking 136th of 510 — a paid-up member of the same one-duck fraternity, though Sunley arrives an established hand rather than a new face. The Week in Brief Four ducks from two matches is a fair week's work for the club's recruiting officer, and the Saturday's last-wicket pairing at Bearsted — both men undone by W E Weber within the same passage of play — will not be forgotten quickly by whoever keeps the Eleven's batting averages. No pairs and no family affairs to report this week, just four honest eggs laid in the ordinary course of cricket. The Duck Gazette — a chronicle for the 15th and 16th of May, 1943

3 ducks
Week 1 · 15 May 1943 – 16 May 1943
A brief innings this week for the Zero Club's recruiting sergeant — three eggs laid across two fixtures, each a tale of its own in the ancient art of not scoring. The First Eleven Saturday's engagement against the Maidstone Fire Service saw the middle and late order do their level best to douse the innings before it caught light. Gordon Fenner, promoted to number eight, was bowled by Andrews for a duck — his first blob of the summer and the first of his career in five innings, placing him 129th of 508 in the club's long and honourable roll of failure. He is not alone in the family trade, either — his sibling Joe Fenner carries three career ducks of his own, so a certain talent for ignominy plainly runs in the blood. Gordon keeps distinguished company besides: A Barker, who turned out for the club between 1885 and 1904 and was crowned Duck of the Year in 1885, sits on precisely the same solitary career duck. One place further down the order, B Westover followed him back to the pavilion, bowled by Porter without troubling the scorers. It was the fifth duck of a career now sixteen innings deep, and it lodges him a lofty tenth of 508 on the all-time list — rarefied ground indeed. He draws level on career ducks with Allan Peach, who plied his trade for the club from 1903 to 1907 and racked up his own five in eleven innings. Sunday brought the eleven up against the Royal Army Service Corps' 533 Division, and here the honour fell to L- Breedon, stumped by Gaines off the bowling of Golder for nought. It was his maiden innings for the club — a debut duck in every sense, and a fine, if unwanted, way to announce oneself to the honours board. He joins A Barker too, on one apiece, in what is fast becoming a well-populated corner of the ledger. The Week in Summary Three ducks, two matches, and not a repeat egg among them — a clean sweep of single failures rather than any grim double this week. The Fire Service accounted for two of the three in one innings, which one imagines they considered fair exchange for whatever blaze they might otherwise have been called to attend. Breedon's arrival is the tale of the week — there can be few gentler introductions to a cricketing life than a stumping for nought on one's very first appearance. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season is yet young, and the table reads accordingly level: - B Westover — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Gordon Fenner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - L- Breedon — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect record of imperfection all round. Plenty of cricket remains in 1943 to separate these three — or, more likely, to be joined by others equally keen to make their name in the club's less celebrated ledger. The next fixture awaits, and with it, no doubt, fresh candidates for the roll of honour. Bats up, eyes down.

3 ducks

A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, but not an idle one. Of the two fixtures played, one innings against the Royal Army Ordnance Corps on the 22nd proved a positively fertile hunting ground, yielding all three ducks of the period — each to the same bowler. A triple strike of that sort does not come along often, and the Duck Club salutes R- Brierley as an honorary patron of the art of not scoring. 1st XI — v Royal Army Ordnance Corps, 22nd June (home) - Richard Harris, opening the innings, was bowled by R- Brierley without troubling the scorers — his first duck's egg of the season and the second of a modest career now standing at two in five innings, a plucky if fruitless knock that leaves him 71st of 502 in the club's dubious all-time reckoning. Curiously, this very day in 1935 saw Percy Brattle likewise stroll back for nought, albeit in different colours against Bearsted CC — history, it seems, keeps a calendar. - J Wenham, sent in at six, fell lbw to the same tireless Brierley — his second duck of the summer, and his second for the career too, from nineteen innings, lodging him 60th of 502 on the honours ledger. Like his captain in misfortune, he shares the curious distinction of a duck falling on this same date back in 1935, when Percy Brattle made his own contribution to the club's archives. - Don Hartridge, at number eight, completed Brierley's morning's work, also bowled for nought — his second duck of the season and the fourth of a career that has now brought him level with several distinguished names, and a lofty 16th of 502 on the all-time list, a place of dubious distinction indeed. The Brattle parallel holds for him too, the 22nd of June evidently being an auspicious date for the art of the duck. The second fixture of the period passed without a single addition to the ledger — a rare instance of the ducks evading capture entirely, though the eleven will no doubt make amends before long. Three ducks, one bowler, one thoroughly sticky wicket for the home side's middle and lower order — a week that will be remembered less for what was scored than for what conspicuously was not. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - B- Vince — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - Arthur Ash — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40% - Don Hartridge — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.22% - Frank Sutton — 12 innings, 2 ducks, 16.67% - J Wenham — 12 innings, 2 ducks, 16.67% The season's leading exponents of the straight bat that met a straighter ball. Members are warmly invited to the next fixture, where the eleven will doubtless offer fresh candidates for the honours board — the ducks, as ever, are only ever one delivery away.

The Duck Report — 14th to 20th June, 1941

8 ducks
Week 5 · 14 Jun 1941 – 20 Jun 1941
🦆 Rise, quackers, and take your caps off — the eleven has had a proper go at surrendering wickets for nothing this week, and eight ducks are safely lodged in the pavilion book. A splendid haul for the connoisseur of failure. 1st XI The Charles Arkcoll match on the 14th opened wretchedly, with G Wood claiming a hat-trick of noughts almost in a single breath. J Wenham went first ball of the collapse, bowled by Wood — his 1st of the season and career, joining a select company on this very day back in 1882 when a whole card of Boxley batsmen also trudged home scoreless. Arthur Ash followed straight after, also bowled Wood, his 2nd season and career duck, keeping company with a long procession of fellow "twos" down the years. Then Dennis Smith, at number ten, completed the misery with his 2nd career duck in 19 innings — Mr Smith carries the solemn distinction of the club's Retirement Duck board, a badge earned in some past farewell rather than this week's dismissal, but a fitting reminder that the art of not scoring runs in some men's blood. Against the Royal Army Service Corps on the 18th, Frank Sutton fell for his 6th career duck in 27 innings, a performance that keeps him at a lofty 5th on the all-time table and a proud holder of the Duck of the Year 1940 honour. Splendidly, on this same date in 1904, one Tom Peach Jnr also perished for nought against Leeds Castle — a coincidence separated by 37 years but united in method. Then came Maidstone Borough Police on the 20th, who bowled the eleven into a positive epidemic. Joe Fenner opened and fell lbw for a duck, his 3rd career effort, level with a healthy crowd of fellow "threes" stretching back to 1893. Percy Brattle went next, bowled, also his 3rd career duck, keeping identical company. Then Frank Sutton returned to complete a grim double for the week — bowled again, his 7th career duck, drawing level with the mighty A Startup of 1868-82 fame, a four-time Duck of the Year and holder of Ducks in a Row. Two ducks in six days is no mean feat, Frank, and the honours board notes it plainly as a pair, without further embellishment needed. Finally R- Lee, on debut, marked his very first innings for the club with a golden nought — bowled — joining the exclusive zero club before he had so much as taken guard for a second ball. A baptism of the purest kind, and a name now etched at the very foot of a long and distinguished list. The week in summary Three matches, eight ducks, and G Wood and G- Baglee sharing the wickets with evident relish. Maidstone Borough Police alone accounted for four of the eight — a fixture the eleven will not remember fondly. Frank Sutton's pair was the standout feat of application, if application is quite the word for it. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - B- Vince — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - Arthur Ash — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40% - Frank Sutton — 10 innings, 2 ducks, 20% - Percy Brattle — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - R- Lee — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 🍩 A fine week's work for the zero club, gentlemen. The next fixture awaits, and no doubt the bowlers will be sharpening their line for fresh additions to this dubious roll of honour. Bat straight, or don't bat at all — either way, the Duck Club welcomes you.

The LPCC Duck Gazette — the weekend of 17th and 18th May, 1941

5 ducks
Week 1 · 17 May 1941 – 18 May 1941
Two fixtures, two afternoons, and the eleven found the art of not scoring practised with rare devotion. Five ducks were laid down for the exclusive zero club this week — a place of dubious distinction, but never short of new members. 1st XI - Herbert Rayner — in at four against the Royal Army Ordnance Corps on the 17th, and undone by Brierley for his first duck's egg of the season. His second of a career now nineteen innings deep, and it lodges him at 51st of 493 in the club's long roll of the dismissed. He draws level on two career ducks with B W Haynes, a name from the club's Edwardian heyday who compiled his own identical pair somewhere between 1891 and 1910 — proof, if any were needed, that this particular failing spans the generations undiminished. - B- Vince — arrived at the crease for the very first time in claret and gold, at nine against the RAOC, and departed for nought before he had properly arrived at all, bowled Brierley. A debut duck, and with the season young he stands, for now, the leading claimant to the club's own Duck of the Year 1941. He joins A Barker, of the 1885 vintage, on a single career duck apiece. But the story did not end there — the very next day, at ten against the Home Guard's Bungs Mob, he was caught off A Stevens for nought once more, completing a grim pair inside forty-eight hours of his arrival. Two innings, two ducks, a full house already — a baptism as chastening as any this correspondent can recall. - R Dann — run out for nought at five against the Home Guard, his tale a touch confused (the striker's end remains, charitably, "unsure"). His first career duck in two innings, placing him 156th of 493. Curiously, on this very day in 1940, Joe Fenner also strolled back for a duck's egg, against Staplehurst CC — the calendar, it seems, has its own sense of humour. - Don Hartridge — stumped by P Richmond off the bowling of George Winter, also against the Home Guard, for his third career nought in fifteen innings, and 28th of 493 on the all-time list. He shares his duck's anniversary with the same Joe Fenner of 1940, who was evidently no stranger to a Saturday spent walking back early. The week in brief Two matches, five ducks, and the Home Guard's Bungs Mob proved especially fond of the eleven's lower order, claiming three of the five between run-out, stumping and catch. The standout performance, if that is the word, belongs to B- Vince, who turned up, introduced himself to the crease twice, and left it twice without troubling the scorer — a pair to mark a debut that will not soon be forgotten. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - B- Vince — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - Herbert Rayner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Don Hartridge — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - R Dann — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season is young and the wickets, by all accounts, still a touch sticky. Week in Summary One match played, nought ducks laid — a rare and faintly suspicious state of affairs for a club whose very purpose is the chronicling of noughts. A modest afternoon at Staplehurst brought the eleven no fewer than four fresh entries to the roll of dishonour. At number six, Bert Buckoke was bowled by D Bearsby, his first duck of this season but the third of a distinguished career spanning fourteen innings — distinguished, that is, by his place on the Duck of the Year honours board for 1928, a title he holds still. He and the venerable A Kent of 1893 stand shoulder to shoulder on three career ducks each. And last but not least, Frank Sutton was caught behind off R Munn without scoring, his second duck of the season and third of his career — a career, one notes, that has already earned him this very season's Duck of the Year honour. A paid-up member of that particular club, and level with A Kent on three career ducks besides. The Week in Brief One match, four ducks, and the Staplehurst bowlers thoroughly enjoying their afternoon's work. A fairly one-sided procession to and from the crease, though it must be said the eleven bore it all with the customary good grace the game demands — there being, after all, a certain nobility in the art of not scoring. A single fixture at home to Bearsted CC has yielded two entries for the honours board this week, both from the 1st XI, both arriving without so much as a run to their name. 1st XI 🍩 Bert Buckoke came in at four and departed bowled by W White for a duck's egg on his very first appearance in club colours — a debut to remember for reasons entirely the wrong way round. His maiden knock joins the ledger at 1 career duck from 1 innings, good for 70th of 430 in the all-time reckoning, and he arrives straight onto the Duck of the Year 1928 board, an honour few manage before their second visit to the crease. He now sits level with the same tally as several old campaigns past — company that includes A Barker, who kept his own solitary duck on the books between 1885 and 1904. 0️⃣ Batting at ten, F Amies also made his bow for the club and was undone by Walter Watcham for nought, a plucky effort in name only. Also 1 career duck from a debut innings, ranked 91st of 430 — the numbers place him not far behind Buckoke on the same page of ignominy, and he too finds himself alongside the historic company of A Barker's single duck of long ago. Week in Summary One match, two ducks, both from the same eleven, both freshly arrived and both departing for nothing at all — a fixture that gave the 1928 season its opening entries in fine style. Whether it was a sticky wicket or simply Bearsted's bowlers finding good order, the eleven's lower and middle order alike found the art of not scoring came rather too naturally this week. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 🥇 Bert Buckoke — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 🥇 F Amies — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Both gentlemen open the 1928 season locked together at the summit of a table nobody wishes to top. The club awaits the next fixture with due anticipation — for the eleven's sake we hope for runs, and for the Gazette's sake we shall not complain if the ducks keep coming home to roost. 🏏

4 ducks

The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, 13th June 1925

3 ducks
Week 1 · 13 Jun 1925
A single fixture on the road at Bearsted, and the Zero Club gathers in three new members at a stroke — one from the top of the order, one from the middle, and one from the tail, as if the whole innings had been arranged for the occasion. The First Eleven, away at Bearsted Opening the innings, C Crundwell fell lbw to W White without troubling the scorers — a maiden knock ending in a maiden's egg, and his very first innings for the club besides. A debut duck of this quality earns him the season's own decoration: he stands newly named Duck of the Year 1925, a distinction not every man is fortunate enough to claim on his first afternoon in flannels. He takes his place at 71st of 415 in the club's long and honourable roll of failure. Curiously, on this very date back in 1900, one X Pike suffered an identical fate against the Royal Engineers — the calendar, it seems, has long memories. At first wicket down, W Merritt was bowled by the same W White, another maiden innings concluding in the same fashion, and he enters the book at 153rd of 415. He too finds himself sharing the date with history — the 13th of June 1900 having claimed X Pike in precisely the same manner, against the same Royal Engineers. Down at number eight, J Fife was bowled by Frank Harnett for his first senior duck, taking up residence at 116th of 415 on the all-time list. And once again the almanack turns up the 13th of June 1900, when X Pike made nought against the Royal Engineers — a date, it would appear, with a settled taste for ducks. The week in brief Three ducks from one visit to Bearsted, and all three debutants besides — a plucky eleven undone at both ends, with W White claiming a brace and Frank Harnett tidying up the tail. A sticky sort of afternoon, though the club's ledger, at least, is thriving. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. C Crundwell — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 2. J Fife — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 3. W Merritt — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% An early season, then, but a full house already at its head. The eleven take the field again before long, and the club awaits its next candidates with its customary warmth — the door of the Zero Club stands ever open, and the pavilion steps are never far away.

A Quiet Week for the Zero Club

0 ducks

Two fixtures were played across the period under review, and the eleven, whatever else may be said of their form with the willow, cannot be charged with any offence against the timbers. Not a single cipher was returned to the pavilion, and the honours board of the exclusive zero club records no new admissions. Whether this reflects a sudden and uncharacteristic soundness of technique, or merely that the bowling of the opposition was insufficiently searching to trouble our men, the correspondent shall not presume to say. The art of not scoring, so carefully cultivated in seasons past, appears this week to have been quite set aside in favour of the more conventional art of scoring runs. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's standings remain as they were, no name having been added nor any tally advanced this week. The board records no runners at present — a state of affairs the correspondent trusts will prove temporary, for a leaderboard without contestants is a dull thing indeed, and the club's honour depends upon its members' continued application to the task. Looking Ahead Members are reminded that fortune at the crease is a fickle mistress, and the eleven's next fixture may yet furnish material for these columns. The correspondent shall maintain his vigil at the scorer's table and report faithfully on any gentleman unfortunate enough to depart before troubling it. Until then, this gazette closes with the ducks, for once, having evaded capture entirely.

A modest week upon the roll of the exclusive zero club, with but a single gentleman required to make the long walk back for nought. Let the record show it properly. It is his first duck of the present season, and the fifth of a career now numbering fourteen innings, which places him ninth upon the club's all-time roll of three hundred and ninety-seven names — a standing not lightly come by. Members will recall he remains a laureate of some distinction, having carried off the Duck of the Year honours as long ago as 1902, a garland that loses none of its lustre for having been won in another age. It may interest the eleven that upon this very date in 1907, Mr Ernest Cruttenden — second upon our all-time roll with ten ducks to his name, and himself Duck of the Year in 1895 — likewise failed to trouble the scorer, against Town Malling CC. History, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. The Week in Summary One match played, one duck recorded, and the Midweek XI may count themselves fortunate that the ducks did not multiply further upon foreign soil. A quiet week for the club's registrars, but a week is a week, and the ledger must be kept regardless of how thin the pickings. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Tom Peach Jnr — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent A leaderboard of but one name this week, Mr Peach standing entirely alone at its head, though whether this reflects distinction or simply an absence of competition, the correspondent leaves to the reader's judgement. The eleven return to the field presently, and the club's registrars stand ready, pencils sharpened, to record whatever further ciphers the coming fixture may yield. Members are reminded that the art of not scoring spares no one, however illustrious, and the honours board awaits new names with its usual patience.

A quiet week for the exclusive zero club: but one gentleman was required to make the short walk back, and he did so with a certain dogged consistency that our readers will find not unfamiliar. 1st XI - Charles Wycherley, sent in at number five in the away fixture against Barming Asylum CC, was bowled by Dr Lewis and returned to the pavilion for a cipher. This is his first duck of the present season, and the fourth of a career now running to ten innings — a record that places him eleventh among the three hundred and ninety gentlemen who have, over the club's long history, achieved this particular species of distinction. He finds himself in close and honourable company with C Amies, who between 1867 and 1870 also compiled precisely four such innings, proving that the art of not scoring has never wanted for practitioners. It may further be recorded, for the historically minded, that Mr Wycherley was Duck of the Year as long ago as 1906, a laurel earned in a season quite separate from this one, and no less becoming for its age. In summary, one match was played and one duck secured — a modest yield, though the club's chroniclers would observe that a single well-turned nought, bowled clean by the good doctor himself, wants for nothing in quality what it lacks in quantity. The ducks, in the main, evaded the net this week, and our correspondent is not ashamed to say he was glad of the one that did not. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Charles Wycherley — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% The season is yet young, and the eleven take the field again before long, at which time the club has every confidence that further candidates for this dubious honour will present themselves. 1908 Season 3 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 12th of August, 1908

0 ducks
Week 11 · 12 Aug 1908
A quiet week, gentlemen, and no cause for the honours board to trouble itself. Our correspondent has scoured the scorebook from every corner of the ground and must report, with something approaching regret, that not a single member of the eleven presented his wicket for a cipher this week. The timbers stood unmolested, the leather went unrewarded, and the art of not scoring was, for once, left entirely unpractised. One match was played, and in it every batsman troubled the scorer at least once — a state of affairs the Duck Club can only note with wry disappointment, for it is rather the business of this gazette to celebrate failure, and failure has this week declined the invitation. We trust our members will not take this as encouragement. The exclusive zero club stands ready to receive new subscribers the moment application is made, and a place of such dubious distinction is never short of interest for long. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. S H Hills — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% Mr Hills leads the field this season by the simplest of arithmetic, having faced the scorer's pencil but once and been sent back to the pavilion on that solitary occasion. A perfect record, of a kind, and one his fellow members are cordially invited to challenge at the earliest opportunity. We look ahead with confidence, if not quite optimism, to the next fixture, where the willow may yet fail our men as reliably as it has failed them in seasons past. The Duck Club awaits its next candidates with open arms and a well-thumbed ledger.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Week Ending the 8th of June, 1908

1 duck
Week 2 · 8 Jun 1908
A single fixture graced our books this week, and a single wicket fell for nought — but what it lacked in number it makes handsomely up for in ceremony. To the wicket, then. The 1st Eleven Opening the innings against Maidstone Cricket Club, Mr S H Hills strode out first to face the bowling and was, alas, promptly caught by E Buss off the bowling of W Simmonds without so much as troubling the scorer. We are given to understand he did survive at least one delivery before his dismissal, so no golden duck attaches to the affair — a small mercy. What does attach is rather grander: this being the very first innings of Mr Hills's career with the club, he has thus been admitted, on his maiden appearance, to the exclusive zero club — a distinction some men labour a decade to earn and he has secured before luncheon on his first day. The honours board records him already for Duck of the Year 1908, a laurel earned this very week and one he may wear, we trust, with the appropriate mixture of pride and mortification. His name now stands 136th of 386 in the club's long roll of the dismissed, a single nought to his single innings — a purity of record, if nothing else. We note also that a Mr A Barker, who turned out for the club between 1885 and 1904 and was himself Duck of the Year in 1885, sits on the very same career tally of one — Mr Hills may consider himself in respectable, if scoreless, company. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, one debutant received into the fold with unusual promptness. There is something to be said for efficiency, even in failure, and Mr Hills has demonstrated it admirably. The bowling figures of Mr Simmonds and the safe hands of Mr Buss are noted with the courtesy due to gentlemen who did their office well. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. S H Hills — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0 per cent A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, an easy table to top, and Mr Hills has done so in a single stroke of misfortune. We look forward with keen anticipation to the season's next fixture, when the bowling attacks of our opponents will no doubt continue their diligent efforts to add further names to this esteemed and ever-growing register. The eleven are cordially reminded that the timbers wait for no man, and that the art of not scoring remains, as ever, very much alive at Linton Park.

The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 30th of May, 1908

0 ducks
Week 1 · 30 May 1908
A single fixture was contested this week, and it is my melancholy duty to report that the ducks proved elusive quarry throughout. Not one gentleman of either eleven was dismissed for a cipher — the timbers stood, the willow connected, and the leather was, on this solitary occasion, denied its usual harvest. One may search the honours boards in vain for a fresh entry this week. The exclusive zero club, that place of dubious distinction to which so many of our members have in seasons past been unwillingly admitted, gained no new subscriber on this occasion. Whether this reflects a sudden and uncharacteristic outbreak of application at the crease, or merely the ordinary caprice of the game, this correspondent will not presume to say. Consistency, it seems, took the week off — even consistency of the particular kind for which the Club exists to celebrate. We trust our members will not take this as any diminishment of the art of not scoring, which remains as noble and as democratic a pursuit as ever, open to novice and veteran alike, and merely resting this week rather than retired. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's returns stand as they were — no fresh figures to report this week, the tally sheet undisturbed by the day's play. Members presently of note in the season's reckoning will find their standing unchanged, and are cordially invited to consider whether such a state of affairs is entirely to their liking. We look with quiet confidence, and no small measure of hope, to the next fixture, at which normal service — by which we mean the entirely abnormal service of being sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer — may reasonably be expected to resume. The Club's doors, as ever, remain open to all comers.

No great surprise, perhaps, but a fitting demonstration of the club's founding principle — that failure, properly and repeatedly borne, is itself a kind of distinction. 1 duck

A quiet week at Linton Park, the eleven engaged in but a single fixture, and the exclusive zero club obliged with only one new member. This stands as his fifth indiscretion of a distinguished career spanning ten innings, and lodges him at the respectable position of seventh in the club's all-time roll of dishonour, a table of some three hundred and eighty names. He carries no honours-board memberships as yet, though on the present showing the committee may wish to keep a place warm. Of interest to the statistically minded: Mr Peach's tally of five now sits precisely alongside that long amassed by Mr F S W Cornwallis, who plied his trade between 1885 and 1906 across four-and-fifty innings before settling on the very same figure — a coincidence of the ledger that the correspondent is only too pleased to record, the two gentlemen now drawing level upon the honours board of nought, separated by but a single place in the all-time reckoning. The Week in Summary A single duck from a single fixture — the willow, on this occasion, proved rather more obliging than usual, and the art of not scoring was practised but the once. Whether this reflects a temporary want of application among the bowling fraternity, or merely good fortune among the batting order, the correspondent declines to speculate. Suffice it to say the ducks proved elusive this week, and the hunting was thin. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Mr Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0 per cent A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, scant sport, but the season is young and the correspondent has every confidence the ranks will swell before long. In Closing The eleven take the field again shortly, and the committee trusts further candidates for the zero club shall present themselves in due course, as they invariably do. Members are cordially reminded that a duck's egg, however unwelcome to the batsman, is always warmly received by this correspondent. Until the next fixture, then — may your bat find the middle, and may Mr Peach find some company at the foot of the table.

Whether this reflects a sudden and regrettable outbreak of competence at the crease, or merely that the bowling was not quite equal to its usual mischief, the Committee declines to speculate. Let it simply be noted, for the historical record, that the 28th of July passed without a single fresh entry to the honours boards — a state of affairs the Club trusts will prove temporary. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard Even in a barren week, the season's standings remain a source of considerable interest, and the following gentlemen continue to distinguish themselves in the art of not scoring: - H Wilson — 2 innings, 2 ducks, a perfect 100 per cent, a record of really quite uncommon thoroughness - Charles Wycherley — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent, seldom troubling the scorer this season - R W Mitchell — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40 per cent, a steadier hand but not without his lapses - D H Luck — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent, an emphatic if brief introduction to the ledger - J W Bowles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent, likewise announcing himself without delay In Closing The Committee extends its compliments to all who batted this week and, somewhat unusually, has nothing further to report against any of them. Members are reminded that such restraint rarely persists for long, and the Secretary awaits next Saturday's fixture with his customary and entirely justified confidence that the timbers will again be rattled for nought.

2 ducks
Week 10 · 14 Jul 1906 – 20 Jul 1906
A chronicle of ciphers, 14th to 20th July, 1906 Two matches were played by the eleven in the week under review, and the willow proved twice unequal to the task, both instances falling to gentlemen of the 1st XI. 1st XI - F E Wallis, sent in at number four against Leeds Castle CC on the 14th, was caught by W Betts off the bowling of W Steadman and returned to the pavilion for a duck's egg. It is his first cipher of the present season and the third of a career now numbering four-and-twenty innings, a showing that places him twenty-second of three hundred and seventy-one in the club's roll of honour. This is his second duck of the season, and the second of a career of but ten innings, a rate of failure that will not have escaped the more attentive members, and stands him fifty-second of three hundred and seventy-one upon the all-time list. Curiously, upon this same date in 1869, a Mr C Amies of this parish also departed for nought, against Horsmonden CC. The Week in Summary Two matches, two ducks, both claimed by our own men and both, it may be observed, at home, where the timbers appear to offer no especial refuge. No gentleman was so unfortunate as to repeat the indignity within the week, and no family party shared in the disgrace on this occasion. A modest week, by the club's usual standards of catastrophe. 2 ducks
Week 9 · 7 Jul 1906
A record of the match played the 7th day of July, 1906, against Sutton Valence School 1st XI Two of our men were sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer this week, and by a pleasing economy of effort the same bowler, Mr H R Tanner of the visiting school, accounted for both. B W Haynes, promoted to first wicket down, had his stumps rearranged by Mr Tanner for a duck's egg — the first cipher of his season and the second of a career that now runs to eighteen innings, a showing that places him thirtieth of the 367 names upon the club's roll of the dismissed. It may interest the gallery that on this very day in the year 1900, one L C Brown was likewise dismissed for nought, against Town Malling CC — history, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. C H Style, coming in at number seven, fared no better and was similarly bowled by Mr Tanner. This was his first duck of the present season and but the second of a career still in its infancy, three innings all told — sufficient nonetheless to place him thirty-third of 367 in the club's dubious company. He, too, shares the distinction of the 7th of July with the aforementioned Mr Brown of 1900, who made his own duck upon this same date six seasons past. In summary A modest yield for the week — two ducks from the single fixture, both at the hand of the same visiting bowler, and both gentlemen of the middle order sent packing before troubling the scorebook. Whether Mr Tanner ought to be congratulated or merely noted with wary respect, the Gazette leaves to the reader's judgement. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. H Wilson — 2 ducks in 2 innings (100%) 2. Charles Wycherley — 2 ducks in 3 innings (66.67%) 3. Allan Peach — 1 duck in 1 innings (100%) 4. D H Luck — 1 duck in 1 innings (100%) 5. J W Bowles — 1 duck in 1 innings (100%) The club extends its compliments to Messrs Haynes and Style upon their contributions to the season's tally, and awaits with interest what fresh candidates the next fixture may deliver unto the exclusive company of the nought.

The Duck Club Chronicle — the fixture of Saturday, 23rd June 1906

8 ducks
Week 7 · 23 Jun 1906
A solitary fixture against Leeds Castle CC yielded no fewer than eight ciphers for the club's ledger this week — a splendid harvest for one afternoon's play, and business enough to keep the scorers' pencils sharp. 1st XI (away, Leeds Castle CC) - Jack Fryer, second man in, was bowled by W Betts for the season's first addition to his account and his twelfth career duck in 67 innings, a tally that stands first of 367 upon the club's roll of dishonour. He remains twice a laureate, having been proclaimed Duck of the Year in both 1891 and 1900. - The Reverend J R Leigh, batting fifth, was caught De Uphaugh, bowled Croucher, for his first duck of the season and, remarkably, only his first in sixteen innings, ranking him 132nd of 367. He now stands level upon exactly one career duck with the venerable A Barker, who kept the identical company between 1885 and 1904 and was himself Duck of the Year in 1885. - Charles Wycherley, seventh man in, was bowled by Betts for his maiden duck of the season, ranking 32nd of 367 and already declared Duck of the Year for 1906, level upon one career duck with A Barker. Sent in again the same day, he was run out without addition, completing a pair and his season's second duck, his career tally now standing at two in a mere four innings — level with C French Snr, who managed the same modest feat between 1860 and 1864. - C Kneller, playing his very first innings for the club, was run out without scoring, opening his career account with a duck in his second innings played, level upon one career duck with A Barker, ranked 68th of 367. - H Wilson, likewise making his debut, was caught De Uphaugh, bowled Betts, and, sent in again, was bowled by Betts a second time without troubling the scorers — a pair upon his very first afternoon in the eleven. His two ducks in two innings, ranked 40th of 367, draw him level with C French Snr on a tally of two. - George Champion, batting fourth, was caught Tillman, bowled Steadman, for his eighth career duck in 63 innings, ranking third of 367 and a paid-up Duck of the Year from 1897. In summary Eight ducks from a single fixture is handsome work, two of them pairs — Wycherley's and young Wilson's, the latter suffered on his very first day in the eleven. Not one of our men departed first ball, each contriving to survive a delivery or more before submitting to the inevitable cipher, which the club's historians will note as consistency of a most particular and unremunerative kind. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Charles Wycherley — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 2. H Wilson — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 3. Allan Peach — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 4. D H Luck — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 5. J W Bowles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% The eleven takes the field again next Saturday, and the Chronicle awaits, with quiet confidence, further additions to the roll.

The Duck Club Gazette — 4th June 1906

2 ducks
Week 4 · 4 Jun 1906
A record of our men sent early back to the pavilion The First Eleven, at home to Maidstone CC Two of our batsmen contrived, within the same innings, to add their names to the club's roll of honour for failing to trouble the scorer. R W Mitchell, in at number four, was caught by C A W Duffield off the bowling of E Larder, and returns to the pavilion bearing his season's first cipher — the club's most exclusive distinction — and his career's first duck in seven innings, placing him 127th of 364 upon the long and undistinguished catalogue the club keeps of such things. He may take some comfort in noting that, on this very day in 1898, one C S Smith performed much the same office against Sutton Valence School, so his ignominy is at least in fine historical company. Following him to the crease, and shortly thereafter following him back, was Allan Peach at number five, caught by E Larder off G W Leng. This is Mr Peach's fourth duck in a career of but six innings, a rate of failure so consistent as to place him ninth of all 364 names ever inscribed upon the roll — a consistency of a very particular kind, and one he can scarcely be proud of, yet cannot now be parted from. He too finds himself in the company of the aforementioned Mr Smith, whose duck of 1898 fell upon this same date. In summary A modest afternoon's work by the standards of the exclusive zero club — a single fixture, two ciphers, both recorded in short order against Maidstone CC. No pairs, no family affairs, and no golden ducks to report this week, merely two gentlemen undone in turn by good bowling and indifferent fortune. The Duck Club Gazette — for the 12th of May, 1906

2 ducks
Week 1 · 12 May 1906
A modest but by no means undistinguished afternoon at Town Malling, where the Eleven, sent thither to try conclusions with the home side, returned with two additions to the club's rolls of honour. The bowlers of Town Malling CC may be congratulated on their part in the proceedings. 1st XI — away to Town Malling CC D H Luck, coming in at number eight, was undone by F B Leney and departed without score — a first innings for the young gentleman, and thus his maiden appearance upon these lists, entered at 75th of 363 in the club's long history of ciphers. He joins A Barker, that veteran of 1885 to 1904 and a Duck of the Year man in his time, on a career tally of one apiece — modest company, but distinguished. J W Bowles, at number ten, was run out for a duck's egg of his own — the fielding, we are given to understand, rather than the bowling, being his undoing. This is his second innings for the club and his first duck, placing him 111th of 363 on the all-time list. He too finds himself level with Mr Barker on one, a tally shared this week, curiously enough, by his own teammate above. In summary Two ciphers from a single fixture, both away from home, both falling to different means — the timbers on one occasion, a mishap in the running on the other. No pairs, no golden ducks, and no family affairs to record this week — a quiet if not entirely blank week for the exclusive zero club. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - D H Luck — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - J W Bowles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Both gentlemen begin the season in what one might call perfect consistency of a very particular kind. 1904 Season 5 reports

The Duck Club Gazette — For the Week Ending Monday, the 25th of August, 1904

2 ducks
Week 11 · 25 Aug 1904
A single fixture is recorded in the period under review, our eleven meeting Leeds Castle Cricket Club, and the willow yielded to the club's collection two further ducks' eggs of note. House Team Mr T Woollett, walking to the wicket at number eight for his very first innings in this eleven's colours, was caught by T Sparks off the bowling of R Startup, and thus took his introduction to the game's sterner disciplines in the most unceremonious fashion available to a debutant — dismissed for a cipher before he had properly taken his guard. It is his maiden innings and, by the same stroke, his maiden duck, a coincidence the honours board records rather less kindly than we do here. He enters the all-time列, or rather the all-time list, at 135th of 359, and in doing so draws level upon a tally of one with the venerable A Barker, whose own solitary duck was taken back in 1885 and earned that gentleman the Duck of the Year garland for his trouble — Mr Woollett may take some comfort in such distinguished, if modest, company. Mr G Pearce, sent in at number ten, was bowled by B Tillman without scoring, his third innings for the club and his first acquaintance with the duck's egg, a distinction he had until now been spared. He stands 93rd of 359 upon the all-time roll of dishonour, and he too finds himself level upon a single duck with the aforementioned A Barker of 1885 vintage — two gentlemen, nineteen years apart, united by the same modest arithmetic. The week in summary Two ducks from a single match, both falling to the lower order of the House Team's innings against Leeds Castle, suggests our tail found the leather rather more troublesome than the top order — no partnerships, no pairs, and mercifully no family misfortune to report this week, the ducks confining themselves to individual, rather than dynastic, disappointment. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season being yet young, five gentlemen stand together at the summit, each having faced the bowling once this season and each having been dismissed without score, for a season average of nought and a duck percentage of a full 100: - Mr Arthur Cornwallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr C H Style — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr G Pearce — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr T Woollett — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A crowded summit, and an early one, but the season is long and the willow fickle. Members are cordially invited to attend the next fixture, where no doubt further candidates shall present themselves for admission to this most exclusive and least sought-after of clubs.

The Duck Club Gazette — a Report for the Week of the 6th to the 9th of August, 1904

1 duck
Week 9 · 6 Aug 1904 – 9 Aug 1904
A quiet week for the timbers, gentlemen, with but a single egg laid across two fixtures — the ducks, it would seem, took their ease this week and left the eleven largely untroubled. House Team - Jack Fryer, first wicket down against Leeds Castle Cricket Club on the 9th, in the away fixture, was bowled by W Thorndycraft for a cipher, and returned to the pavilion with the ledger unimproved. This being his first duck's egg of the 1904 season, and his eleventh in a career now standing at sixty-five innings, he remains ensconced at the very head of the club's all-time roll — first of some three hundred and fifty-five names who have known the particular ignominy of nought. Mr Fryer will further be remembered as a past holder of the Duck of the Year honour, claimed in both 1891 and 1900, proof, if proof were needed, that the art of not scoring may be practised at the very highest level, and practised more than once. A Week in Summary Two fixtures were played in the period under review, and but a single duck's egg was laid between them — a scarcity that will please the batting order rather more than it pleases this correspondent, whose columns are ever the poorer for a quiet week. Mr Fryer alone flew the club's sorry colours, and flew them, it must be said, rather briefly. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Arthur Cornwallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, a full 100 per cent - C H Style — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent - Jack Fryer — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent The season's leading three gentlemen have, it will be observed, achieved a perfect record of imperfection, having faced but the one innings apiece and failed on each occasion to trouble the scorer. Whether such consistency may be sustained, or whether the willow shall yet find its mark, remains a matter for the coming weeks to determine. We commend the eleven to their next fixture, in the confident expectation that the ducks, presently in hiding, shall shortly be flushed once more from cover. The correspondent remains, as ever, at the club's service in the faithful chronicling of such misfortunes as the season may provide.

The Duck Club Gazette — 4th July 1904

3 ducks
Week 4 · 4 Jul 1904
Linton Park v Sutton Valence School The First Eleven Opening the innings, Arthur Cornwallis was caught H W Hunting, bowled N Strickland, without troubling the scorers — his first duck of the present season and the third of a career now spanning six-and-forty innings, a record that places him nineteenth of the three hundred and fifty-three names upon the club's roll of dubious distinction. He is no stranger to such company, having been proclaimed Duck of the Year in 1888 and, it now appears, again in this very season of 1904. Members with long memories will recall that upon this same date in 1891, one Jack Fryer — first of all our three hundred and fifty-three, with ten ducks to his name — likewise returned to the pavilion without score against these same opponents from Sutton Valence. History, it seems, keeps a diary. At number six, Mr C H Style was caught S E Kay, bowled the Reverend R E Lewis, and thus departed for nought on his very first appearance in senior colours — a maiden innings yielding, alas, a maiden duck, and a modest nineteenth-place... rather, sixty-fifth place, entry upon the honours board. He shares, too, the curious coincidence of the calendar, his duck falling on the very anniversary of Jack Fryer's own against Sutton Valence School in 1891. The school's bowlers would seem to keep a long-standing appointment with the fourth of July. Last man in, Allan Peach was caught N Strickland, bowled Rev R E Lewis, for a third career duck taken in but four innings — an economy of effort that carries him to eighteenth of 353 upon the club's register. He too fell upon the same fateful date as Mr Fryer thirteen summers past. The Week in Brief A single fixture, three ducks, and the Reverend R E Lewis doing a fair portion of the damage, claiming two of the three wickets while N Strickland turned his hand to both bowling and catching. That all three should fall on the very day the calendar once favoured Jack Fryer against these same school opponents is the sort of coincidence upon which correspondents are obliged to remark, and members are invited to draw their own conclusions as to the omen. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Allan Peach — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Arthur Cornwallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C H Style — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Tom Peach Jnr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season is yet young, and the table stands wide open to fresh candidates. The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 15th of June, 1904

1 duck
Week 1 · 15 Jun 1904
A single fixture furnished the eleven's ledger this week, and a single name is entered upon it — modest fare, but the exclusive zero club never turns away a new subscriber. 1st XI Away at Town Malling, C Reid came to the wicket at number six and departed shortly after, bowled by F B Leney, without troubling the scorer. It was his maiden appearance in the eleven's colours, and cricket being the courteous game it is, the club has seen fit to mark the occasion with its own peculiar honour rather than the one he might have preferred. A debut duck is a rite few forget and fewer choose to repeat, and Mr Reid may now consider himself formally admitted to a fellowship of dubious distinction. It stands as his first duck in a career of one innings, and he takes his place at seventieth of the three hundred and fifty-one names presently inscribed upon the club's roll — respectable company for an opening entry, and ground enough to build upon, in either direction. By a pleasant trick of the calendar, this very date in 1887 saw Jack Fryer — twice Duck of the Year, in 1891 and again in 1900, and no less than the club's leading exponent of the art with ten to his name — likewise sent back for nought, against East Peckham. Mr Reid may take what comfort he can in such distinguished if accidental fellowship. The Week in Brief One match played, one wicket surrendered without score, and no further casualties reported. A quiet week for the timbers, all told, though the season is young and the leather has claimed finer men than these before now. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent The season's register stands thin as yet, with but a single name upon it, and no cause for alarm among the eleven's more established batsmen. The correspondent trusts the coming fixtures will furnish further material, as they reliably do, and looks forward to reporting whichever gentleman next elects to walk out and walk straight back again.

0 ducks

A single fixture was played this week, and this correspondent is obliged to report a most disappointing state of affairs: not one gentleman of either eleven contrived to be dismissed for a cipher. 4 ducks

A modest week for the willow but a fruitful one for the exclusive zero club, five ciphers being recorded across two fixtures, and two of them upon a single, memorable morning. 1st XI, away to Yalding CC, 15th August C Murdoch, going in first wicket down, was undone lbw to the bowling of F Reeves, and departs with his first duck of the season and the first of his career in ten completed innings, a modest 66th upon the club's roll of 345. On this same date in 1897 one F Smith likewise made a nought, against the Maidstone Conservative Club, and both our new men may take modest comfort in such honourable company. The week in summary Two matches, five ducks, and honours shared between old hands and new arrivals alike — the timbers proving no respecter of experience this week, F Reeves and W Betts between them accounting for the lot. Linton Park Cricket Club — Duck Club Gazette

0 ducks
Week 11 · 14 Aug 1903
Week ending the 14th of August, 1903 Correspondence from the ground brings, this week, a report of scant material — the ducks, it seems, have evaded capture entirely. One fixture was played in the period under review, yet not a single member of either eleven was persuaded to walk back for a cipher. The timbers stood, the leather beat a respectful path around the willow, and every batsman troubled the scorer at least once. A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, and, one might say, a poor one for those of us whose trade is in reporting its exploits. It is not for the correspondent to manufacture drama where none was offered. We record, with the faintest note of disappointment, that the art of not scoring found no fresh practitioners on this occasion. The membership rolls remain unchanged. Let it not be said, however, that the club's honours boards have gone unattended this season — the standings below tell a rather livelier tale. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - George Champion — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0 per cent — a most industrious contributor to the cause - A Grice — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0 per cent — perfection of a very particular kind - G F Vernon — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0 per cent — likewise unblemished in his devotion to nought - Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0 per cent — an even wager each time he takes guard - K McAlpine — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0 per cent — keeping steady company at the head of the table Mr Champion continues to lead the season's proceedings by weight of numbers, though Messrs Grice and Vernon may fairly claim the purer distinction, having yet to trouble the scorer on the single occasion each was called upon. The eleven are cordially reminded that the season is far from concluded, and that the next fixture offers every opportunity for a fresh name — or several — to be added to this distinguished roll. The correspondent, for his part, awaits the next despatch from the ground in the sincere hope of rather more to report.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — a Report of the Willow's Misfortunes, Monday the 3rd of August, 1903

5 ducks
Week 10 · 3 Aug 1903
A melancholy afternoon against Rochester CC has furnished the exclusive zero club with no fewer than five new subscriptions in a single innings, Captain R R Morgan of the visiting eleven proving a positive scourge to our batting order. We proceed to the roll of ignominy. The First Eleven H G Smith, sent in at number two, fell caught and bowled to the Rochester captain without troubling the scorer — his first duck's egg of the season and the third of a career now numbering thirty-one innings, placing him twentieth of the three hundred and thirty-one gentlemen who have graced this list. He arrives at exactly the tally held by the late A Kent, Duck of the Year in 1893, among a distinguished company of some dozen others similarly becalmed on three. The Reverend F A Leveson-Gower followed at first wicket down, bowled by Captain Morgan for his maiden duck of the campaign, the first blemish upon seven innings hitherto respectable. He now stands level upon one career cipher with A Barker of 1885 and a considerable fraternity besides — welcome, Reverend, to a communion of a different order. F Reeves, arriving at seven, was stumped off the same relentless bowler — a mode of dismissal requiring, one notes with some wonder, a batsman to miss the ball by such a margin that even the wicketkeeper could not be denied his moment. His first career duck in eleven innings places him alongside the aforementioned A Barker on a tally of one. K McAlpine, at nine, was bowled by Captain Morgan for his second career duck in a mere ten innings, joining Arthur Cornwallis — a veteran of some forty-five innings across two decades of service — upon that same modest figure. And at eleven, young Allan Peach made his very first appearance for the club and was promptly bowled by Captain Morgan without scoring — a debut duck in the most literal sense, his maiden first-class cipher in what is only his second innings of senior cricket. He, too, finds himself in step with A Barker's solitary duck of 1885. A sobering welcome to the fold, though the honours board stands ready to receive him should the pattern persist. A Note on the Bowling It would be remiss not to record that all five wickets fell to the same bowler, Captain R R Morgan, who appears to have found something in the Linton Park wicket that our batsmen decidedly did not. Whether this reflects credit upon the visiting captain or discredit upon our own eleven is a matter the committee may debate at its leisure over the winter. Week in Summary One match, one innings, five ducks — a thorough dismantling, and a fine harvest for the zero club's ledger. No pairs, no golden ducks and no family affairs to report this week, merely five gentlemen dispatched by the same relentless right arm in the space of a single Rochester innings. Consistency, of a very particular kind. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - George Champion — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - A Grice — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% - G F Vernon — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% - Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% - K McAlpine — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% The season is young yet, and Captain Morgan's afternoon's work may well see fresh names contest this table before long. Members are cordially reminded that the willow offers no guarantees, and are invited to the next fixture, where further additions to the honours board must be considered a distinct probability.

The Duck Club Gazette — Monday, the 4th of July, 1903

0 ducks
Week 6 · 4 Jul 1903
A quiet week, gentlemen, and the honours board goes unmolested. A Week Without Incident It is the correspondent's melancholy duty to report that, upon careful review of the single fixture played this period, not one member of the eleven contrived to be dismissed without troubling the scorer. A most disappointing state of affairs for the club, if a rather more agreeable one for those concerned. The willow was, on this occasion, wielded with sufficient competence throughout to deny us fresh material, and the exclusive zero club welcomes no new initiates this week. One trusts our batsmen will show rather less application at the crease come the next fixture, that the ledger might once again be enlivened. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season standings, however, want for nothing in the way of distinction, and remain a place of considerable dubious honour: - George Champion — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent — a batsman demonstrating consistency of a very particular kind, failing to trouble the scorer in two innings out of three - A Grice — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent — a cipher on the only occasion called upon, and thus perfect in his imperfection - G F Vernon — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent — likewise perfect, and likewise unbothered by his rival Grice's identical feat - Rev W A Carr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent — the reverend gentleman keeping faith with the art of not scoring on exactly half his appearances - P R Burton — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33 per cent — the most modest showing among our leading lights, and modesty is, after all, a virtue In Closing A barren week for the chronicler is, we concede, a triumph of sorts for the eleven, though triumph through adversity remains the club's preferred variety. We look ahead with quiet confidence to the next fixture, in the settled expectation that the timbers will once more be rattled, the leather will once more prevail, and a fresh duck's egg or two will be laid for these pages to record. Until then, the honours board rests, undisturbed but not, we suspect, for long.

A single entry makes for thin copy, but consistency of a very particular kind is, as ever, its own reward. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 1st June, 1903

3 ducks
Week 1 · 1 Jun 1903
Correspondence from the Club's Recorder of Ciphers, upon the occasion of a single fixture against Maidstone Cricket Club, in which our First Eleven contributed three names to the roll of those who failed to trouble the scorer. The First Eleven, in the First Innings of Maidstone C.C. - The Reverend W A Carr, coming in at number two, was bowled by X Hardinge and returned to the pavilion no better acquainted with the scorebook than when he left it. This stands as his first duck in a career of three innings, and places him 115th of 327 upon the Club's honours board of failure. He joins A Barker, Duck of the Year as long ago as 1885, upon that same solitary tally — a fellowship separated by eighteen summers but united in arithmetic. - P R Burton, at number eight, was smartly taken by B W Haynes off the bowling of J H Hobbs, a dismissal executed with more credit to the fielder than to himself. This is his second career duck in four innings, advancing him to 42nd of 327 in the Club's dubious pecking order. He keeps company with Arthur Cornwallis, Duck of the Year 1888 and a veteran of some three and forty innings, likewise settled upon two. - G F Vernon, last man in at number ten, was clean bowled by the same J H Hobbs, whose length appears to have found considerable favour with our lower order this afternoon. This is his first career duck in four innings, and sees him placed 79th of 327. He joins A G Oyler, Duck of the Year in 1899, upon an identical tally of one — proof, if any were needed, that the art of not scoring respects no particular decade. A modest afternoon's harvest, then: three ciphers from a single innings, two of them gathered by the same length of bowling, which speaks either to Mr Hobbs's skill or to a certain want of watchfulness down our order. No pairs were completed, no golden ducks recorded, and no families of ducks graced the same innings — a week of honest, unspectacular failure, which is, after all, the Club's stock in trade. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. G F Vernon — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent 2. P R Burton — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent 3. Rev W A Carr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent The season is yet young, and the leaderboard has ample room for further distinction. Members are cordially reminded that the willow shows no favouritism, and that our next fixture shall doubtless furnish fresh candidates for this exclusive and dubious club. Until then, the Recorder remains, as ever, watchful for the timbers.

1902 Season 4 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette

3 ducks
Week 11 · 16 Aug 1902
Recording the Match of Saturday, 16th August 1902 Our First Eleven, guests of Yalding CC, found the home bowling considerably more troublesome than the home hospitality, and three of our number were sent back to the pavilion without score. The exclusive zero club records its latest subscriptions below, each entered in the ledger with the solemnity such distinction properly deserves. 1st XI, away to Yalding CC Mr W Peach achieved the singular feat of visiting the timbers twice in the one afternoon and troubling the scorers on neither occasion. Opening the innings, he was held by the Reverend J R Leigh off the bowling of Mr F R Allsop, his first duck of the season and the second of a career now standing at eleven innings. Returning at number four, he fell again, caught by Mr H T Manwaring off Mr H Reeves, his second of the season and his third for the club. A plain pair, then, rather than the rarer and more gloriously abject king pair, but a pair nonetheless, and a feat of a very particular consistency. Mr Peach now occupies 25th place of 326 upon the club's roll of ducks. It may interest him to learn that upon this very date in 1893, one George Champion likewise failed to trouble the scorers, against the Free Foresters, so his affliction keeps distinguished company across the years. Mr P R Burton, at number eight, was caught by the Reverend Leigh off Mr R Leney, his first duck of the season and, in only his third innings for the club, his maiden entry upon the ledger. He takes his place 106th of 326. He too shares his misfortune with the calendar, for Mr Champion's duck of 1893, already noted above, fell upon this same sixteenth of August. The Week in Brief One match, three ducks, and the whole business conducted with commendable efficiency by Yalding's attack, Messrs Allsop, Reeves and Leney, with the Reverend Leigh doing rather more work behind the timbers than any of our batsmen managed in front of them. Mr Peach's pair stands as the day's principal ornament, the art of not scoring twice over being no mean accomplishment.
