For the week ending the 19th of July, 1902 At Boxley CC our First Eleven contributed two names to the register of the scoreless this week, each gentleman entering the exclusive company for the very first time in his career. 1st XI — away to Boxley CC F M Hills, sent in at number seven, was bowled by F Pettitt without troubling the scorer at all — a debut innings that yielded a nought, securing in one stroke both his maiden appearance for the club and his maiden failure, and placing him 71st of 324 upon the club's long and melancholy roll of honour. In this he keeps precise company with one A Barker, who managed the identical feat of a single duck in a single innings back in 1885 — a year in which that solitary failure was, remarkably, sufficient to carry off the Duck of the Year itself. A T Benning, at number ten, fell in the same match to C H Style, his own first innings for the club likewise yielding not a run, and taking his place 53rd upon the roll. He too stands level with the aforementioned Mr Barker of 1885 on a single career duck apiece — proof that a gentleman may arrive at nought by many different roads and still find agreeable company waiting for him at the destination. Two ducks, then, from a single fixture, both suffered away from home at Boxley, and both by gentlemen quite new to the fold — a baptism, one might say, conducted in the same coin twice over. Messrs Pettitt and Style will each no doubt fancy himself the more dangerous man; the Duck Club offers no opinion on the matter, only its customary thanks for services rendered. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Tom Peach Jnr — 3 innings, 2 ducks (66.67%) 2. A T Benning — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) 3. F M Hills — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) 4. F E Wallis — 2 innings, 1 duck (50%) 5. W Kennard — 2 innings, 1 duck (50%) The season is yet young, and the timbers remain as inviting as ever to Boxley's bowlers and to all who venture out to face them. The Duck Club Gazette — Week Ending the 11th of June, 1902

4 ducks
Week 1 · 11 Jun 1902
🏏 A single fixture at Town Malling was sufficient to furnish our correspondent with material, four ciphers being registered by the 1st Eleven in the course of the visit, and a family affair to boot. 1st XI — v Town Malling CC (away) Mr Tom Peach Jnr enjoyed the rare, if unwelcome, distinction of being twice sent back to the pavilion in the one match — first at number three, bowled by W H Cooper, and later at number eight, bowled by P Phillips. Neither dismissal came off the first ball, so the gentleman was denied the full ceremony of a king's pair, but a pair it remains nonetheless, his second and first career ducks arriving in the same afternoon, a debut to remember for reasons entirely unconnected with runs. He has been proclaimed Duck of the Year for 1902 already, and now finds himself level upon a tally of two with the veteran Arthur Cornwallis, who compiled his own pair of noughts across a rather more leisurely span of years from 1884 to 1901. Messrs W Kennard and C W Kennard, brothers both, contrived between them one of the more charming curiosities the ledger has to offer this season. W Kennard, at number four, fell to W H Cooper's bowling without troubling the scorer, while C W Kennard, at number six, was accounted for by F Longhurst in like fashion. Each stands debutant to the exclusive zero club, each on a single duck from two innings, and each finds a kindred spirit in the tally of A Barker, whose own solitary duck of 1885 remains, seventeen years on, exactly matched. A Family Notice The correspondent is obliged to record a rarer ceremony still. The Messrs Kennard, being brothers, achieved the distinction of Two of a Quack — both dismissed for nought in the self-same innings against Town Malling. Such fraternal solidarity in failure is not lightly come by, and the club extends its warmest, if faintly mischievous, congratulations to the family upon this shared entry into the honours board. The Week in Brief Four ducks in a single match is respectable industry by any measure, and the 1st Eleven may reflect that consistency, of a very particular kind, was very much the order of the day at Town Malling. Mr Peach's pair alone accounts for half the tally, a feat of concentrated ill fortune not often witnessed in one fixture. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Tom Peach Jnr — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% - C W Kennard — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% - W Kennard — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% The eleven return to the field presently, and the club has every confidence that further additions to the roll of dubious distinction will not be long delayed. Members are cordially reminded that the art of not scoring is one practised by the finest and the humblest alike, and all are welcome to try their hand.

The Duck Club Chronicle — the week ending the 27th of June, 1900

2 ducks
Week 4 · 27 Jun 1900
A quiet week for the willow, gentlemen, for only two of our number were asked to make the short walk back to the pavilion — but a correspondent finds his colour where he may, and the fixture against Brenchley CC did not disappoint. The First Eleven - Mr Arthur Cornwallis, promoted to first wicket down, was undone bowled, the name of his conqueror going unrecorded in the book — no disgrace attaches to falling to a bowler even the scorer could not identify. This is his first cipher of the season and the second of a career now spanning nine and thirty innings, placing him five and twentieth of the two hundred and ninety-eight names upon the club's roll of dubious distinction. He is no stranger to this company, having been crowned Duck of the Year as long ago as 1888, a laurel that ages rather better than most. Curiously, on this very day in the year 1891, one F Danells also returned scoreless to the pavilion, against Hunton CC — the calendar, it seems, has long memory for these things. - Mr F E Wallis followed him to the crease at four, and followed him back again just as promptly, likewise bowled by a hand the scorer declined to name. It is his maiden duck of the summer and but the first blemish upon a card of twelve innings, leaving him four and sixtieth upon the all-time list. He joins a considerable fraternity sitting upon exactly one career cipher apiece — among them Mr A Barker, whose own solitary duck in 1885 was sufficient to earn him that season's dubious crown. In Summary Brenchley CC's bowling claimed two wickets for nought this week from a single fixture, both from the top order and both, it might be observed, by bowlers whose identities the scorebook has chosen discreetly to withhold. Whether this reflects modesty on the bowlers' part or forgetfulness on the scorer's, your correspondent leaves to the reader's judgement. The Duck Hunting Season, Standings to Date 1. F S W Cornwallis — 3 innings, 1 duck (33.3 per cent) The club awaits its next fixture with the usual mixture of hope and foreboding, confident that further names will shortly be added to this ledger of honourable failure.

The Duck Club Gazette — Intelligence from the Match at Yalding, 16th June 1900

3 ducks
Week 3 · 16 Jun 1900
Our correspondent is obliged to report that the visit to Yalding CC yielded, in addition to whatever runs were scored, a modest but respectable harvest for the exclusive zero club. Three of our batsmen were sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer, the bowling of Mr F Reeves proving a particular affliction. 1st XI Mr Jack Fryer, going in at first wicket down, was caught E Wilkins, bowled F Reeves, and thereby entered his second duck's egg of the present season. This is by no means a novel indignity for Mr Fryer, who stands alone at the head of the club's all-time roll with ten career ciphers from five and fifty innings — first of two hundred and ninety-five, a distinction of the most dubious kind. He carries already the Duck of the Year honours of 1891, and appears, on this season's evidence, a strong candidate to add the prize for 1900 to his mantelpiece before the summer is out. Consistency, it must be said, of a very particular kind. Batting at seven, Mr J F Coles was bowled by Mr Reeves for his first duck of the season, and his maiden failure of a fledgling career now numbering three innings. He may take some comfort in joining, on a tally of one career ciphers apiece, the shade of Mr A Barker, who achieved the identical distinction in a single innings for the club back in 1885 and was rewarded, for his trouble, with that year's Duck of the Year honours. At number eight, Mr C S Smith was caught R G Henham, bowled F Reeves, his third career ciphers from a mere eight innings, and the club's seventeenth most prolific duck-getter of all time — a rank he holds partly on the strength of the Duck of the Year prize awarded him in 1898. In this he draws level with Mr A Kent, whose own third duck in 1893 likewise earned him that year's crown. Triumph through adversity, evidently, runs in the family of the willow-wielding unlucky. The Week in Summary One match, one defeat of the scorer's pencil three times over, and the bowling of Mr F Reeves accounting for all three dismissals — a feat of hostile accuracy the club is pleased to record, even as it laments the toll taken upon our own batting order. No pairs of ducks, nor any shared family misfortune, were recorded in this fixture, for which small mercy the eleven may be duly grateful. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Jack Fryer — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0 per cent 2. X Pike — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0 per cent 3. C S Smith — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.3 per cent 4. F S W Cornwallis — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.3 per cent 5. J F Coles — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.3 per cent The season yet has much cricket left in it, and the club trusts its members will continue to apply themselves to the art of not scoring with their customary diligence. Members are cordially invited to the next fixture, where fresh candidates for the timbers, and for these very pages, will no doubt present themselves.

In this he draws level with the veteran F Danells, who between 1881 and 1891 contrived exactly five such dismissals in a mere fifteen visits to the crease, and who rests one place above him upon the all-time list — a swifter road to the same distinguished total, though Mr Cornwallis has taken the longer, and we venture the more scenic, route to it. A Week in Summary One fixture, one wicket of note, one gentleman inducted into this week's proceedings. A quiet week for the art of not scoring, but the club's business is never without its single, solemn entry. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Week 4 · 8 Jul 1899 – 12 Jul 1899
We regret, dear readers, that this week's correspondence must open on a note of quiet disappointment rather than ceremony. Two fixtures were contested by our eleven in the period under review, and in neither did the timbers yield up a single cipher for the Club's honours board. Our batsmen, whether by skill, fortune, or a simple want of ambition in the matter of getting themselves out cheaply, contrived on each occasion to trouble the scorer at least once before their dismissal. The zero club, that most exclusive of fraternities, gained not a single new subscription this week, nor even a repeat visit from an old and valued member. One scarcely knows whether to congratulate the eleven on its unwonted competence or to lament, on the Duck Club's behalf, so barren a stretch. We incline towards the latter view. Consistency of a very particular kind is, after all, what this correspondence exists to celebrate, and a week without a single duck's egg leaves precious little for the diarist's pen. We trust our members will not make a habit of it. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard The season standings remain, for now, undisturbed by the week's events. At the head of the table, five gentlemen stand level, each having faced the willow but the once this season and each dismissed without score upon that solitary occasion — a full one hundred per centum apiece, a record of perfect, if unenviable, symmetry: - A G Oyler — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Ernest Cruttenden — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Rev Thomas Burra — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - W L Meade — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Whether this quintet will be joined, or indeed unseated, by fresher misfortune remains to be seen. History suggests the wait shall not be a long one. We commend our members to the field for the next fixture, in the confident expectation that the Duck Club's ledger shall not long remain so disappointingly quiet. There is, after all, no shortage of gentlemen willing, whether by design or otherwise, to walk back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer — and this correspondent awaits their return with his customary anticipation.

Three of our number were sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer this week, across two fixtures. The exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers. 1st XI Against Sutton Valence School on the 4th, at home, our innings yielded a most economical pair of dismissals from the same hand. Mr C S Smith, in at number nine, was bowled by H Goodban for a cipher — his very first appearance at the wicket in senior colours, and thus a debut of the most particular sort. The Gazette records him at once upon the Duck of the Year board for 1898, a swift elevation to dubious distinction. He stands 54th of 271 in the club's all-time reckoning. Curiously, on this very date in 1886, one Tom Peach Snr likewise returned for nought against The Mote CC — history, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. Following him at number ten came Mr C Marsh, caught H C Pearson off the same Mr Goodban, and likewise dismissed for a duck's egg on his first outing — Goodban may fairly claim a brace of debutants in one afternoon's work. Mr Marsh takes his place at 52nd of 271. He too finds himself in curious company with Tom Peach Snr's duck of the 4th of June 1886 against The Mote CC, the calendar repeating itself twelve years on almost to the hour. Two days later, away at Brenchley CC, Mr F Smith was bowled by R Larkin at number six for a duck — no stranger to this fate, it being his third career nought in seven innings, and his season's first. He rests handsomely at 17th of 271 on the all-time list, level on three career ducks with Mr A Kent of the class of 1893, himself no less than the Duck of the Year for that season. Kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. The week in brief Two matches, three ducks, and a curious symmetry — Sutton Valence School accounted for two of our men in successive deliveries from Mr Goodban, while Brenchley CC claimed the third at the far end of the week. All three fell to the bowler rather than to any misadventure of their own making, which is, we are assured, some small comfort. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - C Marsh — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - C S Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - F Smith — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent The season is yet young, and the timbers await further custom. Members are warmly invited to attend the next fixture, where fresh candidates for the honours board will no doubt present themselves with their customary enthusiasm.

1 duck

A modest bulletin this week, gentlemen, but the exclusive zero club never wants for correspondence, however slender the harvest. In this he draws level with an old and honourable predecessor, C French Snr, who compiled his own brace of naughts between 1860 and 1864 and was, in that latter year, crowned Duck of the Year — proof, if proof were wanted, that the art of not scoring has always run in good company at this club. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, and Mr Smith bears the whole burden of the week's ignominy alone — a solitary sentinel rather than a gathering of the fallen. Consistency, it must be said, of a very particular kind, and no less deserving of note for its modesty. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard Leading the field this season stands Mr George Champion, with two ducks from eight innings, a return of twenty-five per centum, achieved through what one might charitably call triumph through adversity. Close behind, level on a single duck apiece from a single innings — the full hundred per centum, no less — come Messrs A E Leatham, A Heathfield, R Giles and R Tree, each a paid-up member of the season's most emphatic company. We trust the eleven will contrive further material for these columns at the next fixture, and the Gazette stands ready, as ever, to record whatever fresh distinctions of failure the coming Saturday may furnish.

The Duck Report — 11th August 1897

0 ducks
Week 9 · 11 Aug 1897
A quiet week, and no shame whatever attaches to it. Our correspondent must report, with a certain wistfulness, that the ducks evaded capture entirely this week. The eleven took the field on the 11th of August and, whatever else transpired at the wicket, not a single cipher was recorded against our name. The exclusive zero club, so often swollen by Saturday's exertions, admitted no new members this week. Whether this reflects a sudden and uncharacteristic competence with the willow, or merely that the bowling was found wanting, the correspondent declines to speculate. Members of a certain standing on the honours board may rest, or fret, as their temperament inclines them — their records remain, for now, exactly as they were left. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's pursuit of the cipher continues unabated elsewhere, and the standings make sobering reading for the gentlemen concerned: - George Champion — 8 innings, 2 ducks, a rate of 25 per cent. A batsman evidently capable of considerable resistance, interspersed with the occasional lapse into total abstinence. - A E Leatham — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. A perfect record, in its way, and not the sort a man frames for the mantelpiece. - A Heathfield — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. Likewise a cipher at the first time of asking — the scorer had scarcely dipped his pen. - R Giles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. Joins the above gentlemen in that most select and least sought-after fraternity. - R Tree — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. A fourth name added to the same sorry column, and no less welcome to the Club for it. It should be said, in fairness to Messrs Leatham, Heathfield, Giles and Tree, that a single innings is a slender basis upon which to judge a man's cricket, and the season is yet young enough for redemption. The correspondent looks forward, with his customary and entirely unbecoming eagerness, to the next fixture, which may be relied upon to furnish fresh material for these pages. Members are reminded that the timbers care nothing for reputation, and the willow may yet humble even the most watchful of our batsmen before the season is out.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the days 2nd to 4th August, 1897

7 ducks
Week 8 · 2 Aug 1897 – 4 Aug 1897
A fixture against Rochester CC on the 2nd, and a further engagement at Headcorn on the 4th, have furnished the Club with no fewer than seven fresh additions to its roll of dubious distinction. The willow was, on several occasions this week, wielded to no visible purpose whatever. 1st XI Against Rochester, our innings yielded three ciphers in short order. Mr K McAlpine, sent in first wicket down, was smartly taken by H Newsome off X Fellowes for his first duck of the season and the first of his career in five completed innings — 81st of 261 in the club's long roll. On this very day in 1882, one W H Fryer likewise returned a duck's egg, against 1st Innings Boxley CC, a coincidence separated by fifteen years and no improvement in fortune. George Champion followed, bowled by J B Finlayson without scoring, his second duck of the present season and his fourth in a career of three-and-twenty innings — a tally that places him ninth of all who have ever failed to trouble the scorer for the Club, and sufficient, it seems, to have already secured him the Duck of the Year board for 1897. He, too, shares the anniversary with Mr Fryer's 1882 nought. The Reverend Thomas Burra, promoted to bat at nine, was caught by Finlayson off Fellowes for a duck — his second of a career now numbering eleven innings, and the 37th such performer of all time. The reverend gentleman keeps, it might be observed, distinguished company on this same calendar date. At Headcorn on the 4th, the rot continued in earnest. Tom Peach Senior, at number seven, was bowled by E Holland without scoring — his third career duck in seventeen innings, the 21st of all time, and, by pleasant coincidence, a duck struck on this same date in an earlier year of 1869 by one W H Fryer against Horsmonden CC. Mr A Heathfield, appearing for the very first time in club colours, was bowled by W Clinch for a nought on his maiden appearance — a debut duck of the purest and most immediate kind, and one that places him at the modest but respectable rank of 42nd of 261 all-time. R Tree, following at ten, was likewise bowled by Clinch without scoring, his first career duck in a brief innings of two, ranking 92nd of all time. And to close proceedings, R Giles, also making his first appearance for the Club, was bowled by Clinch for nought — a second debutante duck in the very same innings, ranking 88th of all time. Messrs Heathfield, Tree and Giles were all despatched by the same bowler's hand, a fact the correspondent notes without further comment, beyond observing that Mr Clinch appears to have found something in the wicket that our lower order did not. A Word on the Week Two matches, seven ducks — a rate of failure the Club's honours board will record with its customary solemnity rather than alarm. Three wickets fell without score inside a single Headcorn innings, all to the one bowler, which is either misfortune or a want of application, and the correspondent, ever charitable, inclines toward the former. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - George Champion — 7 innings, 2 ducks, 28.57 per cent - A E Leatham — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - A Heathfield — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - R Giles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - R Tree — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent The Club extends its compliments to all who have this week enlarged the roll, and looks forward, with the quiet confidence of long experience, to further additions at the next fixture. The willow, as ever, awaits its next volunteer.

The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 28th of July, 1897

1 duck
Week 7 · 28 Jul 1897
A modest bulletin this week, gentlemen, but the club's honours board is not one to turn away a single contribution, however slender the harvest. 1st XI — away to Brenchley CC Mr Ernest Cruttenden, coming in at number four, was bowled by W J Noakes and returned to the pavilion without addition to the total. It is his first cipher of the present season and the seventh of a distinguished career now standing at thirty-one innings, a return that places him third of two hundred and fifty-eight upon the club's all-time roll of honour — a position, one might observe, not easily dislodged. Readers will recall Mr Cruttenden's name already graces the board as Duck of the Year for 1895, so this latest addition may be taken as a gentleman keeping his hand in rather than any falling away of form. Of particular note, Mr Cruttenden's tally of seven now sits precisely level with that of the venerable A Startup, whose eleven innings between 1868 and 1882 yielded the same figure, and whose own name adorns the board no fewer than three times over as Duck of the Year, together with the rare distinction of five ducks in a row. To draw level with such a figure, even by the unhappy arithmetic of noughts, is scarcely a disgrace. The week in summary One fixture, one dismissal for a cipher, and the willow otherwise behaved itself tolerably well against Brenchley CC. A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, though its members will assure you that quality, not quantity, has always been the club's watchword. Four eggs were laid before the season's sun this week, our men contributing handsomely to that most exclusive of registers, the zero club, across three fixtures. 1st XI - On the 17th, against Mr H Wilson-Smith's eleven, Mr A E Leatham came in at first wicket down and was caught R E Marchant bowled S Mendel without troubling the scorer. His first blemish of the season, though the second upon a career of six innings, it lifts him to 28th of 258. A twelvemonth almost to the day separates him from H W Smith's duck of 1896 against the Royal West Kent Regiment CC, struck upon this same date. - Maidstone completed their afternoon's work by removing Mr George Champion, caught F E Wallis bowled A Boardman for nought at number four — his first duck of the season, his third in a career of twenty innings, and a lofty 17th of 258 upon the roll of dishonour. No pair of misfortunes befell any one gentleman twice, for which small mercy the eleven may be grateful. 🏏 A modest offering from Maidstone on Saturday, where the visitors' willow proved unequal to the task on four separate occasions. This stands as his second duck of the season and his second in a career of eight innings, placing him thirty-fourth of the two hundred and forty-nine names on our roll of dishonour. This is his third duck of the season, his third in a career of only four innings, and it earns him fifteenth place of all who have gone before, together with a place on the Duck of the Year 1896 board — an honour he appears determined to defend without challenge. He joins A Kent, whose identical tally of three was compiled in 1893. - R Kennard, last man in, was bowled outright by W C Betts. Between them they carried the Kennard name to the crease and back again with nothing to show for either journey — one imagines the walk to the pavilion was, at least, companionable. The week in summary — four ducks in a single match, two of them shared by brothers, and W C Betts alone accounting for three of the four dismissals. A bowler in inspired form, and an innings the eleven will be glad to leave behind them. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 15th August 1896

Hard upon his heels came Mr R Kennard at number ten, held by W French off the same F Gilbert, and similarly dismissed for nought. This being his maiden first-class innings, we are obliged to note it as his debut — an inauspicious one, though he joins the club in good and populous company. His name now stands at the eighty-third position of all-time ignominy, itself a curious echo of Mr Norton's own standing at eighty-fourth, and, as with his brother, this day in 1891 saw an identical fate befall the aforementioned Norton against the selfsame Ramblers. We should be remiss not to observe that Mr D H Kennard and Mr R Kennard are brothers, and their twin failures this day at Westborough constitute what the club records as Two of a Quack — a shared and simultaneous descent into scorelessness that we are pleased to solemnise. It is not every week that one family may boast two ducks laid in the same afternoon, and the Kennard household has this day secured that dubious distinction with room to spare. The Week in Summary A single fixture yielded two ducks, both from the same family, both from the same bowler's spell — Mr Gilbert may take some private satisfaction in a family double, though we shall not encourage him further. The Duck Club Gazette — Headcorn CC, 29th July 1896

5 ducks
Week 12 · 29 Jul 1896
A single fixture furnished the Club with five ducks apiece worthy of the honours board, Headcorn's bowlers proving uncommonly parsimonious throughout. 1st XI Ernest Cruttenden did Headcorn the signal courtesy of failing to trouble the scorer twice in the one afternoon. In the first innings he was taken by F Norris off the bowling of the Reverend A C Scott, his fifth career duck in five and twenty innings, and a sitting Duck of the Year for 1895. He shares that exact tally with F Danells, who retired upon it between 1881 and 1891. Sent in again in the second innings, Mr Cruttenden fell lbw to G Knight for his sixth, drawing level with W H Fryer of the 1867-85 vintage, and so completed what the Club terms simply a pair — twice dismissed without score in a single match, a feat demanding rather more application than it might appear. He remains third of all who have ever taken guard for this purpose, out of two hundred and forty-seven. S Smith, at number ten, was held by F E Foreman off G Knight for nought, his first duck in a modest six innings to date. He joins a long and honourable company sitting on the same single duck, among them A Barker, who managed the identical feat in 1885 and was that year's Duck of the Year. H L Andrews, appearing in the eleven for the first time, was bowled by the Reverend A C Scott without troubling the scorer — as warm a welcome to senior cricket as the Club knows how to extend. He too keeps company with A Barker's tally of one, though with his career scarcely begun he may yet better it, for good or ill. D H Kennard, at nine, was bowled by G Knight for a duck on his earliest outing for the Club, and finds himself already proclaimed Duck of the Year for 1896 — an honour arriving rather sooner in the season than he can have hoped for. He stands alongside Messrs Smith and Andrews on a single career duck, level with A Barker's mark of 1885. The afternoon's bowling honours belong chiefly to Headcorn: Mr G Knight accounted for three of the five ciphers and the Reverend A C Scott for the remaining two, a display of the willow's opposite number at its most eloquent. One match, five ducks, and the Reverend proving that the cloth is no bar to menace with the ball. A modest bulletin this week, for the exclusive zero club welcomed but two new members to its dubious ranks, both from the 1st XI, in the fixture against Mr H Wilson-Smith's eleven. 1st XI - G M Style, sent in at number eight, was caught by O Seymour off the bowling of J N Tonge, c O Seymour b J N Tonge, without troubling the scorer. This stands as his first duck of the season and the first of his career in three innings at the wicket, placing him 59th of 235 in the club's roll of honour, a position that finds him keeping company with A Barker, whose lone duck of 1885 secured that gentleman the Duck of the Year and a career tally of exactly one, precisely as Mr Style's now reads. - A L Woodhouse followed his colleague back to the pavilion at number nine, bowled by the same J N Tonge, whose afternoon's figures owe not a little to Linton Park's generosity. A first season duck and a first career duck in two innings at the wicket, Mr Woodhouse joins Mr Style, and indeed the aforementioned A Barker of 1885, in a career tally of exactly one, ranking 35th of 235 on the club's long and honourable list of failures. It is not every match that furnishes two gentlemen undone by the identical bowler in the identical innings, arriving by separate roads at the selfsame distinction. The Week in Summary Two matches were played in the period under review, and but a single innings of true abjection was recorded between them, J N Tonge accounting for both departures, a bowler evidently in determined form against the home eleven. No pairs, no king pairs and no gatherings of kin fell to be reported this week, the ducks confining themselves to solitary appearances, as decorum would demand. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - G M Style, 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - X Gilbert, 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - A L Woodhouse, 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent The season is yet young, and the leaderboard retains ample room for further distinction. Members are cordially reminded that the next fixture stands ready to receive fresh nominations to the zero club, and the correspondent awaits further intelligence with his customary keen anticipation. --- One housekeeping note, unrelated to the above: another machine on the team, turbosammy-Defiance-Pro-16, is well behind on shared updates and flagging a couple of unresolved items — worth a nudge to whoever runs it, next time it's convenient.

The Duck Club Gazette — the Match of the 13th of May, 1896

1 duck
Week 1 · 13 May 1896
A single fixture upon the ground this week, and but one gentleman required to make the short walk back to the pavilion without contributing to the total. A quiet week for the Eleven's registrar of noughts, but a duck is a duck, and the club's business must be recorded all the same. 1st XI - X Gilbert, coming to the wicket at number seven against the Royal West Kent Regiment CC upon our own ground, was bowled by Captain G Marshall, and returned to the pavilion having faced his allotted deliveries without once troubling the scorer. This being his first appearance in the Eleven's colours, it is his maiden innings and his maiden cipher together — a debut conducted, one might say, with rather too much modesty. He enters the club's roll of honour as the 94th name of 230, and in this he keeps distinguished if distant company: Mr A Barker, whose own single duck of the 1885 season earned him that year's Duck of the Year and the 34th place of 230, sits upon exactly the same career total, the two gentlemen united across eleven years by the same solitary nought. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, and precious little else to remark upon. Whether this reflects a want of opportunity or an uncommon steadiness at the wicket among the rest of the Eleven, the correspondent cannot say — only that the ducks, this week, proved elusive quarry, bar the one. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - X Gilbert — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent A modest table this week, Mr Gilbert occupying it entirely by default, though doubtless others will press their claims before the season is out. The next fixture cannot be long delayed, and with it, one trusts, further additions to this list of gentlemen who found the willow uncooperative. Members are encouraged to attend, and to bat rather better than the present correspondent has any right to expect.

1895 Season 3 reports

LPCC Duck Club Gazette — the 10th day of August, 1895

3 ducks
Week 3 · 10 Aug 1895
A single fixture at Maidstone brought the eleven three additions to the club's roll of the dismissed, the exclusive zero club welcoming two new subscribers to go with one old and familiar face. The 1st Eleven J Lampard, at number five, was bowled by H Waghorn after giving the bowling due consideration, only for the timbers to be disturbed all the same. It is his season's first cipher and his first in a senior career now numbering four innings, placing him sixty-sixth of two hundred and twenty-five in the club's honours roll of the dismissed — respectable company, if not company one seeks out. Curiously, on this very day in 1891, L M Richards performed the identical office against the Royal Engineers, proving that the tenth of August has long held a certain fondness for our batting order. D A Kenward, promoted to number six, met a fate the scorer himself could not quite settle — run out, the particulars unresolved — on the occasion of his very first innings for the club. A debut duck is a bold beginning, and Mr Kenward may console himself that he has, at a stroke, secured his place forty-fourth of two hundred and twenty-five on the all-time list without troubling the bowlers in the slightest. He, too, finds himself in step with Mr Richards's exploit of 1891. F Smith, following at number seven, likewise fell to H Waghorn — the same bowler claiming his second victim of the innings — on his own first appearance for the club. Two debutants, two ciphers, one bowler enjoying rather more success than either newcomer would have wished. Mr Smith rests fifty-third of two hundred and twenty-five, and shares, as did his colleagues, the distinction of the tenth of August's historical partiality to nought. The week in summary One match, three ducks, the whole of the misfortune falling upon the 1st Eleven at Maidstone. Of note, two of the three dismissed were making their maiden appearance in club colours, and H Waghorn's bowling accounted for fully two of the three — a fine afternoon's work for Maidstone, and rather a chastening one for the eleven. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Ernest Cruttenden — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent - D A Kenward — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - F Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - H G Smith — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent - J Edmonds — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent The club awaits its next fixture with the usual mixture of hope and resignation, confident that the willow will again prove uncooperative for at least one of our number, and that fresh names will shortly present themselves for consideration upon this ever-lengthening roll.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — a record of ciphers, for the week ending the 5th of August, 1895

2 ducks
Week 2 · 5 Aug 1895
Rochester CC paid our eleven a visit on the 5th, and departed having claimed but two additions to the club's dubious roll of honour. A modest week's harvest, but the honours board is not filled by modesty alone. 1st XI - Ernest Cruttenden (No. 7) was sent back to the pavilion by H M Bathurst, without so much as a run to his name, for the second time this season — his fourth career cipher in nineteen innings, placing him 7th of 220 in the club's melancholy all-time table. He holds the honour of Duck of the Year for 1895, a distinction he is doing his level best to justify. In the matter of career ciphers he now stands level with the estimable C Amies, whose own four noughts were compiled between 1867 and 1870 — a fine piece of company to keep across a gulf of some five-and-twenty years. - Following him to the wicket, and following him back again in short order, was J Edmonds (No. 10), likewise accounting for Bathurst's figures with a duck's egg of his own. It is his maiden season cipher and his first career duck in a brief innings of two, which lands him at 62nd of 220 on the all-time list — a start, one might say, rather than a finish. He now sits level on career ducks with a positively venerable company, headed by A Barker, whose solitary duck of 1885 earned him that season's own Duck of the Year. Mr Bathurst, it should be recorded, accounted for both dismissals — a bowler evidently possessed of a keen eye for the timbers, and one our batting order would do well to treat with greater caution hereafter. The Week in Summary A single fixture, a single wicket-taker among the visitors doing double duty, and two ciphers to show for it — a quiet week by the club's usual generous standards, but every entry on the honours board began somewhere, and both these gentlemen have made their mark upon 1895 regardless. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Ernest Cruttenden — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% 2. H G Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% 3. J Edmonds — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% The season's early running shows a most determined pursuit of the cipher at the top of the table. Members are respectfully reminded that the willow shows no favouritism, and the next fixture promises fresh candidates for the honours board, as it invariably does.

2 ducks

🦆 A modest fixture against Headcorn CC yields but a brace of ducks for the eleven — the timbers were troubled, if not the scorebook. 1st XI v Headcorn CC (home) - Ernest Cruttenden, going in first wicket down, was undone by G Knight and returned to the pavilion with nought to his name. He joins, on this identical tally of three, such esteemed company as A Kent, A Tapsfield, G Sedgwick, J Mallard and T Tomson, a fraternity of the thrice-dismissed-for-nothing. This being his maiden appearance for the eleven, the duck is his very first — an arrival, one might say, announced rather than celebrated, and it places him fifty-seventh of the two hundred and twenty. He has thereby joined, at a stroke, a lengthy roll of members sitting on exactly one career duck, prominent among them A Barker, Arthur Cornwallis and Captain Bowles. Neither gentleman troubled the bowler for more than the compulsory ball or two, and neither achieved the rare distinction of the king pair, for which the club may be quietly grateful, or quietly disappointed, according to taste. The eleven's next fixture awaits, and with it, no doubt, fresh candidates for the honours board — the exclusive zero club welcomes all comers, however reluctantly.

1893 Season 2 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the day's play of 28th August, 1893, versus The Mote CC

3 ducks
Week 3 · 28 Aug 1893
A modest but by no means unworthy showing for the club's exclusive society this week, our men contributing three additions to the roll of dubious distinction in the single fixture played. 1st XI Mr W W Tarrance, promoted to the number four position, was undone caught by F G Stenning off the bowling of A J Thornton — a debut innings, and thus his maiden entry upon the ledger, first of the season and first of a career now standing at one, placing him 85th of 214 in the club's long and melancholy roll. He joins good company on that particular figure: A Barker of the 1885 season, whose solitary duck earned him the Duck of the Year honour that summer, sits level with him at one apiece. At number ten, Mr C A Whittaker fell leg-before to the same indefatigable Mr Thornton, without troubling the scorer. This too was his first appearance upon the club's honours board, his maiden duck in only his second innings for the eleven — an inauspicious beginning, though he keeps distinguished company at one career duck, level again with Mr A Barker of 1885. Mr H Waghorn, at first wicket down, was caught and bowled by the same Mr Thornton, whose afternoon's work read like a benefit performance for the Duck Club. This was no debut mishap but the second nought of an established career now numbering five innings, placing him 26th of the all-time list. He draws level on two career ducks with Mr C French Senior, whose own pair between 1860 and 1864 earned him the Duck of the Year in the latter season. One is bound to observe that Mr A J Thornton, of The Mote CC, appears to have enjoyed a thoroughly satisfactory afternoon at our expense, accounting for all three dismissals himself — a hat-trick of sorts, though not one this correspondent is obliged to celebrate. The Week in Summary Three ducks in the single match played, all falling to one visiting bowler, and all from the 1st XI. No pairs, no golden ducks, and no family ceremonies to report this week — merely three gentlemen returning to the pavilion in steady, unspectacular succession. A quiet week for the club by its own exacting standards, though the timbers and the scorebook alike bore witness to the visitors' evident command of the conditions. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 14th to 18th August, 1893

10 ducks
Week 1 · 14 Aug 1893 – 18 Aug 1893
A full week of misfortune with the willow: three fixtures played, and no fewer than ten ciphers entered upon the club's rolls. The exclusive zero club welcomes its usual mixture of new arrivals and seasoned campaigners. 1st XI Against the Royal Engineers CC on the 14th, the innings unravelled handsomely for our men. A Kent, introducing himself to first-team cricket, was twice sent back to the pavilion without score — bowled by Captain Hamilton, then caught and bowled by A J Woodroffe — a pair on his very arrival that few gentlemen would wish upon themselves. H Waghorn followed at number seven, bowled by A J Woodroffe on his own first outing, and takes his place beside the estimable A Barker of 1885 on a solitary career blemish, 57th of 206 on the club's all-time roll. Further down, Jack Fryer, stumped off Corporal Bayfield in a manner suggesting the willow was scarcely required, recorded the seventh cipher of a career now level with the redoubtable A Startup of the 1870s and 80s — Fryer remains top of the all-time table, 1st of 206, and a past holder of the Duck of the Year honour in 1891. F S W Cornwallis, last man in, fell to Corporal Bayfield for his fourth career duck, keeping distinguished company with C Amies of the 1860s, and stands 7th of 206. Two days later, against the Free Foresters CC, George Champion contrived to be dismissed twice for nought in the one encounter — bowled, then caught by G W Ricketts, both off the bowling of W E W Collins — a grim pair to open his season's account, drawing him level with C French Senior of the 1860s on two career ciphers, 24th of 206. Major Rawson, at number eight, also fell to Collins without troubling the scorer, his maiden duck for the eleven, and joins A Barker's modest company on one, 67th of 206. The Eton Ramblers CC, on the 18th, completed the week's misery. Jack Fryer was bowled by C Heseltine for his second duck of the period and eighth of an ever-lengthening career. A Kent, closing out a week entirely his own, was likewise bowled by Heseltine for a third duck in five short days, drawing level with A Tapsfield of the early 1880s — Kent now stands 12th of 206, and already occupies a place upon this year's Duck of the Year board for 1893. In summary Ten ducks across three matches is a rate of failure the eleven will not care to repeat, though the honours boards are rather better furnished for it. A Kent's three ciphers make him the week's undisputed champion of adversity, with George Champion's pair in a single match running him a close second. The Zero Club Gazette — Tuesday, 8th to Friday, 12th August, 1892

3 ducks
Week 1 · 8 Aug 1892 – 12 Aug 1892
Three visits to the pavilion without troubling the scorer are recorded this week, the whole sorry business confined, as it happens, to the First Eleven. The exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers below. The First Eleven Mr Jack Fryer opened proceedings on the 8th, at home to the Royal Engineers CC, going the way of all willow-wielders at the hands of Mr F G Guggisberg, bowled without addition to the total from the number six position. This is his season's first cipher and his sixth in a career of nineteen innings, a record of consistency that secures him second place of 197 in the club's roll of honour, and he may reflect, with whatever comfort the fact affords, that he was named Duck of the Year for 1891. He finds himself level, on exactly six career ducks, with a Mr W H Fryer, who plied his trade for the club between 1867 and 1885 — a namesake, so far as the records show, rather than a relation, though the coincidence of surname is a pleasing one for the historian. The Eton Ramblers CC proved a most obliging visitor on the 12th, claiming two of our men in the same fixture. Captain Bowles, sent in first, was bowled by Mr C Heseltine without scoring — a maiden innings and a maiden duck together, the gentleman's very first appearance for the club yielding nothing but a cipher, and thereby securing him the Duck of the Year honour for the present season of 1892 at the first attempt. It is recorded that on this very day in 1867, a Mr G a K Simpson likewise returned to the pavilion for nought, against the 1st Innings of Leeds Park CC — history, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. Batting at seven in the same innings, Mr S Christopherson was bowled by Mr G J Foljambe for nought, his first duck of the season and the first of his career, in a modest eight innings to date, placing him 67th of 197 in the club's long ledger of the dismissed. He shares his parallel with the same Mr Simpson of 1867, who made his own duck on this date against Leeds Park CC — a distinguished, if unwitting, anniversary companion. The Week in Summary Three matches, three ducks, and two of our batsmen despatched in a single afternoon by the Eton Ramblers — a fixture that shall not soon be forgotten by those concerned. No pairs, no families of ducks, and no king's ransom of ignominy this week, merely the steady, dependable arithmetic of nought. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Captain Bowles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - Jack Fryer — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent - S Christopherson — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33 per cent The season is young and the willow treacherous. 🏏 A quiet week at the crease, gentlemen and ladies of the Club. No ducks reported this week It grieves the correspondent to record that the eleven, for once, gave the scorers no cipher to note down. 3 ducks

A Chronicle of the Willow's Misfortunes, 10th to 12th August, 1891 To the members of the Club is offered this week's modest harvest — three eggs laid across two fixtures, the eleven having found the art of not scoring practised with its customary devotion. 4 ducks

A modest fixture against Hunton CC on Saturday last has furnished the club's zero register with a fresh quartet of entries, our first eleven contributing the whole of the day's misfortune between them. 1st XI at Hunton CC (away) - F Danells, in at first wicket down, was stumped by the watchful Dr Smart off the bowling of J Foord, and returns to the pavilion for his first duck's egg of the season — his fifth in a career of fifteen innings, placing him third of the club's one hundred and seventy-six honorands. He now sits level upon five with W Goad, whose own accumulation was gathered between 1864 and 1872 — kindred spirits in the art of not scoring, separated by some twenty-seven years but united upon the same solemn total. - Jack Fryer, at first drop, fell caught by H Hubble off the same J Foord — evidently a bowler in fine and unwelcome form — for his first duck of the current season and the fourth of an already distinguished career spanning sixteen innings. He is, be it noted, the reigning holder of the Duck of the Year honour for 1891 itself, a title he may consider well and truly defended by this latest contribution. He draws level upon four with several distinguished names of seasons past, among them J Sedgwick of 1881 and W White of 1869, each themselves former Ducks of the Year. - S Ruck, promoted to the crease at number seven, was bowled by T Hards without troubling the scorer, and does so upon the very occasion of his debut for the club — a duck's egg to mark his arrival, which places him sixty-fourth of one hundred and seventy-six on the all-time roll. He shares his solitary tally with a great many who began thus, among them A Barker of 1885. - H Graves, at number nine, was likewise bowled, by W Galpin, for a duck upon his own first appearance in club colours — a debut shared in ignominy with his colleague Ruck, the pair entering the honours board together. He too stands upon one, in fellowship with A Barker and the long roll of those whose careers began at nought. The Week in Summary Four wickets fell for nought in the single fixture played, the whole harvest gathered by Hunton's bowlers Foord, Hards and Galpin between them — Foord accounting for two of the four, a performance the visiting batting card will not remember fondly. Two debutants and two established campaigners shared the day's disappointments in equal measure, a fair distribution of misfortune by any reckoning. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - F Danells — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - H Graves — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Jack Fryer — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - S Ruck — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% An early season, and the table stands level at its summit — a fine field of candidates for the year's honours, with much cricket yet to be played before the matter is settled. The eleven return to the field presently, and the register of the exclusive zero club remains, as ever, open for further subscription. Members are cordially invited to attend and observe whether fortune favours the willow any better next time out.

1889 Season 1 report

The Duck Report — 21st August 1889

0 ducks
Week 1 · 21 Aug 1889
A quiet week at the wicket, gentle readers. Only one fixture graced the fine August calendar of 1889, and, remarkably, not a single one of our men troubled the exclusive zero club with a fresh entrant. Every batsman who took guard contrived, by hook, crook or simple watchfulness, to trouble the scorer at least once. The eleven, on this occasion, declined to add to the ledger. The Duck Club's committee records this with a measure of relief tempered by mild disappointment — for it is, after all, in the art of not scoring that our members find their truest glory, and a week without a nought is a week the honours board must go without fresh laurels. We are assured the ducks have merely gone to ground, and not retired from the field altogether. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season standings are, alas, not to hand this week — no returns have been lodged. The committee trusts the usual suspects remain in good and scoreless health, and will publish the table the moment the figures are recovered from the pavilion ledger. A quiet week, then, but the season is young yet, and Linton Park's willows have shown before that a duck's egg is never more than one indiscreet stroke away. Members are cordially reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for redemption, or its opposite, and the committee awaits the results with its customary keen and slightly mischievous interest. Until then, we remain, as ever, watchful for the cipher.

The Linton Park Gazette — Tuesday, the 22nd of June, 1887

0 ducks
Week 2 · 22 Jun 1887
It is the melancholy duty of this correspondent to report that the ducks, so reliably plentiful in recent gazettes, evaded the net entirely this week. One fixture was played, and in it not a single member of our eleven had the misfortune, nor indeed the peculiar honour, of being sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer. The exclusive zero club, it seems, held no admissions this week — a state of affairs we note with as much surprise as satisfaction, for a quiet week for the Duck Club is, by its own curious logic, rather a disappointment to the chronicler. Whether this reflects a sudden and uncharacteristic soundness of technique among our batsmen, or merely the bowling of the opposition being insufficiently wicked, this correspondent cannot say. We shall content ourselves that the art of not scoring has, for one week only, gone unpractised at Linton Park. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's standings remain, naturally, undisturbed by a week in which no fresh candidates presented themselves. The roll currently reads thus: - Jack Fryer — 1 innings, 1 duck, a striking 100 per cent — a gentleman who has, thus far in 1887, contrived to be dismissed for a cipher on every single occasion the willow has been placed in his hands. Whether this represents misfortune, consistency, or a design too subtle for lesser minds to fathom, the committee declines to speculate, and merely records the figures as they stand. With but one name upon the list, Mr Fryer holds his position not merely at its head but as its entirety — a solitary sentinel atop a table he has, for want of competitors, no present need to defend. We trust the ducks are merely regrouping, and shall return in greater number at the next fixture, for a Duck Club without its ducks is a curious institution indeed. Members are cordially invited to attend, and — should fortune, or the lack of it, so favour them — to add their names to the roll in the customary fashion. The pavilion door, as ever, stands open in both directions.

The Duck Report — 15th June 1887

1 duck
Week 1 · 15 Jun 1887
A modest bulletin this week, the eleven having contrived but a single dismissal for a cipher in the one fixture played. Still, where there is a duck to be recorded, the Club shall record it with the ceremony it deserves. 1st XI Number eleven Jack Fryer, sent in last as is customary for the lower order, was caught by F W Franks off the bowling of W F Best without so much as troubling the scorer. This marks his third career duck in fourteen innings, placing him thirteenth of the one hundred and fifty-five names on the Club's roll of honour — a respectable, if unenviable, standing among such distinguished company. He faced at least one delivery before his downfall, so no golden egg is to be entered against his name this time, merely a duck of the ordinary, workmanlike variety. By happy coincidence of the calendar, it was on this very day in 1881 that no fewer than eight of the Club's forebears — F Danells, C Fryer, W Wilson, J Mallard, W H Fryer, W White, and W Eggar among them — each made a duck of their own against Collier Street CC. Mr Fryer may take some comfort in such distinguished fellowship across the years, though whether comfort is quite the sentiment a duck deserves remains a matter for debate. It might also be noted, purely as a point of interest, that Messrs Tapsfield, Sedgwick and Tomson of years past each retired from the game with precisely three career ducks to their name, exactly as Mr Fryer now stands — kindred spirits in the art of not scoring, separated by decades but united in tally. In Summary One match, one duck, one gentleman keeping rather select company with the ghosts of 1881. Not a vintage week for the connoisseur of failure, but the Club's records are nothing if not patient, and further additions are anticipated in due course. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Jack Fryer — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% The Club extends its compliments to Mr Fryer on his contribution to the season's tally, and looks forward, as ever, to the next fixture furnishing further candidates for these pages. The willow awaits its next victim.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 3rd and 4th June, 1886

7 ducks
Week 1 · 3 Jun 1886 – 4 Jun 1886
A brisk fixture against The Mote CC on the 4th has furnished the exclusive zero club with no fewer than seven fresh entries, our men finding the art of not scoring rather more congenial than the art of scoring. Let the ledger speak. House Team Batting at seven, Tom Peach Snr was run out without addition, his end unsure but his cipher perfectly certain — a 1st season duck, and his 2nd of a modest career spanning five innings, placing him 27th of 145 in the club's grim roll of honour. He now sits level with C French Snr, that veteran of 1860 to 1864 and Duck of the Year 1864, on an identical career tally of two. F S W Cornwallis, at nine, was first bowled by A J Thornton for nought, and — the innings evidently agreeing with him — returned later in the day to be caught by K McAlpine off the same bowler, again without troubling the scorer. A pair, gentlemen, the grim double so beloved of this establishment, taking him from his 1st to his 2nd season duck in a single afternoon, and to 2 career ducks in four innings, 20th of 145. He joins the estimable C French Snr on that same tally of two. J F Cornish, opening his career at number ten, was leg before to A Hearne for a cipher on his very first appearance at the wicket — a true debutante duck to mark his arrival. Not content with one, he returned to be bowled by A J Thornton for a second, completing his own pair and, being brand new to these pages, arriving already a Duck of the Year 1886 nominee with 2 career ducks from just 2 innings, 24th of 145 — level company indeed with C French Snr on two. A M Streatfield, at four, was run out for a duck, his end likewise unsure. His 1st season duck stands as his 1st career duck from four innings, 30th of 145, drawing level with A Barker, Duck of the Year 1885, on a tally of one. The Hon J B Brownlow, at six and also new to the fixture list, was caught by A Hearne off F M Atkins without scoring — his maiden innings and, fittingly, his maiden duck. His 1st season and 1st career duck from two innings places him 45th of 145, keeping A Barker company on a tally of one apiece. The Week in Brief Seven ducks from two matches, every one of them furnished by the House Team against The Mote CC, and two gentlemen — Cornwallis and Cornish — managing the singular feat of a pair apiece in the same fixture, proof that lightning may strike twice in an afternoon, though never, mercifully, first ball. A fixture to be filed under triumph through adversity, if adversity may be said to triumph twice. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - F S W Cornwallis — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - J F Cornish — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - A M Streatfield — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Hon J B Brownlow — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Tom Peach Snr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season stands young and the willow has spoken plainly this week. 1885 Season 2 reports

The Duck Club Gazette

3 ducks
Week 8 · 12 Aug 1885
A Chronicle of Ciphers — the 12th of August, 1885 Intelligence reaches us of a single fixture played against Hunton CC, in which our First Eleven's willow-wielders contributed no fewer than three additions to the exclusive zero club. A day, in short, in which the art of not scoring was practised with some diligence. 1st XI, away to Hunton CC Mr A Barker opened proceedings at the wicket, only to be run out — the identity of the fielder responsible left, we are told, unrecorded, which is perhaps the kindest mercy the innings afforded him. It marks his very first appearance in senior colours, and what an overture: a maiden innings closed at nought, his name entered at 26th of 137 in the club's roll of dubious distinction. The season bearing his own birth year, 1885, his effort stands credited toward this year's Duck of the Year honours, a race very much open. We note, with the solemnity such coincidences demand, that on this very day in 1867 Mr G a K Simpson likewise departed for a duck's egg, against Leeds Park CC. At number eight, Mr X Latter fared no better, caught by W Crump off the bowling of W Hodges without troubling the scorer. Like Mr Barker, this was his debut innings — a baptism of ciphers, if ever one was witnessed — and he takes his place at 65th of 137 on the all-time list. He too shares his misfortune with the calendar, Mr Simpson's duck of the 12th of August 1867 standing as company for him also. Then, at number nine, came Mr F Danells, no stranger to these proceedings, caught by W Best off the bowling of W Crump. This being his fourth career duck in but fourteen innings, he climbs to a lofty fifth of 137 on the club's all-time register — a veteran, one might fairly say, of the noble failure. His name too falls under the shadow of that same August afternoon in 1867 when Mr Simpson made his own contribution to the calendar of ciphers. The Week in Summary Three ducks from a single fixture is no mean haul, and that two belong to gentlemen quite new to the fold suggests Hunton CC's bowling gave our newer men rather more to consider than they might have wished. Mr Danells, for his part, continues to demonstrate a consistency of a very particular kind. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - A Barker — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F Danells — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - X Latter — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F J Barmby — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - F J Richardson — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% We commend all five gentlemen to the club's continued attention, and await, with our customary mixture of dread and delight, whatever further ciphers the next fixture may add to the register.

A Chronicle of Ciphers — Linton Park Cricket Club, week ending the 26th of June, 1885

5 ducks
Week 1 · 26 Jun 1885
Our fixture against The Mote CC on the 26th proved a fertile afternoon for the ledger of nought, five of our men returning to the pavilion without ever troubling the scorer. The House Eleven F J Barmby, in at four, fell to a catch by G Marsham off the bowling of A Hearne, his maiden entry in the club's books of failure. By curious chance the almanack records that this very date in 1872 also claimed E Skinner for a cipher in the first innings against Sutton Valence CC. Tom Peach Snr, following at five, was run out, the fielder responsible going unrecorded by our scorer, a fate perhaps crueller than dismissal by skill, for it leaves no bowling figures to console him. The date, as before, carries its history, E Skinner having met an identical fate in 1872. N T Nickolls, at seven, was bowled by L E Bligh, his stumps rearranged in a manner permitting no appeal. The 26th of June continues its long acquaintance with the duck's egg, E Skinner having set the precedent some thirteen years before. F J Richardson, at nine, was taken by G Marsham off L E Bligh, Marsham's second catch of the innings and a tidy one by all accounts. Once more the calendar obliges with company from 1872, when E Skinner suffered likewise. O M Leigh, last man in, was caught by the Hon V Parnell off A Hearne, completing the quintet of ciphers for the innings. That this same date in 1872 should furnish a fifth precedent, in the person of E Skinner once again, is a coincidence the club's historians will doubtless wish to note down. In summary A single fixture yielded five ducks, a testament to the home bowling of A Hearne and L E Bligh, who claimed two apiece, and to G Marsham's safe hands, taken twice. All five gentlemen record their first duck of a young season, and indeed the first entered against their names in the club's proper books, each having but one prior innings behind him. The Season's Ledger of Ciphers At this early hour of the season all five ciphered gentlemen stand level at the head of affairs, each with one duck from two innings, a rate of fifty per centum apiece: F J Barmby, F J Richardson, N T Nickolls, O M Leigh and Tom Peach Snr. The next fixture awaits, and with it, no doubt, fresh candidates for this most select and unenviable of confraternities. Members are cordially invited to attend, willow in hand, and try their fortune against the leather.

1883 Season 1 report

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 18th July, 1883

5 ducks
Week 1 · 18 Jul 1883
A single fixture graced our books this week, the eleven at home to the Maidstone Junior Liberal Association, and the exclusive zero club welcomed five new entries into its ledger of dubious distinction. Two completed innings were played in the day, and one of our number contrived to visit the pavilion twice before tea. 1st XI - W Wilson, sent in first to face the bowling, was undone lbw to A E Hickmott without troubling the scorer. His fourth duck in eighteen innings of a career, which places him eighth of all our 120 honoured members. He draws level, curiously enough, with C Amies, who compiled his own four ciphers between 1867 and 1870 in a mere nine innings, and now finds a companion in adversity across the years. - B Small, appearing for the club for the first time, was caught by F Wallis off Hickmott for a maiden duck, a debut of the quieter sort. He enters at 27th of 120, and stands upon the very same mark as A R Simpson of 1881 to 1882, a fellowship of one apiece. - J Danells achieved the rarer distinction of a pair upon his very first appearance for the club, batting at number ten in both innings. First he was taken by R T Nicholson off F Wallis, then, evidently unconvinced by the merits of a second attempt, bowled outright by A E Hickmott. Two ducks in an afternoon and two in a fledgling career, a beginning of the most emphatic kind, and one that earns him a place already among the season's foremost, being a name entered upon the Duck of the Year board for 1883. He now shares his tally with C French Snr, whose own pair of ciphers were gathered between 1860 and 1864, a member of the 1864 Duck of the Year board himself. - F Simmons, last man in, was bowled by F Knight for a debut duck of his own, entering the roll at 33rd of 120, and keeping A R Simpson company at one apiece alongside Master Small. A tidy afternoon's work for the opposing bowlers, then, five ciphers from one match, all confined to the 1st XI, and the singular curiosity of a young debutant contriving to fail twice before luncheon was properly digested. The art of not scoring, it seems, was practised with uncommon thoroughness this week. The Season's Duck-Hunting Ledger - J Danells — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - B Small — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - F Simmons — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - W Wilson — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The committee trusts the eleven will contrive fresh entries at the earliest opportunity, and looks forward to greeting the next fixture's arrivals into this most select and inglorious of fellowships.

1882 Season 5 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Tuesday, 2nd August, 1882

5 ducks
Week 11 · 2 Aug 1882
A day at the wicket against Boxley CC that will be remembered less for runs scored than for runs conspicuously absent. Five of our men returned to the pavilion without troubling the scorer, and the Club's exclusive zero club welcomes its latest — and, in one case, repeat — subscribers. 1st XI W H Fryer, going in at first wicket down, was undone by C Chambers for a cipher — his second duck of the season and the sixth of a distinguished career now spanning four-and-twenty innings, second only on the all-time roll of dishonour. He arrives level with A Startup on six career ducks apiece, a meeting of kindred spirits neither gentleman is likely to toast. Speaking of Mr Startup, his afternoon deserves a paragraph of its own. Bowled by F Atkins for his first duck of the day — the season's first, the career's sixth — he had barely regained the pavilion steps before being sent out again and bowled once more, by F B Hallatt this time, for his second of the match and seventh of his career. A pair, gentlemen, and a chastening one, though we are assured the willow itself bears no blame. Mr Startup may console himself with the season already named in his honour not once but thrice — 1868, 1870 and now 1882 — and a run of five ducks in a row that stands as a monument to consistency of a very particular kind. A R Simpson fell to F B Hallatt for his maiden career duck, a modest debut in the art of not scoring that places him twenty-fifth on the club's roll — good company, for he joins a positively crowded field of gentlemen similarly becalmed on a single nought apiece. J Gurney completed the afternoon's misery, caught by A G Mannering off H Foster's bowling for his first career duck in eight innings, drawing level with Mr Simpson on that same solitary figure — two men, one shared distinction, acquired within minutes of each other. In Summary One match, five ducks, and Mr Startup's pair the undoubted feature of the day — a gentleman who went out to bat twice and returned twice without so much as troubling the umpire's patience. Boxley CC's bowlers, it must be said, appear to have found something in the conditions that suited them handsomely.
